name: Pharmacology
description: Complete study manual · 18 practical class topics

topics.title: The importance of prescription writing in training general practitioners. The prescription and its structure. Solid and soft dosage forms and the rules for prescribing them

goals.text: A general practitioner (GP) writes dozens of prescriptions every day. A single error in a prescription (a misplaced decimal point, a tenfold dose overshoot, a mix-up of dosage forms) can endanger the patient's life. That is why prescription writing is the most practical branch of pharmacology.
The student should know:

items: the concepts of prescription writing, drug substance, medicinal product, drug preparation and dosage form;
the essence of the State Pharmacopoeia, lists A and B, and officinal and magistral drugs;
the types of doses and the rules for writing doses in a prescription;
the parts of a prescription and the procedure for filling in a prescription form;
the abbreviations used in writing prescriptions in Latin and the genitive case;
the classification, advantages and disadvantages of solid and soft dosage forms.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for powders, tablets, dragées, capsules, granules, ointments, pastes, creams, gels, liniments, suppositories and plasters;
calculate the amount of a substance from a percentage concentration;
find and correct errors in a written prescription.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Drug substance → medicinal product → drug preparation. The same drug substance may be produced in different dosage forms: for example, diclofenac is available as tablets, a solution for injection, a gel, suppositories and eye drops.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Common INN stems help to recognize the drug group: **-olol** — beta-blockers (metoprolol), **-pril** — ACE inhibitors (enalapril), **-sartan** — angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan), **-statin** — statins (atorvastatin), **-prazole** — proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole), **-floxacin** — fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), **-mab** — monoclonal antibodies (rituximab).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: There must be at least one digit after the decimal point in a prescription: **1.0** (not “1”), **0.5** (not “.5”). Shifting the decimal point by one place changes the dose 10-fold! Drugs dosed in units of action (U): some antibiotics (benzylpenicillin, nystatin), heparin, insulin, and certain hormones and enzymes.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The formulas above are for rough estimates only. In modern pediatrics, doses for each drug are set in **mg/kg** or **mg/m^2^** (body surface area), based on the package insert and pediatric reference books. For most drugs, calculating a child's dose from age alone can be dangerous.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: A prescription is read “from top to bottom”: **Stamp → Date → Patient → Physician → Rp. → Drug → Instructions → Signatura → Physician's signature**. Initial letters of the Latin names: **I-D-N-N-I-D-S-S-S**. Only **parts 5, 6 and 7** (Rp., drug names, instructions to the pharmacist) are written in Latin; the rest is in the state language.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Vague expressions such as “internally” or “as directed” must not be written in the **signatura**. The amount, the number of times a day, the timing in relation to meals and the duration must be stated clearly: “Take 1 tablet 3 times a day after meals for 5 days”.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Electronic prescription.** In Uzbekistan, the “Electronic prescription” system was launched in December 2025 in Tashkent and a number of pilot districts and is planned to be rolled out nationwide by the end of 2026. The physician confirms the prescription electronically, a QR code is assigned automatically and the prescription is sent to the pharmacy automatically; it was first made mandatory for antibiotics and hormonal preparations. A separate procedure remains for narcotic and potent drugs. Because these rules keep changing, the current orders of the Ministry of Health should be checked. The skill of composing the Latin part of a prescription correctly remains the foundation in the electronic system as well.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Anions of salts belong to the 3rd declension: **-as → -atis** (Natrii sulfas → Natrii sulfatis), **-is → -itis** (Natrii nitris → Natrii nitritis), **-idum → -idi** (Natrii chloridum → Natrii chloridi, 2nd declension). The cation (metal) is always in the genitive: Natrii, Kalii, Calcii, Magnii, Zinci.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Formula for calculating the amount of a substance from a percentage concentration: **amount of substance (g) = total mass × percentage / 100**. This formula is the same for ointments, pastes, liniments and solutions.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Different manuals use different spellings for cream and gel, such as “Crem”, “Cremoris”, “Gel”, “Geli”. According to Latin grammar, Cremor, oris m → genitive **Cremoris**, Gelum, i n → **Geli**. Some Uzbek manuals also give the undeclined form “Gel Troxevasin”. Follow your department's requirements.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: If the amount of base is not specified in a suppository prescription, a rectal suppository is made from 3.0 and a vaginal suppository from 4.0. If the exact amount of base is not known, **q.s.** (quantum satis — as much as needed) is written: Olei Cacao q.s. ut fiat suppositorium.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Fentanyl is a narcotic analgesic. It is prescribed on a **special form** and is strictly accounted for. Cutting or heating the patch (heating pad, sauna) is forbidden: when heated, absorption rises sharply and respiratory depression may occur.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Substances that cannot be prescribed as powders: strongly **hygroscopic** substances (calcium chloride, potassium acetate), substances that **liquefy** when mixed together (eutectic mixtures, e.g., camphor with menthol), and **easily decomposing** and **explosive** combinations (potassium permanganate with organic substances).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **D.t.d. N. ... in tabulettis** — “**D**a **t**ales **d**oses, **N**umero ...” (give such doses, in number ...). The dose of one tablet is written after Rp., and their number after D.t.d.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Common prescription errors: (1) a missing or misplaced decimal point in the dose; (2) writing the substance name in the nominative case (“Analginum 0.5” instead of “Analgini 0.5”); (3) omitting the dosage form or the number in the D.t.d. part; (4) writing the signatura in Latin or vaguely; (5) prescribing a list A or narcotic drug on an ordinary form; (6) no confirmation mark when the maximum dose is exceeded.

sections.title: 1. Prescription writing and its basic concepts

blocks.text: **Prescription writing (recipe writing)** (Lat. recipere — to take) — the branch of pharmacology that studies the rules for prescribing, preparing and dispensing medicines to the patient. It is divided into two parts:

items: **general prescription writing** — dosage forms and the general rules for prescribing them;

**special prescription writing** — prescribing specific drug groups (studied in each subsequent topic). **A prescription** is the physician's **written instruction** to the pharmacist (dispensing chemist) to prepare or dispense a medicinal product in a certain form and dose, and on how to use it. A prescription is simultaneously a medical, legal and financial document.

blocks.title: Table 1.1. Significance of the prescription
head: Aspect
Content
rows: Determines which drug the patient takes, how much and how
The physician who wrote the prescription is legally responsible for the drug's effect; it may serve as evidence in court
The basis for keeping records of substance consumption and of free and subsidized drugs in the pharmacy
A source for conclusions about drug consumption, morbidity and drug effectiveness

blocks.text: Key terms

items: **Drug substance (active substance)** — an individual chemical compound or natural substance that has pharmacological activity and is approved for medical use (e.g., paracetamol).
**Medicinal product** — a substance or mixture of substances approved for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of disease.
**Drug preparation** — a ready-to-use medicinal product brought into a particular dosage form (e.g., “Paracetamol 500 mg tablets”).
**Dosage form** — a state of the medicinal product convenient for use (tablet, solution, ointment, etc.).
**Medicinal plant raw material** — plants or their parts containing biologically active substances.

**Galenic preparations** — preparations obtained by processing medicinal plant raw material and containing ballast substances (infusion, decoction, tincture, extract). **Neogalenic preparations** — preparations maximally purified from ballast substances that can be given parenterally.

parts.text: Drug substance → medicinal product → drug preparation. The same drug substance may be produced in different dosage forms: for example, diclofenac is available as tablets, a solution for injection, a gel, suppositories and eye drops.

blocks.text: State Pharmacopoeia

**Pharmacopoeia** (Gr. pharmacon — drug, poieo — I make) — a collection of state standards **having the force of law** that set the quality requirements for medicines, the methods of preparing, storing and analyzing them, the maximum doses and the lists. Compliance with the pharmacopoeia is mandatory for all pharmaceutical companies and pharmacies. There is also the WHO **International Pharmacopoeia**, which is advisory in nature.
In the pharmacopoeia, drugs are classified by their degree of danger:

items: **List A (Venena — poisonous)** — poisonous drugs that are prescribed, stored and dosed with great care. They are stored separately in a lockable cabinet.
**List B (Heroica — potent)** — drugs that may cause complications when used without medical supervision.

In addition, **narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances and precursors** are controlled by separate legislation. **Officinal drugs** (Lat. officina — pharmacy) — drugs whose composition is set by the pharmacopoeia or a regulatory document and which are produced ready-made in a factory. **Magistral drugs** (Lat. magister — master) — drugs prepared individually in the pharmacy according to a physician's prescription. There are also magistral formulations named after their authors: Votchal's drops, Pavlov's mixture, Vishnevsky's liniment.

parts.text: In modern practice, it is recommended to write prescriptions by the **international nonproprietary name (INN)**. This allows the patient to choose a cheaper generic preparation with the same active substance and prevents the same substance from being prescribed twice under two different trade names (dose duplication).

Common INN stems help to recognize the drug group: **-olol** — beta-blockers (metoprolol), **-pril** — ACE inhibitors (enalapril), **-sartan** — angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan), **-statin** — statins (atorvastatin), **-prazole** — proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole), **-floxacin** — fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), **-mab** — monoclonal antibodies (rituximab).

sections.title: 2. Doses and writing units of measurement in a prescription

blocks.text: **Dose** — the amount of a drug given to the body once or over a certain period that produces the desired effect.

blocks.title: Table 1.3. Types of doses
head: Dose
Latin name
Definition
rows: The total amount taken in one day
The amount over the whole course of treatment
The smallest amount that just begins to produce an effect
The amount that produces the desired effect in most patients
The largest amount considered safe (given in the pharmacopoeia for list A and B drugs)
The amount that causes signs of poisoning
A large initial dose to rapidly achieve the required blood concentration
Subsequent doses to maintain the concentration achieved

blocks.text: **Therapeutic range (therapeutic width)** — the interval between the minimum therapeutic and the minimum toxic doses. The wider it is, the safer the drug (this concept is discussed in detail in topic 3).
Writing amounts in a prescription

In a prescription, the unit of mass is the **gram** and the unit of volume is the **milliliter**. The name of the unit is not written, only the number. Grams are written as whole numbers, and fractions of a gram as decimals.

blocks.text: Doses for children and the elderly
Traditional prescription-writing manuals give simplified formulas for calculating a child's dose from the adult dose:

items: by age: **child's dose = adult dose × child's age / 24**;

by weight: **child's dose = adult dose × child's weight / 70**. Elderly patients (over 60), especially for drugs acting on the CNS, cardiac glycosides and diuretics, are prescribed **1/2–3/4 of the adult dose**.

parts.text: The formulas above are for rough estimates only. In modern pediatrics, doses for each drug are set in **mg/kg** or **mg/m^2^** (body surface area), based on the package insert and pediatric reference books. For most drugs, calculating a child's dose from age alone can be dangerous.

blocks.text: A prescription is written on a special **prescription form** clearly and legibly with a ballpoint pen or ink. Corrections are not allowed. The size of an ordinary form is 105 × 148 mm.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: The prescription form and the parts of a prescription (compiler's diagram, based on the TMA manual “Fundamentals of prescription writing”)

blocks.text: Parts of a prescription

items: **Inscriptio** — the stamp and code of the medical institution.
**Datum** — the date the prescription was written.
**Nomen aegroti** — the patient's surname, first name, patronymic and age.
**Nomen medici** — the physician's surname, first name and patronymic.
**Invocatio** — the physician's address to the pharmacist: **Rp.:** (Recipe — take).
**Designatio materiarum** — the names and amounts of the drug substances (in Latin, in the genitive case).
**Subscriptio** — instructions to the pharmacist about the dosage form and the amount to be dispensed (M.f., D.t.d. N.).
**Signatura** — the method of use for the patient (after S. or D.S., in the state language).
**Signum et sigillum medici** — the physician's signature and personal seal.

parts.text: A prescription is read “from top to bottom”: **Stamp → Date → Patient → Physician → Rp. → Drug → Instructions → Signatura → Physician's signature**. Initial letters of the Latin names: **I-D-N-N-I-D-S-S-S**. Only **parts 5, 6 and 7** (Rp., drug names, instructions to the pharmacist) are written in Latin; the rest is in the state language.

blocks.text: General rules for writing prescriptions

items: Each drug substance is written **on a new line and with a capital letter**.
Drug substances are written **in the genitive case** (Genetivus), because it means “Take [of what?] ...”: Rp.: Analgini 0.5 — “Take 0.5 of analgin”.
Order of the ingredients in compound prescriptions: **main drug (basis) → auxiliary drug (adjuvans) → taste and smell corrector (corrigens) → form-giving substance (constituens)**.
If several substances are prescribed in equal amounts, the amount is placed opposite the last one, preceded by **ana** (**āā**) — “in equal amounts”.
If two drugs are written on one form, they are separated by the **#** sign (except list A and narcotic drugs, which are written on separate forms).
If the drug must be dispensed urgently, **Cito!** (quickly) or **Statim!** (immediately) is written at the top of the form.
If the prescription is to be repeated, **Repetatur!** (let it be repeated) is written.
If the dose of a drug substance exceeds the maximum dose, the physician writes the amount **in words**, puts an exclamation mark and confirms it with a signature.

parts.text: Vague expressions such as “internally” or “as directed” must not be written in the **signatura**. The amount, the number of times a day, the timing in relation to meals and the duration must be stated clearly: “Take 1 tablet 3 times a day after meals for 5 days”.

blocks.text: Types of prescription forms

items: **Ordinary forms** — for most drugs; certified with the institution's “For prescriptions” seal.
**Subsidized and free prescriptions** — the form is stamped “free” or “subsidized” and signed by the physician and the head of the institution.

**Special forms** (serially numbered, strictly accounted for) — for narcotic and psychotropic substances and certain potent drugs. They are certified with the institution's official seal with the coat of arms and are kept in a safe by the chief physician.

parts.text: **Electronic prescription.** In Uzbekistan, the “Electronic prescription” system was launched in December 2025 in Tashkent and a number of pilot districts and is planned to be rolled out nationwide by the end of 2026. The physician confirms the prescription electronically, a QR code is assigned automatically and the prescription is sent to the pharmacy automatically; it was first made mandatory for antibiotics and hormonal preparations. A separate procedure remains for narcotic and potent drugs. Because these rules keep changing, the current orders of the Ministry of Health should be checked. The skill of composing the Latin part of a prescription correctly remains the foundation in the electronic system as well.

blocks.text: Abbreviations used in prescriptions

Abbreviation rule: a word is abbreviated **at a consonant** (extr. — extractum, ung. — unguentum). Names of drug substances, plant names and chemical elements are **not abbreviated** (exceptions: aq. — aqua, sp. — spiritus, ac. — acidum).

The cation (metal) is always in the genitive: Natrii, Kalii, Calcii, Magnii, Zinci.

blocks.text: **Dosage form** — a convenient state given to a medicinal product for use. The dosage form determines the rate of absorption, bioavailability, onset and duration of action of the drug.

blocks.title: Table 1.8. Classification of dosage forms
head: Criterion
Types
rows: Enteral (oral, sublingual, rectal), parenteral (injection), topical (skin, mucous membranes), inhalation
Dosed (tablet, capsule, suppository) and non-dosed (ointment, solution, powder)
Officinal (in a factory) and magistral (in a pharmacy, ex tempore)
Simple (one active substance) and compound (two or more substances)

blocks.text: This topic covers **solid** and **soft** dosage forms; liquid dosage forms are studied in topic 2.

Soft dosage forms include **ointments, pastes, creams, gels, liniments, suppositories and plasters**. They are widely used in dermatology, ophthalmology, proctology, gynecology and surgery; some (nitroglycerin ointment, hormonal patches) are used for a **resorptive** (systemic) effect.
Any soft dosage form consists of two parts:

items: **the active substance (basis)** — has the therapeutic effect;
**the form-giving substance, the base (constituens)** — forms the dosage form and holds the active substance.

blocks.text: 5.1. Ointments (Unguenta)

**Ointment** (Unguentum, i n) — a non-dosed dosage form of soft consistency intended for application to the skin and mucous membranes. The amount of active substance is usually **up to 25%** (if more — a paste).

blocks.title: Table 1.9. Ointment bases (constituens) and their properties
head: Base
Property
Use
rows: Indifferent, does not spoil, not absorbed through the skin
If no base is specified in the prescription, petrolatum is used; for a superficial effect
Obtained from sheep's wool, well absorbed through the skin, absorbs up to 150% water
For a deep and resorptive effect; moist wounds
Well absorbed but quickly turns rancid

blocks.text: Ointments are prescribed in **two** ways:

**Abbreviated form** — if the ointment is officinal or has a single active substance with a petrolatum base. After Rp.: the name of the dosage form in the genitive (Unguenti), the substance name, its concentration and the total amount are written.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.1. TETRACYCLINE EYE OINTMENT** Rp.: Unguenti Tetracyclini ophthalmici 1% — 10.0
D.S. Apply inside the lower eyelid 3 times a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.2. OFFICINAL ZINC OINTMENT** Rp.: Unguenti Zinci 10% — 30.0
D.S. Apply to the affected skin area 2 times a day.

**Extended form** — for magistral ointments, or if the base is not petrolatum, or if there are two or more active substances. Each substance is written on a separate line, the base is brought up to the total mass with “**ad**”, and then **M.f. unguentum** is written.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.3. 1% NEOMYCIN OINTMENT ON A LANOLIN BASE, 50.0** Rp.: Neomycini sulfatis 0.5
Lanolini ad 50.0 M.f. unguentum D.S. Apply to the injured area 2 times a day.
Calculation: 100.0 of ointment contains 1.0 of neomycin; 50.0 of ointment — x; x = 50 × 1 / 100 = **0.5**.

parts.text: Formula for calculating the amount of a substance from a percentage concentration: **amount of substance (g) = total mass × percentage / 100**. This formula is the same for ointments, pastes, liniments and solutions.
Eye ointments are prepared sterile and prescribed in amounts of 5.0–10.0, skin ointments in amounts of 20.0–100.0. The word ophthalmicum is added to the name of an eye ointment.

blocks.text: 5.2. Pastes (Pastae)

**Paste** (Pasta, ae f) — a thick ointment containing **25% to 65%** powdered substances (zinc oxide, talc, starch, white clay). Thanks to the large amount of powder, pastes have an **adsorbing, drying and anti-inflammatory** effect and stay on the skin surface for a long time. They are used for weeping dermatitis, eczema and diaper rash.
If the total powdered substances in the prescription are less than 25%, an indifferent powder (starch, talc) is added to obtain the required consistency.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.4. OFFICINAL ZINC PASTE** Rp.: Pastae Zinci 40.0
D.S. Apply to the affected skin area 2 times a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.5. MAGISTRAL PASTE (5% ANESTHESIN AND 25% ZINC OXIDE, 50.0)** Rp.: Anaesthesini 2.5
Zinci oxydi 12.5 Vaselini ad 50.0 M.f. pasta D.S. Apply to the itching skin area.
5.3. Creams (Cremores) and gels (Gela)

**Cream** — a soft dosage form that is more liquid than an ointment and contains water (emulsion base). It is well absorbed into the skin, cosmetically convenient (not shiny) and convenient for use in skin folds and on the face. **Gel** — a viscous dosage form based on gelling agents such as gelatin, agar-agar and carbomer; it is quickly absorbed by the skin and has a cooling effect. Both are officinal only and are therefore written in the **abbreviated** form.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.6. HYDROCORTISONE CREAM** Rp.: Cremoris Hydrocortisoni 1% — 15.0
D.S. Apply a thin layer to the affected skin area 2 times a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.7. DICLOFENAC GEL** Rp.: Geli Diclofenaci 1% — 50.0
D.S. Apply to the painful joint area 3 times a day.

parts.text: Different manuals use different spellings for cream and gel, such as “Crem”, “Cremoris”, “Gel”, “Geli”. According to Latin grammar, Cremor, oris m → genitive **Cremoris**, Gelum, i n → **Geli**. Some Uzbek manuals also give the undeclined form “Gel Troxevasin”. Follow your department's requirements.

blocks.text: 5.4. Liniments (Linimenta)

**Liniment** (Linimentum, i n) — a dosage form in the form of a **liquid ointment** that melts at body temperature. Vegetable oils (sunflower, cottonseed, castor, peach oil) are used as the base. It is shaken before use. It is used for joint and muscle pain, burns and wounds. Officinal liniments are written in the abbreviated form, magistral liniments in the extended form.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.8. OFFICINAL SYNTHOMYCIN LINIMENT** Rp.: Linimenti Synthomycini 10% — 25.0
D.S. Apply to the wound surface under a dressing.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.9. MAGISTRAL LINIMENT (5% TURPENTINE, 10% METHYL SALICYLATE, 75.0)** Rp.: Olei Terebinthinae 3.75
Methylii salicylatis 7.5 Olei Helianthi ad 75.0 M.f. linimentum D.S. Rub into the painful joint.

parts.text: **Vishnevsky's liniment** (balsamic liniment) — a classic magistral formulation of xeroform, birch tar and castor oil. It is still used to treat purulent wounds and abscesses.

blocks.text: 5.5. Suppositories (Suppositoria)
**Suppository** (Suppositorium, i n) — a dosed dosage form that is solid at room temperature and **melts at body temperature**. It is intended for insertion into body cavities.

blocks.title: Table 1.10. Types of suppositories
head: Type
Shape
Mass
rows: Cone or cylinder with a pointed end
0.5–1.0 g; for the urethra, cervical canal and fistula tracts

blocks.label: Figure 1.2
blocks.caption: Shapes of suppositories: a — rectal; b — vaginal (1 — globule, 2 — ovule, 3 — pessary); c — sticks (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.text: Bases: **cocoa butter** (Oleum Cacao) — the most commonly used base, melts at 30–34 °C; gelatin-glycerin mass; polyethylene oxide bases; butyrol.

parts.text: Rectal suppositories are used for a **local** (hemorrhoids, proctitis) and **resorptive** effect. A drug absorbed from the lower part of the rectum enters the inferior vena cava directly through the inferior and middle rectal veins, bypassing the liver. The drug is therefore protected from partial breakdown in the liver. This route is convenient in vomiting patients, young children (paracetamol suppositories) and unconscious patients.

blocks.text: Officinal suppositories are prescribed in the abbreviated form: Rp.: Suppositorium cum (with …) + the substance name **in the ablative** + dose.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.10. OFFICINAL PARACETAMOL SUPPOSITORIES (FOR A CHILD)** Rp.: Suppositorium cum Paracetamolo 0.25
D.t.d. N. 10 S. Insert 1 suppository into the rectum when the temperature is above 38.5 °C (not more than 4 times a day).
Compound officinal suppositories with a trade name: Rp.: Suppositoria “Anusolum” N. 10.

Magistral suppositories are written in the extended form: the dose of the active substance for one suppository, the amount of base, **M.f. suppositorium rectale (vaginale)**, then **D.t.d. N.** and the signatura.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.11. RECTAL SUPPOSITORIES WITH ANESTHESIN (MAGISTRAL)** Rp.: Anaesthesini 0.3
Olei Cacao 3.0 M.f. suppositorium rectale D.t.d. N. 10 in charta cerata S. Insert 1 suppository into the rectum when in pain.

parts.text: If the amount of base is not specified in a suppository prescription, a rectal suppository is made from 3.0 and a vaginal suppository from 4.0. If the exact amount of base is not known, **q.s.** (quantum satis — as much as needed) is written: Olei Cacao q.s. ut fiat suppositorium.

blocks.text: 5.6. Plasters (Emplastra) and transdermal therapeutic systems

**Plaster** (Emplastrum, i n) — a plastic mass that softens at body temperature and sticks to the skin, or a fabric coated with such a mass. Plasters may consist of the base only (adhesive plaster — for securing a dressing) or contain a drug (pepper and corn plasters).

**Transdermal therapeutic systems (TTS)** — multilayer patches that release the drug through the skin into the blood at a constant, controlled rate. Examples: nitroglycerin, fentanyl, nicotine, estradiol, rivastigmine and scopolamine patches. They bypass the liver and keep the blood concentration steady.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.12. ADHESIVE PLASTER** Rp.: Emplastri adhaesivi 3 cm × 500 cm
D.S. For securing a dressing.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.13. FENTANYL TRANSDERMAL SYSTEM** Rp.: Systematis therapeutici transdermalis Fentanyli 25 mcg/hour
D.t.d. N. 5 S. Apply one patch to the skin of the chest or shoulder every 72 hours.

parts.text: Fentanyl is a narcotic analgesic. It is prescribed on a **special form** and is strictly accounted for. Cutting or heating the patch (heating pad, sauna) is forbidden: when heated, absorption rises sharply and respiratory depression may occur.

blocks.text: Solid dosage forms include **powders, granules, tablets, dragées, capsules, pills, caramels, lozenges (troches), eye films** and medicinal herbal species.

blocks.title: Table 1.11. Advantages and disadvantages of solid dosage forms
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Convenient to store, transport and use
Unsuitable for unconscious or vomiting patients and for children who cannot swallow
Physically and chemically stable, long shelf life
Absorption depends on food, gastric pH and intestinal motility
An unpleasant taste and smell can be masked with a coating
Some drugs are broken down in the liver during first pass

blocks.text: 6.1. Powders (Pulveres)
**Powder** (Pulvis, eris m) — a free-flowing solid dosage form. Types:

items: **by composition:** simple (simplices) and compound (compositi);
**by dosing:** divided into doses (divisi) and undivided (indivisi);
**by fineness:** coarse (grossi), fine (subtiles), very fine (subtilissimi).

blocks.label: Figure 1.3
blocks.caption: Powder (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.text: **Undivided powders** are prescribed for dusting (5.0–100.0) or for substances taken orally in large doses where an exact dose is not important. Undivided powders for oral use are measured with a teaspoon.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.14. SIMPLE UNDIVIDED POWDER FOR DUSTING** Rp.: Pulveris Streptocidi subtilissimi 20.0
D.S. Dust onto the wound surface.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.15. COMPOUND UNDIVIDED POWDER FOR ORAL USE** Rp.: Magnesii oxydi 40.0
Natrii hydrocarbonatis 10.0 M.f. pulvis D.S. Take 1/3 teaspoon 3 times a day 1 hour after meals.

**Divided powders** — each dose is wrapped in a separate paper. The optimal mass of one powder is **0.1–1.0 g** (usually 0.3–0.5 g). If the dose of a substance is less than 0.1, an **indifferent filler** — sugar (Saccharum), glucose or sodium bicarbonate — is added so that the mass of one powder reaches at least 0.3.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.16. CODEINE PHOSPHATE POWDERS (WITH A FILLER)** Rp.: Codeini phosphatis 0.015
Sacchari 0.3 M.f. pulvis D.t.d. N. 12 S. Take 1 powder 3 times a day when coughing.
Powders of hygroscopic, volatile or odorous substances are wrapped in **waxed** (in charta cerata) or **paraffined** (in charta paraffinata) paper: D.t.d. N. 12 in charta cerata.

parts.text: Substances that cannot be prescribed as powders: strongly **hygroscopic** substances (calcium chloride, potassium acetate), substances that **liquefy** when mixed together (eutectic mixtures, e.g., camphor with menthol), and **easily decomposing** and **explosive** combinations (potassium permanganate with organic substances).

blocks.text: 6.2. Granules (Granula)

**Granules** — small uniform grains 0.2–3 mm in size. Substances with an unpleasant taste, irritants and antibiotics for children are often produced as granules; a suspension is prepared from them. All granules are officinal and are therefore written in the abbreviated form.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.17. ACETYLCYSTEINE GRANULES** Rp.: Granulorum Acetylcysteini 0.2
D.t.d. N. 20 S. Dissolve 1 sachet of granules in 1/2 glass of water and take 3 times a day after meals.
6.3. Tablets (Tabulettae)

**Tablet** (Tabuletta, ae f) — a dosed solid dosage form made in a factory by compressing drug and auxiliary substances. All tablets are **officinal**. Their mass is 0.05–1.0 g; if the diameter is more than 9 mm, a score line is made to ease splitting. Auxiliary substances (starch, talc, lactose, magnesium stearate) are **not written** in the prescription.

blocks.label: Figure 1.4
blocks.caption: Tablets and capsules (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.text: Types of tablets:

items: **by route of administration:** oral; sublingual (sublinguales, nitroglycerin); buccal; chewable; water-soluble (solubiles, effervescent); vaginal tablets; tablets for preparing solutions;
**by coating:** uncoated and coated (obductae); enteric-coated; film-coated;
**by drug release:** immediate and extended-release (retard, SR, CR, XL, MR);
**by dose:** forte (increased dose), mite (reduced dose). Tablets can be prescribed in **two ways**.

blocks.text: **First method** (without the name of the dosage form, with D.t.d.):
**PRESCRIPTION 1.18. PARACETAMOL TABLETS (METHOD 1)** Rp.: Paracetamoli 0.5
D.t.d. N. 20 in tabulettis S. Take 1 tablet when the temperature rises (not more than 4 times a day, at least 4 hours apart).
**Second method** (begins with the name of the dosage form in the accusative case — Tabulettas):
**PRESCRIPTION 1.19. PARACETAMOL TABLETS (METHOD 2)** Rp.: Tabulettas Paracetamoli 0.5 N. 20
D.S. Take 1 tablet when the temperature rises.
Tablets of **compound composition** are prescribed by trade name; the dose is not indicated, and the name is in quotation marks in the nominative case:
**PRESCRIPTION 1.20. COMPOUND TABLET WITH A TRADE NAME** Rp.: Tabulettas “Co-trimoxazolum 480” N. 20
D.S. Take 2 tablets 2 times a day after meals for 7 days.
**Coated** tablets: Rp.: Tabulettas Omeprazoli obductas 0.02 N. 14.

parts.text: **Retard**, enteric-coated and film-coated tablets **must not be split, chewed or crushed**: if the coating is damaged, the whole dose may be absorbed at once and cause a toxic effect (nifedipine retard, morphine retard), or the active substance may be destroyed by gastric acid (omeprazole, pancreatin). The patient should be reminded of this in the signatura: “swallow without chewing”.
**D.t.d. N. ... in tabulettis** — “**D**a **t**ales **d**oses, **N**umero ...” (give such doses, in number ...). The dose of one tablet is written after Rp., and their number after D.t.d.

blocks.text: 6.4. Dragées (Dragee)

**Dragée** — a spherical dosed dosage form made in a factory by coating sugar granules layer by layer with drug and auxiliary substances (dragée coating). Its mass is 0.1–0.5 g. The name dragée is not declined in Latin.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.21. DRAGÉE** Rp.: Dragee Drotaverini 0.04
D.t.d. N. 20 S. Take 1 dragée 3 times a day when in pain.
6.5. Capsules (Capsulae)

**Capsule** — a shell that holds powdered, granular, pasty or liquid drugs. The capsule masks the taste and smell of the drug, protects it from light and air, and protects the gastric mucosa from the irritant effect of the drug.

items: **Gelatin capsules** (capsulae gelatinosae): hard (with a cap — operculatae) and soft (elastic — elasticae; for oily solutions).
**Starch capsules** (capsulae amylaceae, cachets) — hardly used now.
**Enteric (glutoid) capsules** — dissolve only in the intestine.

blocks.label: Figure 1.5
blocks.caption: A hard gelatin capsule filled with granules (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.label: Figure 1.6
blocks.caption: A micropellet capsule and types of capped capsules (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.text: **PRESCRIPTION 1.22. AMOXICILLIN CAPSULES** Rp.: Amoxicillini 0.5
D.t.d. N. 21 in capsulis S. Take 1 capsule 3 times a day every 8 hours for 7 days.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.23. OMEPRAZOLE CAPSULES (METHOD 2)** Rp.: Capsulas Omeprazoli 0.02 N. 28
D.S. Take 1 capsule 2 times a day 30 minutes before breakfast and dinner.
6.6. Pills (Pilulae) and other solid forms

**Pill** (Pilula, ae f) — a spherical dosage form weighing 0.1–0.5 g; it is prepared in the pharmacy from a special mass. If its mass is more than 0.5, it is a **bolus**. Today tablets and capsules have almost completely replaced them.
**PRESCRIPTION 1.24. MAGISTRAL PILLS (0.001 STRYCHNINE NITRATE IN EACH)** Rp.: Strychnini nitratis 0.03
Massae pilularum q.s. ut fiant pilulae N. 30 D.S. Take 1 pill 2 times a day.
In pills, the amount of substance is written for the total number: 0.001 × 30 = 0.03.

blocks.label: Figure 1.7
blocks.caption: Pills (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

items: **Caramels** and **lozenges (troches, pastilles)** are sucked in diseases of the mouth and throat: Rp.: Trochiscos “Strepsils” N. 24 / D.S. Dissolve 1 lozenge in the mouth every 2–3 hours.

**Eye films** (Membranulae ophthalmicae) — sterile polymer films that dissolve in tear fluid: Rp.: Membranulas ophthalmicas cum Pilocarpini hydrochlorido N. 30 / D.S. Place 1 film behind the lower eyelid once a day.
**Medicinal herbal species** (Species) — a mixture of crushed plant parts; infusions or decoctions are prepared from them at home.

sections.title: 7. Clinical part: choosing the right dosage form

blocks.text: The effectiveness and safety of the same drug substance depend strongly on the dosage form. The GP chooses the dosage form taking the following into account:

blocks.title: Table 1.12. Choosing the dosage form according to the clinical situation
head: Situation
Appropriate form
Reason
rows: Acts in 1–2 minutes, bypasses the liver
Suspension, syrup, mixture prepared from granules
Cannot swallow tablets; easy to adjust the dose to weight
High local concentration, few systemic adverse effects
The patient forgets to take the drug many times a day

parts.text: **Adherence (compliance).** Patients adhere much better to preparations taken once a day than to those taken 3–4 times a day. That is why, in chronic diseases (arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus), extended-release forms are chosen whenever possible.

Common prescription errors: (1) a missing or misplaced decimal point in the dose; (2) writing the substance name in the nominative case (“Analginum 0.5” instead of “Analgini 0.5”); (3) omitting the dosage form or the number in the D.t.d. part; (4) writing the signatura in Latin or vaguely; (5) prescribing a list A or narcotic drug on an ordinary form; (6) no confirmation mark when the maximum dose is exceeded.

skills.title: Skill 1. Algorithm for prescribing a dosed solid dosage form (tablet, capsule, dragée)

items: Fill in the top part of the form: date, patient's full name and age, physician's full name.
Write the **Rp.:** sign.
Write the name of the drug substance **with a capital letter, in the genitive case** and indicate its **single** dose in grams (Paracetamoli 0.5).
On a new line write **D.t.d. N.** and the number of doses, then add the dosage form with the preposition in in the ablative case (in tabulettis, in capsulis; the form is not written for dragées).
On a new line, after **S.**, write the method of use in the state language: amount, number of doses, timing in relation to meals, duration.
Sign and apply your personal seal.
Compare the dose with the maximum dose; adjust it to age for children and the elderly.

skills.title: Skill 2. Algorithm for writing a prescription for a magistral ointment (paste, liniment)

items: Determine the total mass and the concentration of each active substance.
Calculate the amount of each active substance: **mass × percentage / 100**.
After Rp.: write each active substance on a separate line.
Write the base with **“ad”** up to the total mass (Vaselini ad 50.0).
Write **M.f. unguentum** (pasta, linimentum).
After **D.S.** write the signatura.
For a paste, check that the total of powdered substances is not less than 25%.

skills.title: Skill 3. Algorithm for writing a prescription for a magistral suppository

items: After Rp.: write the dose of the active substance **for one suppository**.
Write the base (Olei Cacao) in the amount for one suppository or with **q.s.**
Write **M.f. suppositorium rectale (vaginale)**.
Write **D.t.d. N.** and the number of suppositories.
In the signatura, state into which cavity, how many times and when it is to be inserted.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A GP found that a 4-year-old child (weight 16 kg) has a temperature of 39 °C during an acute respiratory infection. The child is vomiting and refuses to take medicine by mouth. The physician wants to prescribe paracetamol.
cases.ask: 1) Which dosage form is most appropriate? 2) Calculate the single dose (the single dose of paracetamol is 10–15 mg/kg). 3) Write a prescription.
cases.answer: 1) Because the child is vomiting, a rectal suppository is appropriate: the drug partly bypasses the liver and is absorbed even when oral intake is impossible. 2) 16 kg × 15 mg/kg = 240 mg ≈ 0.25 g. 3) Prescription: ANSWER TO CASE 1 Rp.: Suppositorium cum Paracetamolo 0.25 D.t.d. N. 10 S. Insert 1 suppository into the rectum when the temperature is above 38.5 °C; not more than 4 times a day, at least 6 hours apart.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student wrote the following prescription: Rp.: Neomycinum sulfas 1% 50 / Vaselinum / D.S. for application.
cases.ask: Find the errors in the prescription and write the correct version.
cases.answer: Errors: 1) the substance name is in the nominative case — it should be in the genitive (Neomycini sulfatis); 2) the mass should be “50.0”, not “50”; 3) if the base is petrolatum and there is a single active substance, the abbreviated form is sufficient; in the extended form, the amount of active substance should be calculated in grams (0.5) and “ad” and “M.f. unguentum” written; 4) the signatura is vague — where and how many times to apply is not stated. Correct version: ANSWER TO CASE 2 Rp.: Unguenti Neomycini sulfatis 1% — 50.0 D.S. Apply a thin layer to the infected wound surface 2 times a day.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 68-year-old patient needs a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for knee joint pain caused by gonarthrosis. The history includes a gastric ulcer and arterial hypertension.
cases.ask: 1) Which dosage form is safer and why? 2) Write a prescription.
cases.answer: 1) In an elderly patient with a history of gastric ulcer, a systemic NSAID (tablet) increases the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and of a rise in blood pressure. A topical gel creates a sufficient concentration in the joint area, very little is absorbed into the blood, and the risk of systemic adverse effects is much lower. 2) Prescription: ANSWER TO CASE 3 Rp.: Geli Diclofenaci 1% — 50.0 D.S. Rub a thin layer into the knee joint area 3–4 times a day; do not use for more than 14 days.

cells: Rp.: Moddai 0.5 / D.t.d. N. 20 in tabulettis / S. ... or Rp.: Tabulettas Moddai 0.5 N. 20 / D.S. ...
Rp.: Dragee Moddai 0.05 / D.t.d. N. 20 / S. ...
Rp.: Moddai 0.25 / D.t.d. N. 20 in capsulis / S. ...
Rp.: Moddai 0.3 / D.t.d. N. 10 / S. ... (if the dose is less than 0.1, a filler + M.f. pulvis)
Abbreviated: Rp.: Unguenti Moddai 1% — 30.0 / D.S.; extended: substance / base ad / M.f. unguentum / D.S.
Rp.: Pastae Zinci 40.0 / D.S. or extended + M.f. pasta
Rp.: Linimenti Moddai 10% — 25.0 / D.S. or extended + M.f. linimentum
Officinal: Rp.: Suppositorium cum Moddao 0.25 / D.t.d. N. 10 / S.; magistral: substance / Olei Cacao 3.0 / M.f. suppositorium / D.t.d. N. / S.

topics.cards_title: Table 1.13. Prescribing solid and soft dosage forms — summary

topics.title: Liquid dosage forms for enteral use and the rules for prescribing them. Liquid dosage forms for parenteral and topical use and the rules for prescribing them

goals.text: Liquid dosage forms are used most often in pediatrics, geriatrics and emergency care. A solution is absorbed quickly and its dose is easy to adjust to the patient's weight. However, prescriptions for solutions involve a lot of calculation: concentration, total volume and number of doses depend on one another. A calculation error leads to the patient receiving a dose several times too high.
The student should know:

items: the classification of liquid dosage forms and their advantages and disadvantages;
the types of solutions (aqueous, alcoholic, oily; for oral, topical and injection use) and the ways of expressing concentration;
the properties of infusions, decoctions, tinctures, extracts, mixtures, emulsions, suspensions and mucilages;
the requirements for solutions for injection and eye drops;
the basic concepts of gaseous dosage forms (aerosols, inhalers).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for solutions in the extended, abbreviated and percentage forms;
calculate the total amount of substance and the volume from the single dose and the number of doses;
perform calculations for preparing and diluting solutions of different concentrations;
write prescriptions for drugs in ampoules and vials, including a separate prescription for the solvent.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: If no solvent is specified in the prescription, the solution is prepared in **distilled water**. For an alcoholic solution the word spirituosae is added, for an oily solution oleosae: Solutionis Iodi spirituosae 5%, Solutionis Camphorae oleosae 10%.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Converting a percentage into a ratio: **1% = 1:100**, **0.1% = 1:1000**, **0.02% = 1:5000** (furacilin), **0.01% = 1:10,000**. The second number of the ratio = 100 / percentage.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The three forms express the same drug. The extended form is used for magistral solutions; the abbreviated forms are used more often. In **officinal solutions** (Cordiamine, Validol, dilute hydrochloric acid) the concentration is **not indicated** — only the name and the amount are written: Rp.: Validoli 5 ml.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The standard ratios are used only when the amount of raw material is not given in the prescription (S.S. Azizova, department manual). When the amount of raw material is calculated from the single dose (e.g., thermopsis herb 0.6 — 180 ml), the ratio follows from the prescription itself. Infusions of foxglove, thermopsis and ipecacuanha are hardly ever prescribed in current practice — they have been replaced by standardized tablets and syrups.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Oily solutions, suspensions and ordinary emulsions must not be given intravenously** — risk of fat and particle embolism. **Alcoholic solutions are not given subcutaneously** — tissue necrosis. **Calcium chloride is given only intravenously** (necrosis when given intramuscularly or subcutaneously). **A concentrated potassium chloride solution is not given as an intravenous push** — only diluted, slowly by drip (risk of cardiac arrest).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Ceftriaxone diluted with lidocaine is given **only intramuscularly**; for intravenous use it is dissolved in water for injection. Lidocaine is not used in patients allergic to lidocaine or with impaired cardiac conduction. Giving ceftriaxone in the same line with calcium-containing solutions (Ringer's solution), or simultaneously with calcium solutions in newborns, is forbidden (precipitate formation in the lungs and kidneys).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Rules for using a metered-dose aerosol inhaler:** 1) remove the cap and shake; 2) breathe out fully; 3) seal the lips tightly around the mouthpiece; 4) press the canister once while starting a slow, deep breath; 5) hold the breath for **5–10 seconds**; 6) breathe out slowly. Rinsing the mouth after a glucocorticoid inhaler is mandatory (to prevent oral candidiasis).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Multiply the percentage by ten — you get mg/ml”**: 1% = 10 mg/ml, 2% = 20 mg/ml, 0.1% = 1 mg/ml, 10% = 100 mg/ml, 40% glucose = 400 mg/ml.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The most common error in calculations is **mixing up units** (mg and g, mcg and mg). Before starting a calculation, convert all quantities to one unit. For “high-alert” drugs such as insulin, heparin and potassium chloride, it is recommended that a second staff member independently check the calculation.

blocks.text: **Liquid dosage forms** (Formae medicamentorum fluidae) — dosage forms in which the drug substance is dissolved, suspended or emulsified in a liquid.

blocks.title: Table 2.1. Liquid dosage forms
head: Dosage form
Latin (nominative / genitive)
Brief description
rows: A clear liquid in which the substance is completely dissolved in the solvent
An aqueous extract from the delicate parts of a plant
An aqueous extract from the coarse parts of a plant
An alcoholic extract from a plant (officinal)
A liquid mixture of three or more ingredients
A suspension of oil droplets in water
A suspension of solid particles in a liquid
A viscous colloidal solution; reduces irritant effects
A thick sugar solution; a corrigent or a dosage form
Plant preparations purified from ballast substances
Sterile, pyrogen-free solution, suspension or emulsion

blocks.title: Table 2.2. Advantages and disadvantages of liquid dosage forms
head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Rapid absorption, rapid onset of action
Unstable, spoil quickly (especially infusions and decoctions — 3–4 days)
Convenient for children and patients who cannot swallow
Dosing is less accurate than with tablets (spoons, drops)
Easy to adjust the dose to weight
Taste and smell are harder to mask
Irritant substances can be given diluted
Inconvenient to transport and store, prone to microbial contamination

blocks.text: **Solution** (Solutio, onis f; abbreviated Sol.) — a clear liquid dosage form obtained by dissolving one or more substances in a solvent. A solution consists of two parts: the **solute** and the **solvent**.

Solvents: distilled water (Aqua destillata), purified water (Aqua purificata), ethyl alcohol (Spiritus aethylicus), glycerin (Glycerinum), vegetable oils (peach, almond, olive, sunflower oil), liquid paraffin.

parts.text: If no solvent is specified in the prescription, the solution is prepared in **distilled water**. For an alcoholic solution the word spirituosae is added, for an oily solution oleosae: Solutionis Iodi spirituosae 5%, Solutionis Camphorae oleosae 10%.

blocks.text: 2.1. Ways of expressing the concentration of a solution

blocks.title: Table 2.3. Ways of expressing concentration
head: Method
Meaning
Example
rows: Grams of substance in 100 ml of solution
The ratio of the substance to the volume of solution
Total amount of substance and volume of solution

parts.text: Converting a percentage into a ratio: **1% = 1:100**, **0.1% = 1:1000**, **0.02% = 1:5000** (furacilin), **0.01% = 1:10,000**. The second number of the ratio = 100 / percentage.

blocks.text: 2.2. Solutions for oral use
Solutions for oral use are dosed with a spoon or in drops. Solutions taken by the spoon are usually prescribed **3 times a day for 4 days — 12 doses in total** (the solution does not keep long).
Calculation algorithm:

items: Number of doses: times a day × days (e.g., 3 × 4 = 12).
Amount of substance: single dose × number of doses.

Volume of solution: spoon volume × number of doses (tablespoon: 15 × 12 = 180 ml; dessert spoon: 10 × 12 = 120 ml; teaspoon: 5 × 12 = 60 ml). Example. Write a prescription for a sodium bromide solution with a single dose of 0.3, to be taken 1 tablespoon 3 times a day.

blocks.text: Solutions can be prescribed in **three forms**:
**PRESCRIPTION 2.1. EXTENDED FORM** Rp.: Natrii bromidi 3.6
Aquae destillatae ad 180 ml M.f. solutio D.S. Take 1 tablespoon 3 times a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.2. ABBREVIATED FORM (MASS – VOLUME)** Rp.: Solutionis Natrii bromidi 3.6 — 180 ml
D.S. Take 1 tablespoon 3 times a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.3. ABBREVIATED PERCENTAGE FORM** Rp.: Solutionis Natrii bromidi 2% — 180 ml
D.S. Take 1 tablespoon 3 times a day.

parts.text: The three forms express the same drug. The extended form is used for magistral solutions; the abbreviated forms are used more often. In **officinal solutions** (Cordiamine, Validol, dilute hydrochloric acid) the concentration is **not indicated** — only the name and the amount are written: Rp.: Validoli 5 ml.

blocks.text: 2.3. Drops for oral use
Potent and low-dose substances are given in drops. The single dose is usually **5–20 drops**; the prescription is written for **20 doses**. 1 ml of aqueous solution = 20 drops.
Example. Write a prescription for an atropine sulfate solution with a single dose of 0.0005, to be taken 10 drops at a time.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.4. DROPS (PERCENTAGE FORM)** Rp.: Solutionis Atropini sulfatis 0.1% — 10 ml
D.S. Take 10 drops 2 times a day before meals.

sections.title: 3. Liquid forms prepared from medicinal plant raw material

blocks.text: 3.1. Infusions and decoctions (Infusa et Decocta)

**Infusion** — prepared from the delicate parts of a plant (leaf — folium, flower — flos, herb — herba): the raw material is heated with boiling water in a water bath for **15 minutes**, then cooled for **45 minutes** and strained.

**Decoction** — prepared from coarse parts (bark — cortex, root — radix, rhizome — rhizoma): heated in a water bath for **30 minutes** and strained **while hot**. Exception: bearberry (Uva ursi) leaf is thick, so a decoction is made from it; conversely, an infusion is made from roots containing essential oils (valerian).

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Equipment for preparing an infusion: an infundir pot and a water bath (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.title: Table 2.4. Standard ratios for infusions and decoctions (if not specified in the prescription)
head: Raw material
Ratio
Examples
rows: Chamomile flower, peppermint leaf, oak bark, bearberry leaf
Spring adonis herb, valerian root, lily of the valley herb
Foxglove leaf, thermopsis herb, ipecacuanha root

parts.text: The standard ratios are used only when the amount of raw material is not given in the prescription (S.S. Azizova, department manual). When the amount of raw material is calculated from the single dose (e.g., thermopsis herb 0.6 — 180 ml), the ratio follows from the prescription itself. Infusions of foxglove, thermopsis and ipecacuanha are hardly ever prescribed in current practice — they have been replaced by standardized tablets and syrups.

blocks.text: Infusions and decoctions are prescribed **only in the abbreviated form**: the dosage form (Infusi, Decocti), the plant part with a small letter, the plant name with a capital letter, the mass of raw material and the volume of the finished drug.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.5. INFUSION (SPRING ADONIS HERB, SINGLE DOSE 0.5)** Rp.: Infusi herbae Adonidis vernalis 6.0 — 180 ml
D.S. Take 1 tablespoon 3 times a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.6. DECOCTION (OAK BARK, 1:10)** Rp.: Decocti corticis Quercus 20.0 — 200 ml
D.S. For rinsing the mouth 4–5 times a day.
3.2. Tinctures and extracts

**Tincture** (Tinctura) — a clear, colored extract obtained from plant raw material with 40% or 70% ethyl alcohol. Because alcohol is a preservative, tinctures keep for a long time. All tinctures are **officinal**; they are dosed in drops.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.7. TINCTURE** Rp.: Tincturae Valerianae 30 ml
D.S. Take 20–25 drops 3 times a day.
Several tinctures can be prescribed as a mixture; in that case **M.D.S.** is used:
**PRESCRIPTION 2.8. MIXTURE OF TINCTURES** Rp.: Tincturae Valerianae
Tincturae Leonuri ana 15 ml M.D.S. Take 30 drops 3 times a day.

**Extracts** (Extracta) — concentrated extracts: liquid (fluida, 1:1), thick (spissa, moisture up to 25%) and dry (sicca, moisture up to 5%). Liquid extracts are given in drops; thick and dry extracts are given as part of tablets, capsules and suppositories.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.9. LIQUID EXTRACT** Rp.: Extracti Crataegi fluidi 25 ml
D.S. Take 20–30 drops 3 times a day before meals.
**Neogalenic preparations** — standardized plant preparations maximally purified from ballast substances; some are suitable for injection. Examples: Corglycon, strophanthin, Adonisid.
4.1. Mixture (Mixtura)

**Mixture** — a liquid mixture of **3 or more** ingredients consisting of dissolved solids and various liquid dosage forms (solution, infusion, tincture, syrup). Mixtures that form a precipitate are shaken before use (mixturae agitandae). The word “Mixtura” is not written in the prescription; **M.D.S.** is placed at the end.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.10. MIXTURE (ADONIS INFUSION + SODIUM BROMIDE + CODEINE)** Rp.: Infusi herbae Adonidis vernalis 6.0 — 180 ml
Natrii bromidi 3.6 Codeini phosphatis 0.12 M.D.S. Take 1 tablespoon 3 times a day.

**Corrigents** — substances that improve the taste and smell of a drug: sugar syrups (Sirupus simplex, Sirupus Rubi idaei — raspberry syrup), aromatic waters (Aqua Menthae piperitae — peppermint water). **Mucilages** are added to irritant drugs: starch mucilage (Mucilago Amyli), marshmallow root mucilage (Mucilago radicis Althaeae). Syrups and mucilages are usually added in an amount of **1/3 of** the total volume.
4.2. Emulsions (Emulsa)

**Emulsion** (Emulsum, i n) — a milky dosage form consisting of two immiscible liquids (water and oil). Stability is provided by **emulsifiers**: gelatose, gum arabic, egg yolk, Tweens. The classic ratio for preparing an oil emulsion: **oil : emulsifier : water = 2 : 1 : 17**; if the amount of oil is not specified, the emulsion is prepared at a ratio of 1:10.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.11. OIL EMULSION (ABBREVIATED FORM)** Rp.: Emulsi olei Ricini 20.0 — 200 ml
D.S. Take all at once (as a laxative).

parts.text: In modern practice, the most important emulsions are **emulsions for intravenous use**: propofol (for general anesthesia) and fat emulsions for parenteral nutrition. Oily solutions normally cannot be given intravenously, but special emulsions with very fine particles (less than 1 μm) are an exception.

blocks.text: 4.3. Suspensions (Suspensiones)

**Suspension** (Suspensio, onis f) — solid drug particles that are insoluble in the liquid, held in suspension. It is used orally, topically and intramuscularly. **It must not be given intravenously.** The signatura must include “**Shake before use!**”.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.12. ANTIBIOTIC SUSPENSION FOR A CHILD** Rp.: Suspensionis Amoxicillini 250 mg/5 ml — 100 ml
D.S. Shake before use. Take 5 ml 3 times a day for 7 days.

parts.text: Antibiotics for children are often produced as **powders or granules for oral suspension**. Boiled and cooled water is poured into the bottle up to the mark and shaken. The finished suspension is kept in the refrigerator for 7–14 days. Parents should be taught to use a dosing syringe or spoon: the volume of kitchen spoons is not standard.

sections.title: 5. Liquid dosage forms for topical use

blocks.text: Solutions for topical use are used for wiping the skin, washing wounds, rinsing, compresses (lotions), douching and enemas, and also as eye, ear and nose drops.

blocks.title: Table 2.5. Amounts of solutions for topical use
head: Purpose
Usual amount

blocks.text: **PRESCRIPTION 2.13. NITROFURAL (FURACILIN) SOLUTION (RATIO FORM)** Rp.: Solutionis Furacilini 1:5000 — 200 ml
D.S. Gargle 3–4 times a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.14. ALCOHOLIC SOLUTION** Rp.: Solutionis Viridis nitentis spirituosae 1% — 10 ml
D.S. Apply to the skin around the wound.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.15. OFFICINAL SOLUTION (CONCENTRATION NOT WRITTEN)** Rp.: Solutionis Hydrogenii peroxydi diluti 50 ml
D.S. For washing the wound.
**Prescribing a concentrated solution.** When a large volume is needed (gargling, douching), the patient is prescribed a concentrated solution with instructions for diluting it at home.

Example: the throat needs to be gargled 10 times with a 0.02% potassium permanganate solution (200 ml each time). For one gargle: 200 × 0.02 / 100 = 0.04; for 10 times: **0.4**. Let each dose be contained in 1 tablespoon (15 ml) of concentrated solution: 15 × 10 = **150 ml**.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.16. CONCENTRATED SOLUTION** Rp.: Kalii permanganatis 0.4
Aquae destillatae ad 150 ml M.f. solutio D.S. Dilute 1 tablespoon of the solution in 1 glass of warm water and gargle.
5.1. Eye drops (Guttae ophthalmicae)

Requirements for eye drops: they must be **sterile**, **free of mechanical particles**, as far as possible **isotonic** (osmotic pressure equal to 0.9% NaCl) and close to the pH of tear fluid, and chemically stable. Eye drops are prescribed in 5–10 ml, enough for **20 applications**; 1–2 drops are instilled into each eye at a time.

blocks.label: Figure 2.2
blocks.caption: Eye drops (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.text: **PRESCRIPTION 2.17. EYE DROPS** Rp.: Solutionis Pilocarpini hydrochloridi 1% — 10 ml
D.S. Instill 1–2 drops into each eye 3 times a day.

parts.text: Pressing on the lacrimal duct area (the inner corner of the eye) with a finger for 1–2 minutes after instilling eye drops reduces drainage of the drug into the nasopharynx and its absorption into the blood. This is especially important with beta-blocker drops (timolol) to prevent bronchospasm and bradycardia.

blocks.text: 5.2. Enemas and mucilages

Therapeutic (medicated) enemas are given after a cleansing enema; the single volume does not exceed **50–100 ml**. Irritant substances are given mixed with a mucilage. The prescription is written only in the extended form.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.18. THERAPEUTIC ENEMA** Rp.: Chlorali hydrati 1.0
Mucilaginis Amyli Aquae destillatae ana 25 ml M.D.S. For one enema. Introduce warm into the rectum after a cleansing enema.

sections.title: 6. Dosage forms for injection (Formae medicamentorum pro injectionibus)

blocks.text: For injection, aqueous and oily solutions, suspensions, emulsions and sterile powders to be dissolved before use are used.

blocks.label: Figure 2.3
blocks.caption: Dosage forms for injection: ampoules, vials, infusion solutions (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.title: Table 2.6. Requirements for injection solutions
head: Requirement
Content
rows: No microorganisms; preparation under aseptic conditions or sterilization in an autoclave
No fever-causing substances (bacterial endotoxins); especially important for large-volume infusions
Clarity; prevention of the risk of embolism
Does not decompose during storage; stabilizers may be added
Especially for large volumes given intravenously and into tissues (0.9% NaCl, 5% glucose)

blocks.text: Solvents: water for injection (Aqua pro injectionibus), isotonic sodium chloride solution (Solutio Natrii chloridi isotonica 0.9%), 5% glucose solution, sterile peach or almond oil (intramuscular only).

blocks.title: Table 2.7. Parenteral routes and volumes
head: Route
Single volume
What must not be given
rows: Irritant and hypertonic solutions, alcoholic solutions
Calcium chloride, irritant solutions, large volumes
Oily solutions, suspensions, ordinary emulsions, air bubbles

parts.text: **Oily solutions, suspensions and ordinary emulsions must not be given intravenously** — risk of fat and particle embolism. **Alcoholic solutions are not given subcutaneously** — tissue necrosis. **Calcium chloride is given only intravenously** (necrosis when given intramuscularly or subcutaneously). **A concentrated potassium chloride solution is not given as an intravenous push** — only diluted, slowly by drip (risk of cardiac arrest).

blocks.text: 6.1. Prescribing injection solutions
Solutions in ampoules (divided into doses):
**PRESCRIPTION 2.19. SOLUTION IN AMPOULES (PERCENTAGE FORM)** Rp.: Solutionis Diclofenaci natrii 2.5% — 3 ml
D.t.d. N. 5 in ampullis S. Inject 3 ml deep intramuscularly once a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.20. SOLUTION IN AMPOULES (MASS – VOLUME FORM)** Rp.: Solutionis Dexamethasoni 0.004 — 1 ml
D.t.d. N. 10 in ampullis S. Inject 1 ml intravenously or intramuscularly 1–2 times a day.
Infusion solutions in bottles (not divided into doses) — **only in the percentage form**:
**PRESCRIPTION 2.21. INFUSION SOLUTION** Rp.: Solutionis Natrii chloridi isotonicae 0.9% — 400 ml
D.S. Give by intravenous drip at a rate of 40–60 drops per minute.
Oily solutions are given only intramuscularly or subcutaneously, **warmed to body temperature**:
**PRESCRIPTION 2.22. OILY SOLUTION IN AMPOULES** Rp.: Solutionis Progesteroni oleosae 2.5% — 1 ml
D.t.d. N. 10 in ampullis S. Inject 1 ml intramuscularly (warm to body temperature first).

**Sterile powders.** Drugs that are unstable in solution (most antibiotics) are produced as dry powder in vials and dissolved before use (ex tempore). In this case, **a separate prescription is written for the solvent**, and the two prescriptions are separated by the **#** sign.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.23. STERILE POWDER IN A VIAL AND ITS SOLVENT** Rp.: Ceftriaxoni 1.0
D.t.d. N. 10 S. Dissolve the powder in the vial in 3.5 ml of 1% lidocaine solution and inject intramuscularly once a day. # Rp.: Solutionis Lidocaini hydrochloridi 1% — 3.5 ml
D.t.d. N. 10 in ampullis S. For preparing the ceftriaxone solution.

parts.text: Ceftriaxone diluted with lidocaine is given **only intramuscularly**; for intravenous use it is dissolved in water for injection. Lidocaine is not used in patients allergic to lidocaine or with impaired cardiac conduction. Giving ceftriaxone in the same line with calcium-containing solutions (Ringer's solution), or simultaneously with calcium solutions in newborns, is forbidden (precipitate formation in the lungs and kidneys).

blocks.text: Officinal and neogalenic preparations in ampoules are written by name only: Rp.: Corglyconi 0.06% — 1 ml / D.t.d. N. 10 in ampullis / S. ...

sections.title: 7. Gaseous dosage forms: aerosols and inhalers

blocks.text: **Aerosol** (Aerosolum, i n) — a dosage form in which the drug substance is dispersed as fine particles or droplets in a gaseous medium (air or a propellant). It is produced in pressurized canisters. **Spray** — a propellant-free form sprayed with a mechanical pump.

blocks.title: Table 2.8. Types of inhalation devices
head: Device
Working principle
Advantage / disadvantage
rows: Under propellant pressure, an exact dose is released with each press
Cheap and widespread; requires coordinating the press with inhalation (a spacer helps)
Dry powder inhaler (DPI: Turbuhaler, Diskhaler, capsule-based)
The patient's deep inhalation carries the powder into the lungs
No coordination needed; a strong inhalation is required (unsuitable in a severe attack and in young children)
The energy of a spring creates a slow aerosol cloud
More drug reaches the lungs; a low-velocity cloud
Turns a solution into a fine aerosol
Used at any age and in severe conditions; bulky, requires electricity

blocks.label: Figure 2.4
blocks.caption: Structure of a capsule-based dry powder inhaler (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.label: Figure 2.5
blocks.caption: Structure of a metered-dose aerosol inhaler (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.label: Figure 2.6
blocks.caption: “Respimat” soft mist inhaler (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

blocks.label: Figure 2.7
blocks.caption: Compressor nebulizer (TMA “Fundamentals of prescription writing”, 2020)

parts.text: **Rules for using a metered-dose aerosol inhaler:** 1) remove the cap and shake; 2) breathe out fully; 3) seal the lips tightly around the mouthpiece; 4) press the canister once while starting a slow, deep breath; 5) hold the breath for **5–10 seconds**; 6) breathe out slowly. Rinsing the mouth after a glucocorticoid inhaler is mandatory (to prevent oral candidiasis).

blocks.text: **PRESCRIPTION 2.24. METERED-DOSE AEROSOL** Rp.: Aerosoli Salbutamoli 0.0001/dosi — 200 dosi
D.S. Take 1–2 inhalations during an attack of breathlessness; not more than 8 inhalations a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 2.25. SOLUTION FOR A NEBULIZER** Rp.: Suspensionis Budesonidi pro inhalationibus 0.25 mg/ml — 2 ml
D.t.d. N. 20 S. Inhale 2 ml through a nebulizer 2 times a day.

sections.title: 8. Dose calculation and preparing solutions of different concentrations

blocks.text: This section corresponds to the 5th-semester laboratory class (“Dose calculation. Preparing solutions of different concentrations”).
8.1. Basic formulas

blocks.title: Table 2.9. Basic calculation formulas for working with solutions
head: Quantity sought
Formula

parts.text: **“Multiply the percentage by ten — you get mg/ml”**: 1% = 10 mg/ml, 2% = 20 mg/ml, 0.1% = 1 mg/ml, 10% = 100 mg/ml, 40% glucose = 400 mg/ml.

blocks.text: 8.2. Sample calculations
**Example 1.** An ampoule contains 2 ml of 2% lidocaine solution. How much lidocaine is in the ampoule?
**Example 2.** A patient needs 4 mg of dexamethasone. The ampoule contains a 4 mg/ml solution. How many ml are drawn up?
**Example 3.** 200 ml of a 5% solution must be prepared from a 40% glucose solution. How much of the 40% solution is taken?
C~1~ × V~1~ = C~2~ × V~2~ → 40 × V~1~ = 5 × 200 → V~1~ = **25 ml**; the remaining 175 ml of water for injection is added.
**Example 4.** A 1000 ml infusion must be given over 8 hours. The drip set gives 1 ml = 20 drops. What is the rate?
**Example 5.** A child weighing 12 kg is prescribed amoxicillin 25 mg/kg 2 times a day. The suspension is 250 mg/5 ml. How many ml are given at a time?
**Example 6.** How many tablets are needed for 500 ml of a 0.02% nitrofural (furacilin) solution (1 tablet = 20 mg)?

parts.text: The most common error in calculations is **mixing up units** (mg and g, mcg and mg). Before starting a calculation, convert all quantities to one unit. For “high-alert” drugs such as insulin, heparin and potassium chloride, it is recommended that a second staff member independently check the calculation.

sections.title: 9. Clinical part: choosing the liquid dosage form and the route of administration

blocks.title: Table 2.10. Comparison of routes of administration
head: Route
Onset of action
Bioavailability
Main indications
rows: When oral intake is impossible; depot preparations

parts.text: In emergencies (anaphylactic shock, status epilepticus, severe hypoglycemia), the **intravenous** or intramuscular route is chosen. In anaphylaxis, giving epinephrine (adrenaline) **intramuscularly** (into the anterolateral thigh) is the first choice: it acts quickly and carries no risk of the arrhythmias seen with intravenous use.

skills.title: Skill 1. Algorithm for prescribing a solution for oral use

items: Determine the single dose (g) and the method of intake (spoon or drops).
Set the number of doses: usually 12 for a spoon, 20 for drops.
Total amount of substance = single dose × number of doses.
Total volume = spoon volume × 12 (or number of drops × 20 / 20).
If necessary, calculate the percentage: substance × 100 / volume.
Write the prescription in the chosen form and state the type of spoon and the number of doses in the signatura.

skills.title: Skill 2. Algorithm for prescribing an injection

items: Determine whether the drug comes in an ampoule (dosed) or a bottle (non-dosed).
For a solution in ampoules: Solutionis ... % — ... ml / D.t.d. N. ... in ampullis.
For an infusion solution in a bottle: percentage form only, D.S.
For a dry powder: a prescription for the powder (D.t.d. N.), then **#** and a separate prescription for the solvent.
State clearly in the signatura the route (intravenously, intramuscularly, subcutaneously), the rate and the number of injections.
Check that no oily solution or suspension is prescribed intravenously.

skills.title: Skill 3. Preparing the required concentration from a concentrated solution

items: Write down the volume and concentration of the required solution (C~2~, V~2~).
Write down the concentration of the available solution (C1).
Find the required volume from the formula V~1~ = C~2~ × V~2~ / C~1~.
Add solvent in a volume of V~2~ – V~1~.
Check the result with a reverse calculation.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 2-year-old child (weight 12 kg) presents with acute otitis media. The pediatrician wants to prescribe amoxicillin at a daily dose of 90 mg/kg, divided into 2 doses, for 10 days. The pharmacy has powder for preparing a 400 mg/5 ml suspension (70 ml of finished suspension).
cases.ask: 1) Calculate the single dose in mg and ml. 2) How many bottles are needed for 10 days? 3) Write a prescription.
cases.answer: 1) Daily dose 12 × 90 = 1080 mg; single dose — 540 mg; 400 mg — 5 ml, 540 mg — x; x = 540 × 5 / 400 ≈ 6.75 ml (in practice 6.8 ml). 2) Daily volume ≈ 13.5 ml; over 10 days ≈ 135 ml → 2 bottles (2 × 70 ml). 3) Prescription: ANSWER TO CASE 1 Rp.: Pulveris pro suspensione Amoxicillini 400 mg/5 ml — 70 ml D.t.d. N. 2 S. Add cold boiled water to the bottle up to the mark and shake. Give 6.8 ml 2 times a day (every 12 hours) for 10 days with a dosing syringe. Shake before use. Store in the refrigerator.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A nurse was about to give 10 ml of a 7.5% potassium chloride solution (in an ampoule) as an intravenous push to a patient with hypokalemia.
cases.ask: 1) What is the nurse's error and what is the danger? 2) State the correct method of administration.
cases.answer: 1) An intravenous push of concentrated potassium chloride sharply raises the blood potassium concentration and creates a risk of cardiac arrest (asystole, ventricular fibrillation). 2) Potassium chloride must always be diluted (e.g., in 400–500 ml of 0.9% NaCl or 5% glucose solution) and given slowly by drip (into a peripheral vein usually not more than 10 mmol per hour), under ECG and blood potassium monitoring. 10 ml of the 7.5% solution contains ≈ 750 mg KCl ≈ 10 mmol of potassium.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A patient needs a 1:10,000 potassium permanganate solution for washing a wound. It is used at 1 liter a day for 10 days. A concentrated solution should be obtained from the pharmacy, with the daily dose in 1 tablespoon.
cases.ask: 1) Calculate the total amount of substance and the volume of the concentrated solution. 2) Write a prescription.
cases.answer: 1) 1:10,000 → 0.1 g in 1 liter; for 10 days 1.0 g. If the daily dose is 1 tablespoon (15 ml), the total volume is 15 × 10 = 150 ml. 2) Prescription: ANSWER TO CASE 3 Rp.: Kalii permanganatis 1.0 Aquae destillatae ad 150 ml M.f. solutio D.S. Dilute 1 tablespoon of the solution in 1 liter of warm boiled water and use once a day for washing the wound.
