topics.cards_title: Table 2.11. Prescribing liquid dosage forms — summary

topics.title: General pharmacology. Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of drug substances. Drugs acting on the afferent nervous system

goals.text: General pharmacology is the “grammar” of all pharmacology. When studying each drug group, we keep returning to the same questions: how the drug is absorbed, where it is distributed, how it is broken down and excreted (pharmacokinetics); which target it acts on and what effect it produces (pharmacodynamics). A student who knows these concepts can understand even a new drug logically.
The student should know:

items: the tasks and branches of pharmacology;
the routes of drug administration, the mechanisms of absorption, bioavailability and the first-pass effect;
the principles of distribution, biological barriers, biotransformation and excretion;
the main pharmacokinetic parameters (Cmax, AUC, Vd, Cl, t½, Css);
the types of drug action, drug targets, the types of receptors, and the concepts of agonist and antagonist;
the dose–effect relationship, the therapeutic index, phenomena on repeated use and drug interactions;
the classification of drugs acting on the afferent nervous system, and the mechanism and use of local anesthetics.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: calculate the time to reach steady-state concentration from the half-life;
calculate the maximum dose of local anesthetics according to the patient's weight;
write prescriptions for local anesthetics, astringents, coating agents, adsorbents and irritants.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The four stages of pharmacokinetics — **ADME**: **A**bsorption, **D**istribution, **M**etabolism (biotransformation), **E**limination (excretion). Pharmacokinetics is “the drug's journey”, pharmacodynamics is “the drug's work”.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **“Like is absorbed in like, trapped in the opposite”**: an acid is non-ionized (absorbed) in an acidic medium and ionized (trapped and excreted) in an alkaline medium. By this rule, alkalinizing the urine (sodium bicarbonate) in poisoning speeds up the excretion of **weak acids** (salicylates, phenobarbital).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Displacement from protein binding.** Drugs that are more than 90% protein-bound (warfarin, sulfonylureas, phenytoin), when given together with another strongly bound drug (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, valproate), may have a sharp rise in their free fraction: risk of bleeding or hypoglycemia. In newborns, sulfonamides and ceftriaxone can displace bilirubin from albumin and cause **bilirubin encephalopathy**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Prodrug** — a drug that is inactive itself and is converted into an active substance in the body: enalapril → enalaprilat, clopidogrel → active thiol metabolite, levodopa → dopamine, codeine → morphine (CYP2D6), prednisone → prednisolone. Some metabolites are toxic: paracetamol → N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) — hepatotoxic.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Inducers: **“Rifa, Pheno, Carba and Pheny drank, smoked and ate St John's wort”** — rifampicin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, alcohol, smoking, St John's wort. Inhibitors: **“MAKC CIMA GRAPE”** — **MA**crolides, **K**etoconazole (azoles), **C**iprofloxacin, **CIM**etidine, **A**miodarone, **GRAPE**fruit.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The “4–5 half-lives” rule:** with repeated use at a constant dose, steady-state concentration (Css) is reached after about **4–5 × t½**; when the drug is stopped, it also takes **4–5 × t½** for it to be almost completely (94–97%) eliminated from the body. 1 t½ → 50%, 2 → 75%, 3 → 87.5%, 4 → 93.75%, 5 → 96.9%.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Zero-order kinetics: **“PEA”** — **P**henytoin, **E**thanol, **A**spirin (at high doses). Zero order is a “saturated pump” that removes the same amount every hour.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: G proteins and receptors: **“QISS”** — **Q**q (α~1~, M~1~, M~3~, H~1~), **I**i (α~2~, M~2~, D~2~), **S**s (β~1~, β~2~, D~1~, H~2~, V~2~). Odd-numbered M receptors (M~1~, M~3~) — G~q~; even (M~2~) — G~i~.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Do not confuse potency with efficacy: furosemide 40 mg is **more effective** than hydrochlorothiazide (25 mg) (it produces a stronger diuresis), even though it is less potent per mg. Bumetanide (1 mg) is **more potent** than furosemide (40 mg), but their efficacy is the same.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Amide anesthetics have two “i”s in their names**: l**i**doca**i**ne, art**i**ca**i**ne, bup**i**vaca**i**ne, rop**i**vaca**i**ne, mep**i**vaca**i**ne. Esters have one “i”: procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Maximum doses differ slightly between sources (especially for procaine). Always calculate the dose in **mg/kg** and reduce it according to the patient's condition (old age, liver disease, pregnancy, heart failure). The doses of anesthetics injected into different sites at the same time **add up**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Management of systemic toxicity:** 1) stop injecting the anesthetic, call for help; 2) secure the airway, 100% oxygen; 3) for seizures — **benzodiazepines** (midazolam, diazepam); 4) **20% lipid emulsion** intravenously: 1.5 ml/kg bolus, then an infusion of 0.25 ml/kg/min; 5) in cardiac arrest — resuscitation (epinephrine in small doses; lidocaine is **not used** as an antiarrhythmic).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The procaine metabolite **PABA** **reduces** the antibacterial effect of sulfonamides (competitive antagonism). Because procaine is broken down by pseudocholinesterase, its effect and toxicity increase in patients with an atypical form of this enzyme and in those taking anticholinesterase agents.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Adsorbents also bind other drugs and reduce their absorption. Therefore, other drugs are taken **at least 1–2 hours before or after** the adsorbent.

sections.title: 1. Pharmacology as a science and its branches

blocks.text: **Pharmacology** (Gr. pharmacon — drug, logos — study) — the science that studies the interaction of chemical compounds with the living organism. Its main task is to search for new effective and safe medicines and to justify the rational use of existing ones.

blocks.title: Table 3.1. Main branches of pharmacology
head: Branch
What it studies
rows: What the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, biotransformation, excretion
What the drug does to the body: site of action, mechanism, effects
The influence of hereditary factors on drug action
The use and effects of drugs in the population
The toxic effects of substances and the treatment of poisoning
The effects of drugs in the patient's body; rational pharmacotherapy

parts.text: The four stages of pharmacokinetics — **ADME**: **A**bsorption, **D**istribution, **M**etabolism (biotransformation), **E**limination (excretion). Pharmacokinetics is “the drug's journey”, pharmacodynamics is “the drug's work”.

blocks.caption: General scheme of drug pharmacokinetics: absorption, distribution to plasma and tissues, depot, metabolism and excretion (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: 2.2. Mechanisms of absorption
**Absorption** — the passage of a drug from the site of administration into the blood. Main mechanisms:

items: **Passive diffusion** — along the concentration gradient, without energy expenditure, through the lipid membrane. The most common mechanism. Lipophilic and **non-ionized** substances pass well.
**Filtration** (through aqueous pores) — water-soluble substances of small molecular weight (up to 100–200 Da).
**Active transport** — with the help of carrier proteins, with energy (ATP) expenditure, against the gradient; it can be saturated and competitively inhibited (levodopa, iron, 5-fluorouracil).
**Facilitated diffusion** — with a carrier but along the gradient, without energy (glucose).

**Pinocytosis (endocytosis)** — engulfment of large molecules by the membrane (vitamin B~12~ — intrinsic factor complex). **Ionization and pH.** Most drugs are weak acids or bases. Their non-ionized (lipophilic) fraction crosses the membrane. The degree of ionization depends on the pH of the medium and the pKa of the substance (**Henderson–Hasselbalch equation**):
weak **acids** (acetylsalicylic acid, barbiturates) are poorly ionized in an **acidic** medium and are well absorbed;
weak **bases** (alkaloids: morphine, atropine) are poorly ionized in an **alkaline** medium.

parts.text: **“Like is absorbed in like, trapped in the opposite”**: an acid is non-ionized (absorbed) in an acidic medium and ionized (trapped and excreted) in an alkaline medium. By this rule, alkalinizing the urine (sodium bicarbonate) in poisoning speeds up the excretion of **weak acids** (salicylates, phenobarbital).

blocks.text: 2.3. Bioavailability and the first-pass effect

**Bioavailability (F)** — the fraction (%) of the administered dose that reaches the **systemic circulation** unchanged. With intravenous administration, F = 100%. With oral intake, F depends on: the dosage form, completeness of absorption, and metabolism in the intestinal wall and liver.

**First-pass effect (presystemic elimination)** — a drug absorbed from the intestine first reaches the liver through the portal vein, and part of it is broken down before reaching the systemic circulation. Drugs with a strong first-pass effect: nitroglycerin (given sublingually), propranolol, morphine, lidocaine (unsuitable for oral use), verapamil.

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Serum concentration curve of an orally administered drug: Cmax — maximum concentration, T — time to reach it; the area under the curve (AUC) reflects bioavailability (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

parts.text: **Bioequivalence** — two preparations with the same active substance (original and generic) at the same dose produce the same Cmax, Tmax and AUC in the blood. Generic preparations must prove their bioequivalence to be registered.

blocks.text: 2.4. Distribution
After absorption, the drug is distributed to the tissues through the blood. Factors affecting distribution:

items: **blood flow** (the brain, heart, kidneys and liver are saturated quickly; adipose tissue slowly);
**lipophilicity** and molecular size;
**binding to plasma proteins** (acidic drugs — to albumin, basic drugs — to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein). Only the **free (unbound) fraction** is active, is metabolized and is filtered;
**biological barriers**: the blood–brain barrier (BBB), the placental barrier, the blood–ocular and blood–testis barriers.

parts.text: **Displacement from protein binding.** Drugs that are more than 90% protein-bound (warfarin, sulfonylureas, phenytoin), when given together with another strongly bound drug (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, valproate), may have a sharp rise in their free fraction: risk of bleeding or hypoglycemia. In newborns, sulfonamides and ceftriaxone can displace bilirubin from albumin and cause **bilirubin encephalopathy**.

blocks.text: **The blood–brain barrier** — tight junctions of the endothelium of brain capillaries and the P-glycoprotein pump. Lipophilic substances (diazepam, thiopental) cross well; quaternary ammonium compounds (neostigmine, metocinium) and many antibiotics cross poorly. In inflammation (meningitis), the permeability of the barrier increases — benzylpenicillin reaches the cerebrospinal fluid.
**The placental barrier** — lipophilic, small-molecule drugs cross easily. Therefore, during pregnancy any drug is regarded as potentially dangerous.

**Volume of distribution (Vd)** — a notional volume that relates the amount of drug in the body to its plasma concentration: **Vd = D / C~0~**. Small Vd (5–15 l) — the drug is mainly in the blood (heparin, warfarin); large Vd (hundreds of liters) — the drug accumulates in the tissues (digoxin, amiodarone, chloroquine). In poisoning with drugs of large Vd, hemodialysis is ineffective.
**Depot formation** — accumulation of a drug in a tissue: thiopental — in adipose tissue, tetracyclines — in bone and teeth, iodine — in the thyroid gland, amiodarone — in fat and the lungs.
2.5. Biotransformation (metabolism)

Biotransformation takes place mainly in the **liver** (also in the intestinal wall, lungs, kidneys and blood). Its aim is to make a lipophilic substance **hydrophilic** (water-soluble) and so make its excretion easier.

parts.text: **Prodrug** — a drug that is inactive itself and is converted into an active substance in the body: enalapril → enalaprilat, clopidogrel → active thiol metabolite, levodopa → dopamine, codeine → morphine (CYP2D6), prednisone → prednisolone. Some metabolites are toxic: paracetamol → N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) — hepatotoxic.

blocks.title: Table 3.4. Inducers and inhibitors of microsomal enzymes (clinically important)
head: Inducers (reduce the effect of other drugs)

parts.text: Inducers: **“Rifa, Pheno, Carba and Pheny drank, smoked and ate St John's wort”** — rifampicin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, alcohol, smoking, St John's wort. Inhibitors: **“MAKC CIMA GRAPE”** — **MA**crolides, **K**etoconazole (azoles), **C**iprofloxacin, **CIM**etidine, **A**miodarone, **GRAPE**fruit.

Rifampicin speeds up the metabolism of oral contraceptives and can lead to **unintended pregnancy**. When clarithromycin is given together with simvastatin, the statin concentration rises and there is a risk of **rhabdomyolysis**. Ciprofloxacin can raise the theophylline concentration and lead to seizures.

blocks.text: 2.6. Excretion
Drugs are excreted mainly through the **kidneys**, and also with the **bile** through the intestine, through the lungs (volatile substances — ether, halothane), sweat, saliva and **breast milk**.
**Renal excretion** is the sum of three processes:

items: **Glomerular filtration** — small-molecule substances not bound to protein;
**Tubular secretion** (in the proximal tubule, active) — separate carriers for acids (penicillins, diuretics) and bases. Probenecid competitively inhibits penicillin secretion;
**Tubular reabsorption** (passive) — lipophilic, non-ionized substances are reabsorbed. Reabsorption can be controlled by changing the urine pH.

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Processes of drug excretion in the nephron: filtration, secretion, reabsorption (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.label: Figure 3.4
blocks.caption: Enterohepatic circulation (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: **Enterohepatic circulation** — a conjugate excreted into the intestine with the bile is broken down by intestinal bacteria, and the drug is reabsorbed. This prolongs the action of drugs (digitoxin, estrogens, morphine). Antibiotics can alter the intestinal flora and reduce the enterohepatic circulation of estrogen-containing contraceptives.

parts.text: **In renal failure**, the doses of drugs excreted unchanged mainly by the kidneys are reduced according to creatinine clearance: aminoglycosides, vancomycin, digoxin, metformin, lithium, enoxaparin. **In hepatic failure** — drugs that undergo extensive hepatic metabolism (morphine, benzodiazepines, propranolol).

blocks.text: 2.7. Main pharmacokinetic parameters

blocks.title: Table 3.5. Pharmacokinetic parameters
head: Parameter
Symbol
Meaning
rows: The highest concentration in the blood
The total amount of drug that has entered the body
The volume of plasma completely cleared of the drug per unit of time (ml/min): Cl = Vd × kel
The fraction of drug eliminated per unit of time
The time it takes for the plasma concentration to fall by half: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Cl
The state in which intake and elimination are balanced

parts.text: **The “4–5 half-lives” rule:** with repeated use at a constant dose, steady-state concentration (Css) is reached after about **4–5 × t½**; when the drug is stopped, it also takes **4–5 × t½** for it to be almost completely (94–97%) eliminated from the body. 1 t½ → 50%, 2 → 75%, 3 → 87.5%, 4 → 93.75%, 5 → 96.9%.

blocks.label: Figure 3.5
blocks.caption: Change in plasma concentration with repeated use: steady state and the therapeutic window (compiler's diagram)

blocks.text: **Loading dose** — a large initial dose for drugs with a long t½ (amiodarone, digoxin) to reach Css quickly: **Dload = Css × Vd / F**. **Maintenance dose** — to maintain Css: **Dmaint = Css × Cl × τ / F** (τ — dosing interval).
Elimination kinetics:

items: **First-order** (most drugs) — a **constant fraction** of the drug is eliminated per unit of time; t½ is constant.

**Zero-order (saturation)** — a **constant amount** is eliminated per unit of time; the enzymes are saturated. Examples: **ethanol, phenytoin, high-dose salicylates**. A small increase in dose leads to a sharp rise in concentration.

parts.text: Zero-order kinetics: **“PEA”** — **P**henytoin, **E**thanol, **A**spirin (at high doses). Zero order is a “saturated pump” that removes the same amount every hour.

blocks.text: 3.2. Molecular targets of drug action

items: **Receptors** — specialized proteins that bind endogenous ligands (mediators, hormones).
**Ion channels** — local anesthetics (Na^+^ channels), calcium antagonists (L-type Ca^2+^ channels), sulfonylureas (ATP-dependent K^+^ channels).
**Enzymes** — NSAIDs (cyclooxygenase), ACE inhibitors, neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase), statins (HMG-CoA reductase).
**Transport systems** — omeprazole (H^+^/K^+^-ATPase), digoxin (Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase), furosemide (Na^+^-K^+^-2Cl– cotransporter), antidepressants (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake).
**Nucleic acids and other targets** — cytostatics (DNA), antacids (chemical neutralization), osmotic diuretics (physicochemical action).

blocks.text: 3.3. Agonists and antagonists
**Affinity** — the ability of a substance to bind to a receptor. **Intrinsic activity** — the ability, after binding, to activate the receptor and produce a response.

blocks.text: **Types of antagonism:** competitive (can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — atropine and acetylcholine), noncompetitive (cannot be overcome), **physiological** (opposite effects through different receptors — epinephrine against histamine in anaphylaxis), **chemical** (direct binding — protamine sulfate neutralizes heparin), **physical** (adsorption — activated charcoal).
3.4. The dose–effect relationship

blocks.label: Figure 3.7
blocks.caption: The dose–effect relationship: a — potency (EC50) and efficacy (Emax), b — therapeutic index (compiler's diagram)

items: **Potency** — the smaller the dose that produces the desired effect, the more potent the drug. Its measure is **EC50** (the concentration that produces 50% of the maximal effect).
**Efficacy** — the **maximal** effect a drug can produce (**Emax**). Clinically, efficacy is more important than potency.

**Therapeutic index (TI)** = TD50 / ED50 (in animals LD50 / ED50). Drugs with a small TI (**“with a narrow therapeutic range”**): digoxin, lithium, theophylline, warfarin, aminoglycosides, phenytoin, carbamazepine — their blood concentrations are monitored.

parts.text: Do not confuse potency with efficacy: furosemide 40 mg is **more effective** than hydrochlorothiazide (25 mg) (it produces a stronger diuresis), even though it is less potent per mg. Bumetanide (1 mg) is **more potent** than furosemide (40 mg), but their efficacy is the same.

blocks.text: 3.6. Drug interactions

items: **Pharmaceutical** — outside the body, in one syringe or solution (precipitate, inactivation).
**Pharmacokinetic** — absorption (antacids reduce the absorption of tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones), distribution (displacement from proteins), metabolism (induction, inhibition), excretion.
**Pharmacodynamic** — **synergism** (additive — the sum; potentiation — more than the sum) and **antagonism**.

parts.text: Examples of dangerous interactions: MAO inhibitors + tyramine-containing foods (cheese) → hypertensive crisis; SSRIs + tramadol or MAO inhibitors → **serotonin syndrome**; sildenafil + nitrates → severe hypotension; warfarin + NSAIDs → bleeding; ACE inhibitors + potassium-sparing diuretics → hyperkalemia.

blocks.text: 3.7. Factors affecting drug action

items: **Age.** In newborns, liver enzymes (glucuronosyltransferase) are immature — chloramphenicol (Levomycetin) causes the “gray baby syndrome”; the BBB is permeable; renal function is low. In the elderly, renal and hepatic clearance decrease, adipose tissue increases (the Vd of lipophilic drugs rises), and CNS sensitivity increases.
**Pregnancy and lactation.** Teratogenic drugs: thalidomide, isotretinoin, warfarin, valproate, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines, methotrexate.

**Pharmacogenetics.** Slow and fast **acetylators** (isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide); **G6PD deficiency** (primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin → hemolysis); the atypical form of **pseudocholinesterase** (suxamethonium → prolonged apnea); CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers (codeine → much more morphine is formed — respiratory arrest in children).
**Diseases** (renal, hepatic, heart failure), diet, circadian rhythms, the placebo effect.

blocks.text: 3.8. Adverse effects

items: **Type A** (dose-related, predictable) — an exaggeration of the pharmacological effect: insulin — hypoglycemia, anticoagulant — bleeding.
**Type B** (not dose-related, unexpected) — **allergic reactions** (anaphylaxis, Stevens–Johnson syndrome) and **idiosyncrasy** (an unusual response associated with a hereditary enzyme defect).

**Toxic effects** — nephrotoxicity (aminoglycosides), ototoxicity (aminoglycosides, furosemide), hepatotoxicity (paracetamol, isoniazid), cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin), myelotoxicity (cytostatics, chloramphenicol).
**Teratogenic, embryotoxic, fetotoxic, mutagenic and carcinogenic** effects.
**Dysbiosis, superinfection** — with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

blocks.text: 3.9. General principles of treating acute drug poisoning

items: **Stopping absorption:** gastric lavage (within 1 hour, in a conscious patient, in the absence of corrosive substances), **activated charcoal** (1 g/kg), washing the skin and eyes.

**Speeding up the elimination of absorbed poison:** forced diuresis, alkalinization of the urine (salicylates, phenobarbital), hemodialysis (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates), hemosorption.
**Antidote therapy** (specific neutralization).
**Symptomatic support of vital functions:** airway, breathing, circulation, stopping seizures.

sections.title: 4. Drugs acting on the afferent nervous system

blocks.text: **Afferent (sensory) nerves** — fibers that carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. The drugs of this group are divided into two large groups.

blocks.text: 4.1. Local anesthetics
**Local anesthetics** — drugs that **reversibly** abolish pain sensation (and later other sensations) at the site of application. They do not cause loss of consciousness.

**History.** In 1879, the Russian scientist **V.K. Anrep** discovered the local anesthetic effect of cocaine; in 1884, K. Koller introduced it into ophthalmology. In 1905, A. Einhorn synthesized **procaine (Novocain)**, which is less toxic than cocaine; in 1943, N. Löfgren created the first amide anesthetic — **lidocaine**.

**Chemical structure.** The molecule consists of three parts: **a lipophilic aromatic ring** — **an intermediate chain (ester or amide bond)** — **a hydrophilic amine group**. Two groups are distinguished according to the intermediate bond.

blocks.label: Figure 3.9
blocks.caption: Chemical structure of local anesthetics: cocaine, novocaine, dicaine (esters), lidocaine and trimecaine (amides) (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.title: Table 3.12. Differences between the ester and amide groups
head: Feature
Esters (procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine)
Amides (lidocaine, articaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, mepivacaine)
rows: In the blood by pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase), rapid
In the liver by microsomal enzymes, slower

parts.text: **Amide anesthetics have two “i”s in their names**: l**i**doca**i**ne, art**i**ca**i**ne, bup**i**vaca**i**ne, rop**i**vaca**i**ne, mep**i**vaca**i**ne. Esters have one “i”: procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine.

blocks.text: **Mechanism of action.** Local anesthetics block the **voltage-gated sodium channels** of the nerve fiber membrane from the inside. Sodium ions stop entering the cell, no action potential is generated, and impulse conduction is blocked.

blocks.label: Figure 3.10
blocks.caption: Effect of anesthetics on conduction of excitation along a nerve fiber: A — normal Na^+^ entry; B — anesthetic molecules block the sodium channels (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: Important details of the mechanism:

items: The anesthetic crosses the membrane **in the non-ionized (base) form**, and inside the cell it blocks the channel **in the ionized (cationic) form**.
In inflamed tissue (pus), the medium is **acidic**, the anesthetic is more ionized and crosses the membrane poorly — anesthesia is **weak**.
Channels are blocked better in the **open and inactivated state** (**“use-dependent block”**) — pain fibers that conduct impulses frequently are blocked first.

**Sensitivity of fibers:** thin unmyelinated C fibers and A-delta fibers (pain, temperature) are blocked first, then touch and pressure, and **motor** (thick A-alpha) fibers last. Order of loss of sensations: **pain → temperature → touch → deep pressure → motor function**.

parts.text: **Adding a vasoconstrictor.** If **epinephrine** (adrenaline, usually 1:100,000 – 1:200,000) is added to a local anesthetic solution: 1) the blood vessels constrict, the anesthetic is absorbed slowly — the effect is **prolonged**; 2) less enters the blood — **systemic toxicity decreases**, and the maximum dose is increased; 3) bleeding decreases. However, epinephrine-containing solutions are **not used** for anesthesia of the **fingers, auricle, tip of the nose and penis** (end arteries — risk of necrosis), in severe heart disease, thyrotoxicosis and in patients taking MAO inhibitors.

Always calculate the dose in **mg/kg** and reduce it according to the patient's condition (old age, liver disease, pregnancy, heart failure). The doses of anesthetics injected into different sites at the same time **add up**.

blocks.text: 4.4. Systemic toxicity of local anesthetics
When the anesthetic accidentally enters a **vessel** or the dose is exceeded, a systemic toxic effect develops (LAST — local anesthetic systemic toxicity).

items: **CNS signs** (first): numbness of the lips and tongue, a metallic taste in the mouth, tinnitus, dizziness, restlessness, speech disturbance, muscle twitching → **seizures** → CNS depression, coma, respiratory arrest.
**Cardiovascular signs:** bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmias, **cardiac arrest** (typical of bupivacaine — it dissociates from sodium channels very slowly).

parts.text: **Management of systemic toxicity:** 1) stop injecting the anesthetic, call for help; 2) secure the airway, 100% oxygen; 3) for seizures — **benzodiazepines** (midazolam, diazepam); 4) **20% lipid emulsion** intravenously: 1.5 ml/kg bolus, then an infusion of 0.25 ml/kg/min; 5) in cardiac arrest — resuscitation (epinephrine in small doses; lidocaine is **not used** as an antiarrhythmic).

blocks.text: **Allergic reactions** are typical mainly of esters (PABA metabolite). Allergy to amides is very rare; it is usually due to a preservative (methylparaben) or sulfites (in epinephrine-containing solutions).

parts.text: The procaine metabolite **PABA** **reduces** the antibacterial effect of sulfonamides (competitive antagonism). Because procaine is broken down by pseudocholinesterase, its effect and toxicity increase in patients with an atypical form of this enzyme and in those taking anticholinesterase agents.

blocks.text: 4.5. Astringents

**Astringents** **partly and reversibly denature** proteins on the surface of a mucous membrane or wound and form a thin protective film. As a result, sensory nerve endings are protected, pain decreases, the vessels constrict, and exudation and inflammation decrease.

items: **Organic:** tannin (5–10% solution — for rinsing the mouth, in burns), oak bark decoction, infusions of chamomile, sage and St John's wort, blackcurrant berries.

**Inorganic (metal salts):** basic bismuth nitrate, bismuth tripotassium dicitrate (De-Nol — for gastric ulcer, topic 12), zinc sulfate (eye drops), zinc oxide, aluminum potassium sulfate (alum), lead acetate, silver nitrate (astringent at low concentration, caustic at high concentration).

parts.text: The effect of metal salts depends on concentration: at **low** concentration — astringent, at **moderate** — irritant, at **high** — caustic (necrosis). For example, silver nitrate 0.05–0.1% is astringent, 2–5% is caustic (excess granulation tissue, warts).

blocks.text: 4.6. Coating agents
**Coating agents** form colloidal solutions in water, cover the mucous membrane and protect it from irritation. They have no resorptive effect.

items: starch mucilage, flaxseed mucilage, marshmallow root mucilage, salep;

aluminum hydroxide, magnesium trisilicate, Almagel (topic 12). Uses: gastritis, gastric ulcer, enteritis, colitis; together with irritant drugs (chloral hydrate) — to soften their local effect; in poisoning — to reduce absorption.

blocks.text: 4.7. Adsorbents (enterosorbents)
**Adsorbents** — water-insoluble, chemically inert powders with a large surface area. They bind gases, toxins, bacteria and drug substances on their surface.

blocks.title: Table 3.16. Main adsorbents
head: Preparation
Property
Use
rows: The surface of 1 g is up to 1000 m^2^
Acute poisoning (1 g/kg), dyspepsia, flatulence; binds lithium, iron, alcohols, acids and alkalis poorly
A natural aluminosilicate; also coats the mucous membrane
Sweating of the skin, dermatitis (in powders and pastes)

parts.text: Adsorbents also bind other drugs and reduce their absorption. Therefore, other drugs are taken **at least 1–2 hours before or after** the adsorbent.

blocks.text: 4.8. Irritants
**Irritants** stimulate sensory nerve endings in the skin and mucous membranes. Their effect is mainly **reflex**:

items: **“Distracting” effect** — excitation from the skin competes in the spinal cord with pain impulses coming from internal organs (**gate control theory**), thereby reducing pain; endorphins and enkephalins are released.
**Trophic effect** — blood circulation and trophism improve in the internal organs belonging to the same segment as the irritated skin area (according to the **Zakharyin–Head zones**).
**Reflex stimulating effect** — ammonia vapor stimulates the trigeminal nerve endings in the nasal mucosa and reflexly stimulates the respiratory and vasomotor centers (in fainting).

blocks.text: 5.2. Practical application of clinical pharmacokinetics

parts.text: **Knowing the time to reach steady state has practical importance.** The t½ of digoxin is ≈ 36–48 hours — at an ordinary dose, steady state is reached after 7–10 days; if a rapid effect is needed, a **loading dose** is given. The t½ of amiodarone is several weeks, so treatment is started with a loading dose, and its effect persists for months after it is stopped. In contrast, drugs with a short t½ (adenosine — less than 10 seconds) are used only as a bolus, for an immediate effect.

skills.title: Skill 1. Algorithm for calculating the maximum volume of a local anesthetic

items: Determine the patient's weight (kg).
Choose the maximum dose (mg/kg) of the anesthetic for the solution without or with epinephrine.
Maximum dose (mg) = weight × mg/kg (but not exceeding the absolute maximum dose).
Convert the solution concentration to mg/ml (percentage × 10).
Maximum volume (ml) = maximum dose (mg) / concentration (mg/ml). **Example:** a 60 kg patient, 1% lidocaine without epinephrine. 60 × 4.5 = 270 mg; 1% = 10 mg/ml; 270 / 10 = **27 ml**.

skills.title: Skill 2. Calculating the time to reach steady-state concentration

items: Determine the t½ of the drug.
Time to reach Css ≈ 4–5 × t½.
Time for complete elimination after the drug is stopped ≈ 4–5 × t½. **Example:** t½ = 6 hours → Css after 24–30 hours.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 55-year-old patient (70 kg) came to outpatient surgery to have a lipoma removed from the forearm. The surgeon wants to use 1% lidocaine with epinephrine for infiltration anesthesia. After 25 ml had been injected during the procedure, the patient reported numbness of the tongue, a metallic taste in the mouth and ringing in the ears, and then his hands began to tremble.
cases.ask: 1) What complication has developed? 2) What is the maximum dose for this patient? Has the dose been exceeded? 3) What emergency measures are needed?
cases.answer: 1) Systemic toxicity of the local anesthetic (early CNS signs) — the solution probably partly entered a vessel. 2) The maximum dose of lidocaine with epinephrine is 7 mg/kg → 70 × 7 = 490 mg ≈ 49 ml of 1% solution. The 250 mg injected did not exceed the maximum dose, so the main cause is intravascular injection (injection without an aspiration test). 3) Stop the injection, call for help, give 100% oxygen, establish intravenous access; if seizures begin — midazolam or diazepam; if the condition worsens — 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 ml/kg bolus and infusion; ECG and BP monitoring. Prevention: an aspiration test before each injection, injecting the solution slowly in small portions.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 32-year-old woman is taking rifampicin for tuberculosis. She also takes a combined oral contraceptive. Two months after the start of treatment, pregnancy was diagnosed.
cases.ask: 1) What is the pharmacological cause of the pregnancy? 2) What measures should have been taken?
cases.answer: 1) Rifampicin is a strong inducer of hepatic microsomal enzymes (CYP3A4); it accelerated the metabolism of estrogens and progestins and lowered their blood concentrations — the contraceptive became ineffective. 2) Non-hormonal contraception (intrauterine device, condom) should have been recommended during treatment with rifampicin and for at least 4 weeks after it. This example shows the need to check for pharmacokinetic interactions every time a prescription is written.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 3-year-old child (15 kg) swallowed an unknown number of tablets from his grandfather's medicine box at home; 40 minutes have passed since the incident. The child is conscious and his condition is satisfactory for now. The box contained digoxin and amlodipine tablets.
cases.ask: 1) According to the general principles of treating poisoning, what are the first measures? 2) What is the specific antidote in digoxin poisoning? 3) Why must such a child be observed for a long time?
cases.answer: 1) Call emergency services; activated charcoal to reduce absorption (1 g/kg = 15 g, most effective within 1 hour of the incident); monitoring of vital signs (pulse, BP, ECG); determining blood potassium and digoxin levels. 2) Fab fragments of digoxin-specific antibodies; in addition, correction of arrhythmias and hyperkalemia. 3) Digoxin has a large volume of distribution and saturates the tissues slowly, and amlodipine has a long t½ (30–50 hours) — the toxic effect may intensify after several hours; therefore the child must be monitored in hospital for at least 24 hours.

topics.cards_title: Table 3.19. General pharmacology and drugs acting on the afferent nervous system — summary

topics.title: Drugs acting on M- and M-N-cholinergic receptors

goals.text: Drugs acting on the cholinergic system appear in almost every area of clinical medicine: treatment of glaucoma and myasthenia gravis, postoperative intestinal atony, bradycardia, bronchial obstruction, intestinal and renal colic, urinary incontinence, Alzheimer's disease. Poisoning with organophosphorus compounds (insecticides) and atropine poisoning are classic emergencies. This topic is the foundation of autonomic nervous system pharmacology.
The student should know:

items: the structure of efferent innervation, the physiology of the cholinergic synapse and the types of cholinergic receptors;
the classification, mechanism, pharmacological effects, uses and adverse effects of M-cholinomimetics, anticholinesterase agents and M-cholinergic blockers;
the clinical picture and treatment of poisoning with organophosphorus compounds, muscarine and atropine.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for preparations such as pilocarpine, neostigmine, pyridostigmine, galantamine, atropine, platyphylline, ipratropium and tropicamide;
distinguish drugs that cause miosis from those that cause mydriasis;
recognize OPC and atropine poisoning by their clinical signs and draw up a treatment plan.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Acetylcholine** is the mediator of all **preganglionic** fibers, all **parasympathetic postganglionic** fibers, **somatic** nerves and the sympathetic fibers innervating the sweat glands. Norepinephrine is the mediator of most **sympathetic postganglionic** fibers only.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: M-cholinomimetic effect — **“DUMBELS”**: **D**iarrhea, **U**rination, **M**iosis, **B**radycardia and **B**ronchorrhea/**B**ronchospasm, **E**mesis (vomiting), **L**acrimation, **S**alivation and **S**weating (secretion).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: General **contraindications** to M-cholinomimetics and anticholinesterase agents: bronchial asthma, bradycardia and AV block, ischemic heart disease, gastric ulcer, epilepsy, pregnancy (uterine tone increases), **mechanical** obstruction of the urinary and intestinal tracts (peritonitis, intestinal obstruction).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Quaternary ammonium compounds** (neostigmine, pyridostigmine, metocinium, ipratropium, hyoscine butylbromide) carry a permanent positive charge: they are **poorly absorbed** from the intestine, **do not cross the BBB** and do not act on the CNS. **Tertiary amines** (physostigmine, galantamine, atropine, scopolamine) are well absorbed and act **on the CNS**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Myasthenic and cholinergic crisis** — both present with muscle weakness and respiratory failure. In a myasthenic crisis, the anticholinesterase drug is **insufficient**; in a cholinergic crisis — **excessive** (DUMBELS signs: miosis, salivation, bradycardia, diarrhea, fasciculations). They used to be distinguished by the edrophonium test; now the airway is secured first and anticholinesterase agents are temporarily stopped.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Causes of death in OPC poisoning** — respiratory failure: bronchorrhea and bronchospasm + paralysis of the respiratory muscles + depression of the respiratory center.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Treatment of OPC poisoning — **“A-R-D”**: **A**tropine (blocks M), **R**eactivator (restores the enzyme), **D**iazepam (stops seizures). Atropine does not eliminate the N effect (muscle paralysis) — only a reactivator can do this.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Dose dependence** of atropine effects: the most sensitive are the salivary, bronchial and sweat glands (0.5 mg) → eye and heart (1–2 mg) → bladder and intestine (2–5 mg) → gastric secretion (the highest dose; that is why atropine is ineffective in gastric ulcer and has many adverse effects). At doses above 10 mg — CNS disturbances.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: A pupil dilated by atropine stays dilated for **7–10 days** (and even longer); for diagnostic purposes, short-acting tropicamide (4–6 hours) or cyclopentolate (up to 24 hours) is now preferred. **Contraindications** to atropine and other M-cholinergic blockers: **angle-closure glaucoma**, prostatic hypertrophy (urinary retention), tachyarrhythmias, intestinal atony and paralytic ileus, severe heart failure, hot climate and febrile children (hyperthermia).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Atropine poisoning, in the classic English phrase: **“Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, full as a flask”** (hyperthermia, dry skin, flushing, mydriasis and inability to see near objects, delirium, urinary retention).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Eye muscles: **“Circular — parasympathetic, radial — sympathetic”**. The circular (sphincter) muscle constricts the pupil through M receptors; the radial (dilator) muscle dilates it through alpha-1. M blockers cause **both mydriasis and cycloplegia**; phenylephrine — mydriasis only.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Conclusion of the experiment: atropine abolishes only spasm induced **through M-cholinergic receptors** (**neurotropic antispasmodic**). Papaverine and drotaverine act directly on the smooth muscle cell (**myotropic antispasmodics**) and relax spasm of any cause. Platyphylline has both mechanisms.

sections.title: 1. Efferent innervation and the cholinergic synapse

blocks.text: 1.1. Structure of the autonomic nervous system

The efferent nervous system consists of the **somatic** (skeletal muscles) and **autonomic** (internal organs, vessels, glands) parts. The autonomic nervous system is divided into the **parasympathetic** and **sympathetic** divisions.

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: General scheme of cholinergic and adrenergic innervation (C, Th, L, S — spinal cord segments) (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

parts.text: **Acetylcholine** is the mediator of all **preganglionic** fibers, all **parasympathetic postganglionic** fibers, **somatic** nerves and the sympathetic fibers innervating the sweat glands. Norepinephrine is the mediator of most **sympathetic postganglionic** fibers only.

blocks.text: 1.2. How the cholinergic synapse works

items: **Synthesis:** in the cytoplasm of the nerve ending, acetylcholine (ACh) is formed from choline and acetyl-CoA with the participation of **choline acetyltransferase**. Choline is taken back up into the cell by a special carrier (hemicholinium blocks this process).
**Storage:** ACh is collected into vesicles (vesamicol blocks this).

**Release:** when a nerve impulse arrives, Ca^2+^ enters, the vesicles fuse with the membrane and release ACh into the synaptic cleft (exocytosis). **Botulinum toxin** cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks ACh release.
**Action on receptors:** ACh stimulates the postsynaptic M or N cholinergic receptors.

**Inactivation:** in the synaptic cleft, **acetylcholinesterase** (true cholinesterase) breaks ACh down into choline and acetic acid within a few milliseconds. Blood plasma and the liver contain **butyrylcholinesterase** (pseudocholinesterase).

blocks.text: **M-cholinomimetics** — drugs that stimulate M-cholinergic receptors **directly**. They reproduce the muscarinic effects of ACh.
2.1. Pilocarpine
**Pilocarpine** — an alkaloid of the South American plant Pilocarpus jaborandi, a tertiary amine. It is used mainly **topically in ophthalmology**.

items: **Miosis** — the pupillary constrictor muscle contracts.

**Lowering of intraocular pressure** — the iris becomes thinner and stretched, the anterior chamber angle opens, and outflow of fluid into Schlemm's canal improves; the ciliary muscle contracts and pulls the trabecular meshwork.

**Spasm of accommodation** — the eye adjusts to near vision, and distance vision temporarily worsens. **Uses:** glaucoma (especially in an attack of angle-closure glaucoma), retinal artery thrombosis, constriction of a pupil dilated by atropine; orally — for **xerostomia** (dry mouth) in Sjögren's syndrome and after radiation.

parts.text: **Acute attack of angle-closure glaucoma** — an emergency: severe eye pain, redness, sharp loss of vision, “colored halos”, headache, vomiting. Treatment: pilocarpine 1–2% drops (every 15 minutes), acetazolamide orally or intravenously, osmotic diuretics, beta-blocker drops (timolol); then laser iridotomy. **M-cholinergic blockers (atropine) are absolutely contraindicated** in such patients.

blocks.text: 2.2. Aceclidine and bethanechol

**Aceclidine** — a synthetic M-cholinomimetic. It is less irritating than pilocarpine. It is used as eye drops in glaucoma and given subcutaneously for postoperative **atony of the intestine and bladder**.
**Bethanechol** — is not broken down by cholinesterase and acts mainly on the intestine and bladder; for postoperative urinary retention.

parts.text: General **contraindications** to M-cholinomimetics and anticholinesterase agents: bronchial asthma, bradycardia and AV block, ischemic heart disease, gastric ulcer, epilepsy, pregnancy (uterine tone increases), **mechanical** obstruction of the urinary and intestinal tracts (peritonitis, intestinal obstruction).

blocks.text: 2.3. Muscarine poisoning

Some mushrooms (Inocybe and Clitocybe species; little in fly agaric) contain **muscarine**. Poisoning begins after 15–30 minutes: profuse salivation, sweating, lacrimation, miosis, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, colicky abdominal pain, bradycardia, hypotension. **Antidote — atropine** (intravenously or intramuscularly, until the signs disappear).

**Anticholinesterase agents** inhibit acetylcholinesterase. As a result, ACh is not broken down in the synapses, it accumulates, and the action on **all** cholinergic receptors (M and N) increases. Their effect therefore consists of **muscarinic** (DUMBELS) and **nicotinic** (fibrillary twitching of skeletal muscles, improved neuromuscular transmission, at high doses — depolarizing block) components.

parts.text: **Quaternary ammonium compounds** (neostigmine, pyridostigmine, metocinium, ipratropium, hyoscine butylbromide) carry a permanent positive charge: they are **poorly absorbed** from the intestine, **do not cross the BBB** and do not act on the CNS. **Tertiary amines** (physostigmine, galantamine, atropine, scopolamine) are well absorbed and act **on the CNS**.

**Myasthenia gravis** — an autoimmune disease in which autoantibodies against N~M~ cholinergic receptors are formed: pathological fatigability of the extraocular muscles (ptosis, diplopia), the muscles of swallowing and speech, and the limb muscles. Treatment: pyridostigmine (symptomatic), glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, thymectomy. In a severe **myasthenic crisis** — respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation, plasmapheresis or immunoglobulin.

**Myasthenic and cholinergic crisis** — both present with muscle weakness and respiratory failure. In a myasthenic crisis, the anticholinesterase drug is **insufficient**; in a cholinergic crisis — **excessive** (DUMBELS signs: miosis, salivation, bradycardia, diarrhea, fasciculations). They used to be distinguished by the edrophonium test; now the airway is secured first and anticholinesterase agents are temporarily stopped.

blocks.text: 3.2. Irreversible anticholinesterase agents — organophosphorus compounds (OPCs)

OPCs **phosphorylate** the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase; the bond is very strong. Over time, the enzyme–OPC complex **“ages”** (an alkyl group is cleaved off) and can then no longer be restored even by reactivators. Enzyme activity recovers only when new enzyme is synthesized (weeks).

Of the OPCs, only **Armin** and **ecothiopate** (in glaucoma) have been used as drugs; their main importance lies in **poisoning**: agricultural insecticides (trichlorfon, malathion, dichlorvos, parathion), household insecticides and chemical warfare agents (sarin, soman, tabun, VX).
3.3. Acute OPC poisoning
OPCs are rapidly absorbed through the skin, mucous membranes, and the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

blocks.title: Table 4.6. Clinical picture of OPC poisoning
head: Effect
Signs
rows: Miosis (“pinpoint pupils”), blurred vision, profuse salivation, sweating, lacrimation, bronchorrhea and bronchospasm (resembling pulmonary edema), bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal colic, involuntary urination
Muscle fasciculations (fibrillary twitching), seizures, then muscle weakness and paralysis, paralysis of the respiratory muscles; tachycardia and hypertension (through the ganglia) may occur
Restlessness, fear, headache, ataxia, seizures, coma, paralysis of the respiratory center

parts.text: **Causes of death in OPC poisoning** — respiratory failure: bronchorrhea and bronchospasm + paralysis of the respiratory muscles + depression of the respiratory center.

blocks.text: Treatment:

items: **Removing the poison:** remove the victim from the contaminated environment, take off the clothes, wash the skin with soap and water (or with 2–5% sodium bicarbonate solution); if ingested — gastric lavage, activated charcoal. The medical worker must protect himself or herself (gloves).
**Securing breathing:** suctioning the airway, oxygen, if necessary intubation and mechanical ventilation. Suxamethonium is **not used** (prolonged apnea).

**Atropine** — the main treatment (eliminates the M effect): for adults **2–4 mg intravenously**, then every 5–10 minutes **doubling the dose** until signs of **“atropinization”** appear (cessation of bronchial secretion, disappearance of crackles in the lungs, heart rate above 80, dry skin). In severe poisoning, the daily dose may reach tens or even hundreds of milligrams. Miosis is not a criterion of atropinization.

**Cholinesterase reactivators** — pralidoxime, dipyroxime (trimedoxime), alloxime: they detach the phosphoryl group from the enzyme and restore it. They also act on the **N effect** (muscle weakness). They are effective before the enzyme “ages”, i.e. **as early as possible** (in the first hours).
**Against seizures** — diazepam or midazolam.

parts.text: Treatment of OPC poisoning — **“A-R-D”**: **A**tropine (blocks M), **R**eactivator (restores the enzyme), **D**iazepam (stops seizures). Atropine does not eliminate the N effect (muscle paralysis) — only a reactivator can do this.

blocks.text: **M-cholinergic blockers** block M-cholinergic receptors **competitively** and eliminate the effects of ACh and M-cholinomimetics. Their effect resembles “switching off” the parasympathetic innervation.
4.1. Atropine

**Atropine** — an alkaloid of plants of the nightshade family: belladonna (Atropa belladonna), henbane (Hyoscyamus niger), jimsonweed (Datura stramonium). A tertiary amine; it nonselectively blocks all types of M-cholinergic receptors.

Tone and peristalsis decrease (antispasmodic), salivary and gastric secretion decrease
The bladder detrusor and urinary tract relax — urinary retention may occur
Secretion of the salivary, sweat, bronchial and lacrimal glands decreases sharply; loss of sweating raises body temperature
At therapeutic doses — little; at toxic doses — excitation, hallucinations, delirium, then depression

parts.text: **Dose dependence** of atropine effects: the most sensitive are the salivary, bronchial and sweat glands (0.5 mg) → eye and heart (1–2 mg) → bladder and intestine (2–5 mg) → gastric secretion (the highest dose; that is why atropine is ineffective in gastric ulcer and has many adverse effects). At doses above 10 mg — CNS disturbances.

blocks.text: Uses of atropine:

items: **Bradycardia and AV block** (with increased vagal tone, in the first hours of myocardial infarction): 0.5–1 mg intravenously every 3–5 minutes, up to 3 mg in total;
**premedication** — before anesthesia, to reduce salivary and bronchial secretion and prevent reflex bradycardia (glycopyrronium is now used more often);
**OPC and muscarine poisoning**, overdose of anticholinesterase agents;
**smooth muscle spasms** — renal and biliary colic, intestinal colic (platyphylline and hyoscine butylbromide are often preferred);
**ophthalmology** — examining the fundus and determining refraction (in children), **in iritis and iridocyclitis** (to dilate the pupil, prevent synechiae and rest the ciliary muscle);
when reversing nondepolarizing muscle relaxants with neostigmine — for protection against the M effects of neostigmine.

parts.text: A pupil dilated by atropine stays dilated for **7–10 days** (and even longer); for diagnostic purposes, short-acting tropicamide (4–6 hours) or cyclopentolate (up to 24 hours) is now preferred. **Contraindications** to atropine and other M-cholinergic blockers: **angle-closure glaucoma**, prostatic hypertrophy (urinary retention), tachyarrhythmias, intestinal atony and paralytic ileus, severe heart failure, hot climate and febrile children (hyperthermia).

blocks.text: 4.2. Atropine poisoning
Poisoning is often seen in children who eat the berries and seeds of belladonna, jimsonweed and henbane, and also with drug overdose.

**Clinical picture:** dryness of the skin and mucous membranes, difficulty swallowing, hoarseness, **flushing** of the skin of the face and neck, **hyperthermia** (especially in children), marked **mydriasis** and photophobia, inability to see near objects, **tachycardia**, urinary retention, intestinal atony; CNS excitation — restlessness, speech and motor excitation, **hallucinations**, delirium, seizures; in severe cases — coma, paralysis of the respiratory center.

parts.text: Atropine poisoning, in the classic English phrase: **“Hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, full as a flask”** (hyperthermia, dry skin, flushing, mydriasis and inability to see near objects, delirium, urinary retention).

blocks.text: Treatment:

items: Gastric lavage (useful even late, because atropine slows intestinal motility), activated charcoal.
**Antidote — physostigmine** (a tertiary amine that enters the CNS) 0.5–2 mg intravenously, slowly; it eliminates central and peripheral signs. Neostigmine acts only on peripheral signs.
For agitation and seizures — **diazepam** (phenothiazines are contraindicated — they themselves have M-blocking activity).
For hyperthermia — physical cooling (ice, wet sponging).
For urinary retention — catheterization; for respiratory disturbance — mechanical ventilation.

parts.text: **“Anticholinergic burden” in the elderly.** Many drugs have M-blocking properties: tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), first-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine, Dimedrol), phenothiazines, oxybutynin, trihexyphenidyl. In the elderly, their combined effect causes **cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, urinary retention, constipation** and attacks of glaucoma. Such drugs should be prescribed to the elderly as little as possible (Beers criteria).

parts.text: Eye muscles: **“Circular — parasympathetic, radial — sympathetic”**. The circular (sphincter) muscle constricts the pupil through M receptors; the radial (dilator) muscle dilates it through alpha-1. M blockers cause **both mydriasis and cycloplegia**; phenylephrine — mydriasis only.

sections.title: 5. Laboratory class: studying the antispasmodic effect of M-cholinergic blockers

blocks.text: This section corresponds to the 5th-semester class “Laboratory study of the antispasmodic effect of M-cholinergic blockers”.
**Essence of the experiment.** An isolated segment of intestine (usually guinea pig ileum) is placed in warm (37 °C) oxygenated Tyrode's solution, and its contractions are recorded.

items: Baseline contractions are recorded.
**Acetylcholine** is added to the bath — the intestine contracts strongly (tone and amplitude increase).
After washing, **atropine** is added to the bath and then acetylcholine is given again — the contracting effect of ACh **weakens or disappears**.
It is shown that the block can be overcome by increasing the ACh dose — a sign of **competitive antagonism** (the dose–effect curve shifts to the right, Emax is unchanged).
For comparison, a spasm caused by **barium chloride** (a direct myotropic contractor) is not abolished by atropine but is abolished by **papaverine** (a myotropic antispasmodic).

parts.text: Conclusion of the experiment: atropine abolishes only spasm induced **through M-cholinergic receptors** (**neurotropic antispasmodic**). Papaverine and drotaverine act directly on the smooth muscle cell (**myotropic antispasmodics**) and relax spasm of any cause. Platyphylline has both mechanisms.

parts.text: **The combination of neostigmine + atropine** is used to reverse the residual effect of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants (rocuronium, vecuronium): neostigmine accumulates ACh at the neuromuscular junction and restores muscle strength, while atropine (or glycopyrronium) prevents its M effects such as bradycardia, bronchorrhea and salivation. The modern specific antidote for rocuronium is **sugammadex**.

skills.title: Skill 1. Algorithm of emergency care for a patient poisoned with OPCs

items: Protect yourself (gloves, mask) and remove the patient from the contaminated environment.
Take off the clothes, wash the skin with soap and plenty of water.
Clear the airway and give oxygen; if necessary, intubate (without suxamethonium).
Establish intravenous access; **atropine 2–4 mg intravenously**, doubling the dose every 5–10 minutes until atropinization (dry bronchi, HR > 80).
Give a **cholinesterase reactivator** (pralidoxime or dipyroxime) as early as possible.
For seizures — diazepam 10 mg intravenously.
If ingested (after the airway has been secured) — gastric lavage, activated charcoal.
Determine serum cholinesterase activity and observe for at least 24–48 hours (delayed conditions, “intermediate syndrome”).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 45-year-old farmer was brought to the emergency department 2 hours after spraying insecticide in a cotton field. Complaints: blurred vision, shortness of breath, nausea. On examination: pinpoint pupils, profuse salivation and sweating, numerous moist crackles in the lungs, HR 48/min, BP 90/60 mm Hg, fibrillary twitching of the face and arm muscles.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) Divide the signs into M, N and central effects. 3) Draw up a treatment plan.
cases.answer: 1) Acute poisoning with an organophosphorus compound (insecticide). 2) M signs: miosis, salivation and sweating, bronchorrhea (moist crackles), bradycardia, hypotension, nausea; N signs: muscle fasciculations; central: mild so far (seizures and coma may follow). 3) Remove the clothes, wash the skin with soap; oxygen, airway toilet; atropine 2–4 mg intravenously, doubling the dose every 5–10 minutes until bronchial secretion stops and HR > 80; pralidoxime (or dipyroxime) as early as possible; diazepam for seizures; monitoring in the intensive care unit.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 4-year-old child ate jimsonweed seeds growing in the village. An hour later the child is restless and hallucinating; the skin is dry and red, temperature 39.2 °C, the pupils are dilated and unreactive to light, HR 160/min, and he has not urinated for 6 hours.
cases.ask: 1) What kind of poisoning is this? 2) The antidote and the reason for choosing it. 3) Which drugs are contraindicated?
cases.answer: 1) Poisoning with atropine-like (anticholinergic) alkaloids. 2) Physostigmine — being a tertiary amine, it crosses the BBB and eliminates central (delirium, hallucinations) and peripheral signs; in children 0.02 mg/kg intravenously, slowly (under ECG monitoring). In addition: gastric lavage, activated charcoal, physical cooling, bladder catheterization, diazepam for agitation. 3) Phenothiazines (chlorpromazine), diphenhydramine (Dimedrol), tricyclic antidepressants — they themselves have M-cholinergic blocking properties and worsen the poisoning.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 70-year-old man was prescribed diphenhydramine (Dimedrol) for insomnia and oxybutynin for overactive bladder; in addition, he takes amitriptyline for depression. In recent days, his relatives have noticed confusion, memory impairment, constipation and difficulty urinating. He has a history of prostatic adenoma.
cases.ask: 1) What is the cause of this condition? 2) What would you recommend?
cases.answer: 1) Anticholinergic burden — all three drugs (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, amitriptyline) have M-cholinergic blocking activity; in the elderly, their combined effect has caused delirium, cognitive impairment, constipation and, against the background of prostatic adenoma, urinary retention. 2) Stop diphenhydramine (sleep hygiene, if necessary drugs with little M-blocking activity); replace amitriptyline with an SSRI (sertraline); consider the beta-3 adrenomimetic mirabegron, which has no M-blocking activity, instead of oxybutynin; urologist consultation for the prostatic adenoma; regular review of all prescribed drugs.

topics.title: Drugs acting on N-cholinergic receptors

goals.text: N-cholinergic receptors play a decisive role in two places: **in the autonomic ganglia** (NN) and **at the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscles** (NM). The drugs acting on these receptors are the main drugs of modern anesthesiology (muscle relaxants), smoking cessation drugs (cytisine, varenicline) and ganglionic blockers of historical importance. Working with muscle relaxants requires full control of breathing and circulation, so knowing their mechanism and complications is mandatory for every physician.
The student should know:

items: the structure and types of N-cholinergic receptors (neuronal and muscular);
the effects and uses of N-cholinomimetics (nicotine, cytisine, lobeline, varenicline) and the toxicology of nicotine;
the mechanism, effects, uses and complications of ganglionic blockers;
the classification of peripheral muscle relaxants, the difference between the mechanisms of nondepolarizing and depolarizing agents, and their antagonists;
the complications of muscle relaxants (prolonged apnea, malignant hyperthermia, hyperkalemia) and their management.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for preparations such as cytisine, azamethonium, rocuronium, suxamethonium, neostigmine and sugammadex;
match the choice of muscle relaxant to the clinical situation;
draw up a pharmacotherapy plan for smoking cessation.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks recommended cytisine (Cytiton) and lobeline as **reflex respiratory analeptics** (carbon monoxide poisoning, asphyxia). In modern practice, respiratory failure is treated with oxygen and mechanical ventilation; analeptics are considered ineffective and dangerous. The main current importance of cytisine is **smoking cessation**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Ganglionic blockers **“switch off the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems at once”**: in the vessels — loss of sympathetic tone (hypotension); in most other organs — loss of parasympathetic tone (atropine-like effects). That is why they have many adverse effects.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: After a ganglionic blocker has been given, the patient must lie **horizontally for 2 hours**; if he gets up suddenly, orthostatic collapse develops. Today ganglionic blockers are hardly used to treat hypertension — they have been replaced by modern antihypertensive drugs with fewer adverse effects (topic 11).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Hofmann elimination — “ATRA and CIS”**: **atra**curium and **cis**atracurium break down spontaneously in the blood independently of organ function — the agents of choice in renal and hepatic failure.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Neostigmine does not reverse a suxamethonium block but, on the contrary, enhances it** — because it accumulates ACh and also inhibits pseudocholinesterase. There is no specific antagonist of a depolarizing block; its effect wears off quickly on its own.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Treatment of malignant hyperthermia:** immediately stop all triggering agents (inhalational anesthetics, suxamethonium), hyperventilation with 100% oxygen, **dantrolene** intravenously (2.5 mg/kg, repeated up to 10 mg/kg; blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum), physical cooling, correction of acidosis and hyperkalemia.

blocks.text: The N-cholinergic receptor is a **ligand-gated ion channel** (ionotropic receptor). It consists of five subunits (alpha, beta, gamma or epsilon, delta), with a channel in the center that conducts Na^+^ and K^+^ ions. When two molecules of acetylcholine bind to **the two alpha subunits**, the channel opens and the membrane depolarizes.

blocks.text: 2.1. Nicotine

**Nicotine** — an alkaloid of tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum), a liquid tertiary amine; it is absorbed very quickly from the skin, mucous membranes and lungs. As a drug, it is used only in **nicotine replacement therapy** (smoking cessation).
**Biphasic action:** at small doses it **stimulates** N-cholinergic receptors, at large doses it **blocks** them through prolonged depolarization.

blocks.title: Table 5.3. Effects of nicotine (at doses seen in smokers)
head: System
Effect
rows: Excitation, improved attention and mood (dopamine release in the mesolimbic system — the basis of dependence), reduced appetite; at large doses — tremor, seizures
Stimulation of the sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla — tachycardia, rise in BP, constriction of peripheral vessels, increased myocardial oxygen demand
Stimulation of the parasympathetic ganglia — increased salivation and peristalsis, nausea (with the first cigarette)
Reflex stimulation of breathing through the carotid bodies

blocks.text: **The harm of smoking** is due mainly not to nicotine but to **more than 4000** substances in tobacco smoke (tars, benzpyrene and other carcinogens, carbon monoxide, cyanides): lung cancer, COPD, atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, stroke, impaired fetal development.

**Acute nicotine poisoning** (when children swallow cigarettes or nicotine liquid, e-cigarette liquid): nausea, vomiting, salivation, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dizziness, tachycardia, then bradycardia and hypotension, seizures, **paralysis of the respiratory muscles**. Treatment: activated charcoal, respiratory support, diazepam for seizures, atropine for M signs.
2.2. Cytisine and lobeline

**Cytisine** — an alkaloid of thermopsis and laburnum (Cytisus laburnum, the “golden rain” shrub); it stimulates N-cholinergic receptors, but more weakly and more selectively than nicotine. **Tabex** tablets — for smoking cessation: by partly occupying nicotinic receptors, it softens withdrawal symptoms and reduces the “pleasure” obtained from smoking.
**Lobeline** — an alkaloid of lobelia. It was formerly used as a reflex respiratory analeptic; it is hardly used now.

parts.text: Older textbooks recommended cytisine (Cytiton) and lobeline as **reflex respiratory analeptics** (carbon monoxide poisoning, asphyxia). In modern practice, respiratory failure is treated with oxygen and mechanical ventilation; analeptics are considered ineffective and dangerous. The main current importance of cytisine is **smoking cessation**.

parts.text: Smoking cessation is the most effective preventive measure for reducing cardiovascular disease and lung cancer. Pharmacotherapy **combined with brief counseling** increases the chance of quitting 2–3-fold. Every GP should offer smoking cessation to a smoking patient at every visit.

blocks.text: **Ganglionic blockers** block the N~N~-cholinergic receptors in the autonomic ganglia and simultaneously stop impulse transmission in **sympathetic and parasympathetic** ganglia; they also reduce epinephrine release from the adrenal medulla.

parts.text: Ganglionic blockers **“switch off the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems at once”**: in the vessels — loss of sympathetic tone (hypotension); in most other organs — loss of parasympathetic tone (atropine-like effects). That is why they have many adverse effects.

blocks.text: Uses (mainly historical):

items: hypertensive crisis (intravenously or intramuscularly, in the horizontal position);
**controlled (deliberate) hypotension** — during surgery to reduce blood loss;
pulmonary edema against the background of arterial hypertension (they “unload” the pulmonary circulation);

peripheral vasospasm (Raynaud's disease). **Adverse effects: orthostatic collapse** (the most dangerous), tachycardia, dry mouth, disturbed accommodation, constipation and paralytic ileus, urinary retention, development of tolerance.

parts.text: After a ganglionic blocker has been given, the patient must lie **horizontally for 2 hours**; if he gets up suddenly, orthostatic collapse develops. Today ganglionic blockers are hardly used to treat hypertension — they have been replaced by modern antihypertensive drugs with fewer adverse effects (topic 11).

blocks.text: **Peripheral muscle relaxants** block N~M~-cholinergic receptors at the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscles and cause **muscle relaxation (paralysis)**. They do not act on the CNS — the patient does not lose consciousness and feels pain. Therefore muscle relaxants are used **only during general anesthesia** and with mechanical ventilation.
**History.** Curare is the arrow poison of South American Indians. In 1942, Griffith and Johnson first used tubocurarine during surgery; this was a revolution in anesthesiology.

**Order of muscle relaxation:** first the **facial and eye** muscles, then the **fingers**, limbs, neck and trunk muscles, the **intercostal muscles** and, last of all, the **diaphragm**. Recovery is in the reverse order.

blocks.label: Figure 5.3
blocks.caption: Mechanism of action of curare-like agents: a — nondepolarizing (competitive) block; b — depolarizing block (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: 4.1. Nondepolarizing (competitive) muscle relaxants

**Mechanism:** they block N~M~ receptors **competitively** with ACh and do not cause depolarization themselves. No end-plate potential is generated. Increasing the ACh concentration in the synapse (anticholinesterase agents — **neostigmine**) reverses the block.

blocks.label: Figure 5.4
blocks.caption: Chemical structure of some curare-like agents: tubocurarine, pancuronium, pipecuronium, anatruxonium, Ditilin (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

parts.text: **Hofmann elimination — “ATRA and CIS”**: **atra**curium and **cis**atracurium break down spontaneously in the blood independently of organ function — the agents of choice in renal and hepatic failure.

blocks.text: **Factors that enhance a competitive block:** inhalational anesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane), **aminoglycosides** (gentamicin — reduces ACh release), polymyxins, lincosamides, magnesium sulfate, calcium antagonists, hypothermia, acidosis, hypokalemia, myasthenia gravis (these patients are very sensitive to competitive relaxants).
Antagonists:

items: **Neostigmine** (0.04–0.07 mg/kg intravenously) — together with **atropine** or glycopyrronium (to prevent M effects). Effective only after partial recovery has begun; ineffective in a deep block.

**Sugammadex** — a modified gamma-cyclodextrin; it **encapsulates** (“wraps up”) **rocuronium** and vecuronium molecules in the blood, forming an inactive complex. It rapidly (within 2–3 minutes) reverses a block of any depth, without M effects.

blocks.text: 4.2. Depolarizing muscle relaxant — suxamethonium (Ditilin)

**Suxamethonium** — a compound of two ACh molecules. It **stimulates** N~M~ receptors and causes **prolonged depolarization** of the end plate. First, brief **muscle fasciculations** (disorganized contractions) are seen, then the membrane remains depolarized and does not respond to new impulses — **paralysis** (phase I block). With prolonged or repeated administration, the block may become competitive in character (**phase II** block).

items: The action begins **very quickly** (**30–60 seconds**) and is **short** (5–10 minutes).
It is rapidly broken down in the blood by **pseudocholinesterase** (butyrylcholinesterase).
Uses: **rapid sequence intubation** (full stomach, emergency surgery), short procedures (laryngospasm, endoscopy, electrical cardioversion).

parts.text: **Neostigmine does not reverse a suxamethonium block but, on the contrary, enhances it** — because it accumulates ACh and also inhibits pseudocholinesterase. There is no specific antagonist of a depolarizing block; its effect wears off quickly on its own.

head: Adverse effect
Cause and risk group
rows: Hereditary atypical form or deficiency of pseudocholinesterase (liver disease, pregnancy, OPC poisoning, anticholinesterase agents)

Hereditary (RYR1 gene mutation) — suxamethonium and inhalational anesthetics trigger uncontrolled release of Ca^2+^ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum: muscle rigidity, hypercapnia, tachycardia, a sharp rise in temperature
Burns, extensive injuries, prolonged immobilization, denervation, muscular dystrophies — the number of receptors increases
After surgery, as a result of fasciculations
Increased intraocular, intragastric and intracranial pressure
Fasciculations and contraction of the extraocular muscles; dangerous in penetrating eye injuries
Stimulates cardiac M~2~ receptors (especially in children and with repeated doses)

parts.text: **Treatment of malignant hyperthermia:** immediately stop all triggering agents (inhalational anesthetics, suxamethonium), hyperventilation with 100% oxygen, **dantrolene** intravenously (2.5 mg/kg, repeated up to 10 mg/kg; blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum), physical cooling, correction of acidosis and hyperkalemia.

Therefore neuromuscular transmission is monitored (acceleromyography, TOF test), and antagonists are given if necessary. Mechanical ventilation continues until the patient recovers.

blocks.text: 4.4. Other drugs affecting neuromuscular transmission

items: **Botulinum toxin A** — blocks ACh release from the presynaptic nerve ending (cleaves SNARE proteins). It is injected locally: blepharospasm, spasticity, dystonias, hyperhidrosis, overactive bladder, chronic migraine, cosmetology. Its effect lasts 3–6 months.
**Dantrolene** — blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum inside skeletal muscle; for malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

**Central muscle relaxants** (inhibit polysynaptic reflexes in the CNS): baclofen (GABA-B agonist), tizanidine (alpha-2 agonist), tolperisone — for spasticity, muscle spasm, low back pain; benzodiazepines (diazepam).

parts.text: Before surgery, it is mandatory to ask about cases in **relatives of prolonged failure to wake up after anesthesia** or of **high fever of unknown cause**: this may indicate pseudocholinesterase deficiency or a predisposition to malignant hyperthermia.

skills.title: Skill 1. Smoking cessation counseling (the 5 A's rule)

items: **Ask** — ask about and record smoking status at every visit.
**Advise** — explain the need to stop smoking clearly and in a personalized way.
**Assess** — assess the patient's readiness to quit.
**Assist** — set a quit date and prescribe pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement therapy, cytisine or varenicline).
**Arrange follow-up** — schedule follow-up visits after 1–2 weeks and after 1 month.

options: General anesthesia and the availability of mechanical ventilation

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 28-year-old patient underwent general anesthesia for appendectomy; suxamethonium was used for intubation. The operation ended in 30 minutes, but 2 hours later spontaneous breathing had still not returned. The patient's uncle had also previously “not woken up for a long time” after anesthesia.
cases.ask: 1) What is the probable cause? 2) Can neostigmine be given in this situation? 3) Management.
cases.answer: 1) A hereditary atypical form (deficiency) of pseudocholinesterase — suxamethonium is not broken down and acts for a long time. 2) No — neostigmine also inhibits pseudocholinesterase and may enhance the depolarizing block. 3) Keep the patient on mechanical ventilation under sedation and wait until the block wears off on its own (several hours); if necessary, fresh frozen plasma (a source of pseudocholinesterase); test the patient and relatives (dibucaine number), avoid suxamethonium and mivacurium in the future, and make a note in the medical records.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 19-year-old man was given sevoflurane anesthesia and suxamethonium for intubation during knee arthroscopy. After 20 minutes, rigidity of the masticatory muscles, tachycardia of 150/min, a sharp rise in end-tidal CO~2~ and a rise in temperature to 39.5 °C were observed.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) Pathogenesis? 3) Emergency treatment.
cases.answer: 1) Malignant hyperthermia. 2) Because of a hereditary (RYR1) defect, suxamethonium and the inhalational anesthetic triggered uncontrolled release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle — hypermetabolism, muscle rigidity, excessive production of CO~2~ and heat, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia. 3) Stop sevoflurane immediately, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenously (repeated), physical cooling, correction of acidosis and hyperkalemia, support of diuresis; observation in intensive care; warn the patient and his family about future anesthesia.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 52-year-old man has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes a day for 30 years. He had a myocardial infarction two years ago. He wants to stop smoking, but previous attempts have failed (irritability, insomnia, strong craving to smoke).
cases.ask: 1) What pharmacotherapy would you offer? 2) What causes the withdrawal symptoms?
cases.answer: 1) Together with counseling — varenicline (12 weeks) or cytisine (25 days), or combined nicotine replacement therapy (patch + gum). In stable ischemic heart disease, nicotine replacement therapy is much safer than smoking (no carbon monoxide or other harmful substances from smoke). 2) Chronic exposure to nicotine changes the number and sensitivity of N-cholinergic receptors in the CNS, and dopamine release in the mesolimbic system becomes nicotine-dependent; when nicotine is stopped, the dopamine deficit causes irritability, depression, insomnia and strong craving. Partial agonists stimulate the receptors moderately and soften these symptoms.
