topics.title: Drugs acting on adrenergic receptors

goals.text: Drugs acting on the adrenergic system are the main drugs of emergency medicine (anaphylactic shock, cardiac arrest, cardiogenic and septic shock) and cardiology (arterial hypertension, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, arrhythmias). Stopping anaphylaxis with epinephrine and choosing beta-blockers correctly are skills every GP must master.
The student should know:

items: the structure of the adrenergic synapse and the synthesis, release and inactivation of catecholamines;
the types of adrenergic receptors, their location and the effects of their stimulation;
the classification, mechanism, uses and adverse effects of adrenomimetics, sympathomimetics, adrenergic blockers and sympatholytics;
the algorithm of emergency care in anaphylactic shock.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for preparations such as epinephrine, norepinephrine, phenylephrine, salbutamol, xylometazoline, prazosin, tamsulosin, metoprolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol and timolol;
calculate and give the dose of epinephrine in anaphylaxis;
choose a beta-blocker according to the clinical situation.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the beta receptor numbers by the number of organs: **beta-1 — 1 heart**, **beta-2 — 2 lungs**. Alpha-1 — “**constriction**” (vessels, sphincters), alpha-2 — “**brake**” (self-limitation, central sympathetic tone).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Dale's phenomenon (vasomotor reversal).** If epinephrine is given against the background of an alpha-blocker, BP **does not rise but falls**: the alpha receptors are blocked and only beta-2-mediated vasodilation remains. Therefore epinephrine is not given for hypotension caused by alpha-blockers or neuroleptics (chlorpromazine has alpha-blocking properties) — **norepinephrine** or phenylephrine is chosen.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **“Renal-dose dopamine”** (1–3 mcg/kg/min) was formerly widely prescribed to prevent acute renal failure. Clinical studies have shown that it does not protect the kidneys or reduce mortality; it is now **not recommended** for this purpose. In septic shock, dopamine causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine, so norepinephrine is preferred.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Using decongestants for **more than 5–7 days** leads to **tachyphylaxis** and **“rebound”** swelling — **drug-induced rhinitis** develops (naphazoline dependence). In young children, imidazolines are absorbed into the blood and depress the CNS: drowsiness, **bradycardia, hypothermia, coma** (naphazoline poisoning). Only pediatric concentrations (xylometazoline 0.05%) are used in children; naphazoline 0.1% is contraindicated in children.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **The three beta-blockers that reduce mortality in heart failure — “BMC”**: **B**isoprolol, **M**etoprolol succinate, **C**arvedilol (+ nebivolol in the elderly). Cardioselective ones run alphabetically **“A–M”**: **A**tenolol, **B**isoprolol, **B**etaxolol, **E**smolol, **M**etoprolol (all begin with letters from A to M) + nebivolol.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **A beta-blocker must not be stopped abruptly** — “rebound” syndrome: the number of receptors has increased (up-regulation), and when the drug is stopped, sensitivity to catecholamines rises sharply — tachycardia, angina attacks, **myocardial infarction**, hypertensive crisis. The dose is reduced gradually over 1–2 weeks.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Beta-blocker poisoning** (bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, hypoglycemia, seizures): atropine (often of little effect), **glucagon** (activates adenylate cyclase independently of beta receptors), high-dose insulin + glucose, catecholamines (epinephrine, isoprenaline), cardiac pacing; in propranolol poisoning (wide QRS) — sodium bicarbonate.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks gave reserpine and Octadine (guanethidine) as the main drugs for hypertension. In modern recommendations (topic 11), they are **not used**: they have many adverse effects, and a reduction in cardiovascular complications has not been proven.

blocks.text: 1.1. Synthesis, release and inactivation of catecholamines

items: **Synthesis** (in the nerve ending): **tyrosine** → (tyrosine hydroxylase — the slowest, rate-limiting step) → **DOPA** → (DOPA decarboxylase) → **dopamine** → (dopamine beta-hydroxylase in the vesicles) → **norepinephrine**. In the adrenal medulla, norepinephrine is converted into **epinephrine** by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase.
**Storage:** norepinephrine is stored in vesicles together with ATP and chromogranins (VMAT carrier; **reserpine** blocks it).
**Release:** Ca^2+^-dependent exocytosis when a nerve impulse arrives.
**Action on receptors:** postsynaptic alpha and beta receptors, presynaptic alpha-2 (negative feedback — reduces release) and beta-2 (enhances release) receptors.

**Inactivation:** mainly (70–90%) by **neuronal reuptake** (NET, “uptake 1”; blocked by cocaine and tricyclic antidepressants); the rest — breakdown by the enzymes mitochondrial **MAO** (in the nerve ending) and **COMT** (in the effector cell and the liver). Metabolites — vanillylmandelic acid and metanephrines (measured in the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma).

blocks.text: 2.1. Epinephrine (adrenaline)

**Epinephrine** — a hormone of the adrenal medulla; it directly stimulates all **alpha and beta** receptors. It is destroyed in the gastrointestinal tract — it is used only parenterally, by inhalation and topically. Its action is short (intravenously — 5 minutes, subcutaneously — 30 minutes) because of reuptake and breakdown by COMT/MAO.

blocks.title: Table 6.3. Pharmacological effects of epinephrine
head: Organ / system
Effect
Receptor
rows: The force and rate of contraction increase, conduction and automaticity increase; myocardial oxygen demand increases; arrhythmias are possible
Vessels of the skin, mucous membranes and kidneys constrict; skeletal muscle and coronary vessels dilate
Systolic pressure rises; at small doses diastolic pressure may fall (beta-2), at large doses it rises (alpha-1)
Hyperglycemia (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, reduced insulin secretion), lipolysis, hypokalemia
Reduces the release of histamine and other mediators

parts.text: **Dale's phenomenon (vasomotor reversal).** If epinephrine is given against the background of an alpha-blocker, BP **does not rise but falls**: the alpha receptors are blocked and only beta-2-mediated vasodilation remains. Therefore epinephrine is not given for hypotension caused by alpha-blockers or neuroleptics (chlorpromazine has alpha-blocking properties) — **norepinephrine** or phenylephrine is chosen.

blocks.text: Uses of epinephrine:

items: **anaphylactic shock and severe allergic reactions** — the drug of first choice;
**cardiac arrest** (asystole, pulseless electrical activity, ventricular fibrillation refractory to defibrillation) — 1 mg intravenously every 3–5 minutes;
adding to local anesthetic solutions (vasoconstriction);
stopping bleeding from the nose and small vessels (topically);
in an attack of bronchial asthma — now only when other agents are unavailable (beta-2 agonists are preferred);
open-angle glaucoma (historically).

parts.text: **Epinephrine dose in anaphylaxis:** for adults **0.5 mg** (0.5 ml of 0.1% solution), for children **0.01 mg/kg** (maximum 0.5 mg; 6–12 years — 0.3 mg, under 6 years — 0.15 mg), **intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh**; if there is no effect, it is repeated every **5 minutes**. Intravenous administration only in a resuscitation setting, diluted and under monitoring (risk of arrhythmia). In anaphylaxis, epinephrine is given **before** all other drugs; antihistamines and glucocorticoids are only adjuncts.

blocks.text: **Adverse effects:** tachycardia, arrhythmias (especially with halothane), angina, hypertension, headache, fear, tremor, hyperglycemia; with repeated subcutaneous injection — necrosis.
2.2. Norepinephrine (noradrenaline)

**Norepinephrine** stimulates alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta-1 receptors; **its effect on beta-2 is very weak**. As a result, all vessels constrict and **systolic and diastolic BP rise**. Although it directly stimulates beta-1 receptors in the heart, **reflex bradycardia** develops through the baroreceptors.

items: **Uses: septic shock** (the vasopressor of first choice), other types of shock and severe hypotension (after adequate fluid replacement); only **by intravenous drip**, under BP monitoring.
**Complication:** if the solution leaks out of the vessel — **tissue necrosis**. Treatment: infiltration of the area with **phentolamine** (an alpha-blocker) solution.

blocks.text: 2.3. Dopamine and dobutamine
**Dopamine** — a precursor of norepinephrine; its effects depend on the dose.

blocks.title: Table 6.4. Dose-dependent effects of dopamine
head: Dose (mcg/kg/min)
Main receptors
Effect
rows: Dilation of renal and mesenteric vessels, increased diuresis

parts.text: **“Renal-dose dopamine”** (1–3 mcg/kg/min) was formerly widely prescribed to prevent acute renal failure. Clinical studies have shown that it does not protect the kidneys or reduce mortality; it is now **not recommended** for this purpose. In septic shock, dopamine causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine, so norepinephrine is preferred.

blocks.text: **Dobutamine** — mainly a **beta-1** adrenomimetic; it increases the force of cardiac contraction, speeds up the heart rate less and hardly changes BP. Uses: **cardiogenic shock** and acute decompensated heart failure (low cardiac output), stress echocardiography.
2.4. Alpha-adrenomimetics

**Phenylephrine (Mesaton)** — an alpha-1 agonist; it is not broken down by COMT and acts longer than epinephrine. It constricts the vessels, raises BP and causes reflex bradycardia. Uses: hypotension (during anesthesia), as a **mydriatic** (does not affect accommodation), rhinitis (in nasal drops).
**Midodrine** — orally for orthostatic hypotension.

**Imidazoline derivatives — decongestants** (xylometazoline, oxymetazoline, naphazoline, tetrahydrozoline) — alpha-2 (and alpha-1) agonists; they constrict the vessels of the nasal mucosa and reduce swelling. They are instilled into the nose in rhinitis, sinusitis and otitis.

parts.text: Using decongestants for **more than 5–7 days** leads to **tachyphylaxis** and **“rebound”** swelling — **drug-induced rhinitis** develops (naphazoline dependence). In young children, imidazolines are absorbed into the blood and depress the CNS: drowsiness, **bradycardia, hypothermia, coma** (naphazoline poisoning). Only pediatric concentrations (xylometazoline 0.05%) are used in children; naphazoline 0.1% is contraindicated in children.

blocks.text: 2.5. Beta-adrenomimetics
**Isoprenaline (Isadrin)** — a beta-1 and beta-2 agonist. Tachycardia and bronchodilation. Rarely used now (temporarily in AV block, in bradycardia).
**Beta-2 adrenomimetics** — the main drugs for bronchial asthma and COPD (in detail in topic 9):

items: **short-acting** (4–6 hours; for relieving attacks): salbutamol, fenoterol, terbutaline;
**long-acting** (12 hours): salmeterol, formoterol (formoterol has a rapid onset); **ultra-long-acting** (24 hours): indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol;

**tocolytics** (relaxing the uterus when there is a risk of preterm labor): hexoprenaline (Ginipral), salbutamol. **Adverse effects:** hand tremor (beta-2 of skeletal muscles), tachycardia and arrhythmias (at high doses they also act on beta-1), **hypokalemia**, hyperglycemia, headache; tachyphylaxis.

blocks.text: 2.6. Indirect sympathomimetics

**Ephedrine** — an alkaloid of the ephedra plant; it has a **mixed** action: it enhances norepinephrine release from the nerve ending (the main action) and also stimulates alpha and beta receptors directly. It resembles epinephrine but acts more weakly and **longer**; it is active orally; it stimulates the CNS. With repeated doses, **tachyphylaxis** develops (norepinephrine stores are depleted). Uses: hypotension during spinal anesthesia, narcolepsy (historically). As a precursor of narcotic substances (methamphetamine), it is under strict control.
**Amphetamine**, **methylphenidate** — CNS stimulants (topic 8).

**Tyramine** — found in cheese, wine and smoked products; in patients taking MAO inhibitors it is not broken down, releases a large amount of norepinephrine and causes a **hypertensive crisis** (“cheese reaction”).
3.1. Alpha-blockers

blocks.label: Figure 6.3
blocks.caption: Sites of action of adrenergic blockers: phentolamine, Tropaphen — alpha-1 and alpha-2; prazosin — alpha-1 (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: **Nonselective alpha-1 and alpha-2 blockers** (phentolamine, Tropaphen, phenoxybenzamine): they dilate the vessels and lower BP. Because presynaptic alpha-2 receptors are also blocked, norepinephrine release increases and **tachycardia** is marked.

items: **Phentolamine** — short-acting; hypertensive crises during the diagnosis and surgery of **pheochromocytoma**, norepinephrine extravasation.
**Phenoxybenzamine** — irreversible (covalent) block; preparation of pheochromocytoma for surgery.
**Dihydroergotoxine, nicergoline** (derivatives of ergot alkaloids) — for cerebral and peripheral circulatory disorders.

blocks.text: **Selective alpha-1 blockers** (prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin): little reflex tachycardia (alpha-2 remains open), slightly improve the lipid profile.

items: **Uses:** arterial hypertension (as an add-on drug, especially together with prostatic hyperplasia), **benign prostatic hyperplasia** (urination improves), Raynaud's syndrome.

**“First-dose phenomenon”** — marked **orthostatic hypotension** and fainting after the first dose. Prevention: start with a small dose, **at bedtime**. **Uroselective alpha-1A blockers** (tamsulosin, silodosin, alfuzosin) act selectively on the smooth muscle of the prostate and bladder neck; they have little effect on BP. Used for prostatic hyperplasia and to ease the passage of urinary stones. Adverse effects: retrograde ejaculation, “floppy iris” syndrome during cataract surgery.

parts.text: In a patient with **pheochromocytoma** (a catecholamine-producing tumor), a beta-blocker must not be given **without an alpha-blocker**: beta-2 vasodilation is lost and alpha vasoconstriction is left unopposed — **a severe hypertensive crisis**. An alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine, doxazosin) is given first, and only then is a beta-blocker added for tachycardia.

blocks.text: 3.2. Beta-blockers
**Beta-blockers** competitively block the action of catecholamines on beta receptors. This is one of the most important groups in cardiology.

blocks.title: Table 6.5. Main effects of beta-blockers

Mechanism
Clinical result
rows: Heart rate and contractility decrease, myocardial oxygen demand decreases (antianginal)
Conduction in the AV node slows
Cardiac output decreases, renin secretion decreases (beta-1), central sympathetic tone decreases
The toxic effect of catecholamines on the myocardium and remodeling decrease
Reduce mortality in heart failure and after infarction
Fluid production by the ciliary body epithelium decreases
Mask the signs of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremor) and slow recovery from hypoglycemia

blocks.title: Table 6.6. Classification and properties of beta-blockers
head: Preparation
Selectivity
Additional property
Feature of use
rows: Tremor, migraine prophylaxis, thyrotoxicosis, portal hypertension, somatic signs of anxiety, hemangiomas (in children)
Hypertension, angina, infarction; metoprolol succinate (extended-release) — heart failure
Dilates the vessels by releasing NO
Intravenously — for tachycardia and hypertension during surgery

parts.text: **The three beta-blockers that reduce mortality in heart failure — “BMC”**: **B**isoprolol, **M**etoprolol succinate, **C**arvedilol (+ nebivolol in the elderly). Cardioselective ones run alphabetically **“A–M”**: **A**tenolol, **B**isoprolol, **B**etaxolol, **E**smolol, **M**etoprolol (all begin with letters from A to M) + nebivolol.

blocks.text: Uses:

items: arterial hypertension;
ischemic heart disease: stable angina, the period after myocardial infarction (reduce mortality);
chronic heart failure (in a stable state, increasing gradually from a small dose);
tachyarrhythmias (rate control in atrial fibrillation, extrasystoles);
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dissecting aortic aneurysm;
signs of thyrotoxicosis (tachycardia, tremor), pheochromocytoma (after an alpha-blocker);
migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, “stage fright”;
glaucoma (timolol, betaxolol drops);
portal hypertension in liver cirrhosis (prevention of bleeding from esophageal varices — propranolol, carvedilol).

blocks.title: Table 6.7. Contraindications to beta-blockers
head: Absolute
Relative (with caution)
rows: Bronchial asthma (nonselective agents, including eye drops)
COPD (cardioselective agents in small doses are possible)
Second- or third-degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome (without a pacemaker)
Acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic shock
Pregnancy (labetalol and metoprolol are possible; atenolol — slows fetal growth)

parts.text: **A beta-blocker must not be stopped abruptly** — “rebound” syndrome: the number of receptors has increased (up-regulation), and when the drug is stopped, sensitivity to catecholamines rises sharply — tachycardia, angina attacks, **myocardial infarction**, hypertensive crisis. The dose is reduced gradually over 1–2 weeks.

blocks.text: **Adverse effects:** bradycardia, AV block, worsening of heart failure (in decompensation), hypotension, bronchospasm, cold extremities, fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance, sleep disturbances and nightmares (with lipophilic agents), erectile dysfunction, masking of hypoglycemia, worsening of the lipid profile (with nonselective agents).

parts.text: **Beta-blocker poisoning** (bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, hypoglycemia, seizures): atropine (often of little effect), **glucagon** (activates adenylate cyclase independently of beta receptors), high-dose insulin + glucose, catecholamines (epinephrine, isoprenaline), cardiac pacing; in propranolol poisoning (wide QRS) — sodium bicarbonate.

blocks.text: **Sympatholytics** reduce norepinephrine stores in adrenergic nerve endings or stop its release; they do not act on receptors.

items: **Reserpine** — an alkaloid of Rauwolfia; it blocks the uptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin into vesicles (VMAT), the mediators are broken down by MAO, and the stores are depleted. The hypotensive effect develops slowly (over 1–2 weeks). Adverse effects: **depression** (risk of suicide), parkinsonism, nasal congestion, bradycardia, exacerbation of gastric ulcer (parasympathetic predominance). It is hardly used now; it remains in some combination tablets (Adelphane).
**Guanethidine (Octadine)** — blocks norepinephrine release; does not enter the CNS. It causes severe orthostatic hypotension. It is of historical importance.

parts.text: Older textbooks gave reserpine and Octadine (guanethidine) as the main drugs for hypertension. In modern recommendations (topic 11), they are **not used**: they have many adverse effects, and a reduction in cardiovascular complications has not been proven.

blocks.text: 5.1. Emergency care in anaphylactic shock

blocks.title: Table 6.8. Algorithm of care in anaphylaxis (adults)
head: Step
Action
rows: Stop contact with the allergen (stop the drug infusion); call for help
Epinephrine 0.5 mg (0.1% — 0.5 ml) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh; may be repeated every 5 minutes
Lay the patient down with the legs raised (half-sitting if breathing is difficult); do not let him stand up suddenly
Establish intravenous access and rapidly infuse 500–1000 ml of crystalloids (0.9% NaCl) (for children 10–20 ml/kg)
Additionally: an H~1~ antihistamine (for allergic skin signs), a glucocorticoid (to prevent a delayed reaction — its effectiveness has not been proven)
If there is no response to two doses of epinephrine — an epinephrine infusion in the intensive care unit; in patients taking beta-blockers who do not respond to epinephrine — glucagon
Observation for at least 6–12 hours (biphasic reaction); an epinephrine auto-injector and allergist consultation for the patient

parts.text: The most common error in anaphylaxis is giving epinephrine **late** or not at all and giving only prednisolone and diphenhydramine instead. The effect of glucocorticoids begins after hours, and they do not stop shock. Only epinephrine given in time saves life.

blocks.text: 5.2. Choosing a vasopressor and an inotrope

blocks.title: Table 6.9. Adrenergic drugs in types of shock
head: Type of shock
First choice
Additional
rows: Dobutamine (when BP is relatively preserved); norepinephrine (in hypotension)

items: Open an ampoule of 0.1% (1 mg/ml) epinephrine.
Calculate the dose: 0.01 mg/kg = 0.01 ml/kg (maximum 0.5 ml for adults, 0.3 ml for children).
Draw it into a syringe; the needle must be long enough to reach the muscle.
Inject **intramuscularly** into the middle third of the anterolateral thigh; this can be done through clothing.
Record the time; if there is no effect after 5 minutes, repeat.

skills.title: Skill 2. Algorithm for choosing a beta-blocker

items: Determine the indication (hypertension, angina, heart failure, arrhythmia, migraine, glaucoma).
Check for contraindications (asthma, AV block, bradycardia, decompensation).
In heart failure — only bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate, carvedilol or nebivolol; start with a very small dose and double it once every 2 weeks.
In COPD and diabetes — a cardioselective preparation (bisoprolol, nebivolol).
In pregnancy — labetalol or metoprolol.
Warn the patient not to stop the drug abruptly.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Ten minutes after taking amoxicillin at the dentist's, a 25-year-old woman developed itching, urticaria, swelling of the lips and eyelids, hoarseness, shortness of breath and dizziness. BP 70/40 mm Hg, HR 128/min.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) The first-line drug, its dose and route? 3) Further measures.
cases.answer: 1) Anaphylactic shock (to amoxicillin). 2) Epinephrine 0.5 mg (0.5 ml of 0.1% solution) intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh; if there is no effect, repeat every 5 minutes. 3) Call for help, lay the patient down with the legs raised (half-sitting if breathing is difficult), oxygen, establish intravenous access and rapidly infuse 0.9% NaCl; if bronchospasm persists — salbutamol; additionally — an antihistamine and a glucocorticoid; observation for at least 12 hours; record the penicillin allergy in the medical records and provide an epinephrine auto-injector.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 62-year-old patient takes propranolol for arterial hypertension and angina. It turned out that the patient also has bronchial asthma; in recent weeks the attacks of breathlessness have become more frequent. In addition, the patient stopped taking propranolol 3 days ago because he ran out of the drug, and yesterday he had a severe angina attack.
cases.ask: 1) What caused the attacks of breathlessness to become more frequent? 2) What caused the angina attack? 3) How should the treatment be changed?
cases.answer: 1) Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker; it blocks beta-2 receptors in the bronchi and causes bronchospasm — it is contraindicated in asthma. 2) Abrupt withdrawal of the beta-blocker — rebound syndrome (increased sensitivity to catecholamines against the background of receptor up-regulation). 3) If a beta-blocker is needed in a patient with asthma — a highly cardioselective one (bisoprolol, nebivolol) in a small dose and under the supervision of a pulmonologist; or an alternative to beta-blockers for angina (verapamil, diltiazem or a dihydropyridine calcium antagonist + nitrates); explain to the patient never to stop the drug abruptly.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 2-year-old child's mother instilled 0.1% naphazoline drops intended for adults into his nose many times for nasal congestion. A few hours later the child is drowsy, the skin is pale and cold, HR 70/min, body temperature 35.4 °C, and breathing has become infrequent.
cases.ask: 1) What is this condition? 2) Its mechanism? 3) Treatment and prevention.
cases.answer: 1) Poisoning with an imidazoline derivative (naphazoline). 2) In a young child, a large amount of naphazoline absorbed from the nasal mucosa crosses the BBB and stimulates central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors — sympathetic tone falls: CNS depression, bradycardia, hypothermia, respiratory depression (similar to clonidine poisoning). 3) Urgent hospitalization, monitoring of breathing and circulation, warming, atropine for bradycardia, oxygen and respiratory support for respiratory failure; recovery usually occurs within 12–24 hours. Prevention: only pediatric concentrations for children (xylometazoline 0.05%), not more than 2–3 times a day and for not more than 3–5 days; keep drugs out of the reach of children.

cells: Anaphylaxis (0.5 mg i/m), cardiac arrest (1 mg i/v)
Not more than 5–7 days; poisoning in children

topics.title: General anesthetics. Neuroleptics. Anxiolytics

goals.text: This topic brings together three important groups that depress the central nervous system (CNS). **General anesthetics** made surgery painless and safe. **Neuroleptics (antipsychotics)** revolutionized the treatment of schizophrenia and other psychoses. **Anxiolytics (tranquilizers)** are among the most frequently prescribed drugs, but they carry a high risk of dependence. The GP must recognize the adverse effects of these drugs (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, extrapyramidal disorders, benzodiazepine dependence) and provide help in poisoning.
The student should know:

items: the classification of drugs acting on the CNS, the theories of anesthesia and the stages of anesthesia;
the properties of inhalational and non-inhalational anesthetics and the principles of combined anesthesia and premedication;
the classification of neuroleptics (typical and atypical), their mechanism of action, uses and adverse effects;
the mechanism and uses of anxiolytics (benzodiazepines and others), dependence and poisoning.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for preparations such as propofol, ketamine, haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, diazepam, alprazolam and buspirone;
determine the stages of anesthesia in a laboratory experiment;
provide help in benzodiazepine poisoning and in acute adverse effects of neuroleptics.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Components of modern general anesthesia: **hypnosis** (loss of consciousness), **analgesia**, **amnesia**, **muscle relaxation** and **suppression of unwanted autonomic reflexes**. No single drug can safely provide all of these, so **combined (balanced) anesthesia** is used.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The therapeutic range of anesthesia (the difference between the surgical stage and stage IV) is relatively narrow for inhalational anesthetics. The excitement stage is dangerous (aspiration of vomit, arrhythmias), so in modern anesthesia, anesthesia is started with fast-acting intravenous agents (**induction**), and stage II is hardly seen.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Sevo is a child's friend”**: sevoflurane is pleasant and non-irritating, so it is the main agent for mask induction in children. **“Halothane is the enemy of the heart and liver”**: arrhythmias and hepatitis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Main criteria of the depth of anesthesia in the laboratory: the **righting reflex** (consciousness), **response to pain**, the **corneal reflex**, **muscle tone**, and **respiratory rate and pattern**. A sharp slowing of breathing is a sign of the danger of passing into stage IV.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The 4 dopamine pathways — **“Limbic — Cortex — Substantia nigra — Pituitary”**: meso**limbic** (psychosis decreases), meso**cortical** (negative symptoms), nigrostriatal — **substantia nigra** (movement disorders), tuberoinfundibular — **pituitary** (prolactin increases). The therapeutic effect is only in the first; the others are a source of adverse effects.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)** — a rare but life-threatening complication (mortality up to 10%): **high fever**, **“lead-pipe” muscle rigidity**, impaired consciousness, autonomic instability (tachycardia, fluctuating BP, sweating), a **sharp rise in blood creatine kinase**, leukocytosis, rhabdomyolysis and renal failure. **Treatment:** stop the neuroleptic immediately, intensive care, cooling, fluids, **dantrolene** and/or **bromocriptine** (a dopamine agonist), benzodiazepines.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Benzodiazepines** increase the **frequency** of chloride channel opening, while **barbiturates** increase its **duration**. At large doses, barbiturates open the channel even without GABA — that is why their therapeutic range is narrow and they can paralyze the respiratory center.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Benzodiazepines are prescribed in **short courses** (not more than 2–4 weeks). In chronic anxiety disorders, the first choice is **antidepressants** (SSRIs) and psychotherapy. When long-term benzodiazepines are stopped, the dose must be reduced gradually over several weeks to months. **Combination with opioids** is one of the main causes of overdose deaths.

sections.title: 1. General classification of drugs acting on the CNS

blocks.title: Table 7.1. Drugs acting on the CNS
head: Direction of action
Groups
rows: General anesthetics, hypnotics, ethyl alcohol, antiepileptics, antiparkinsonian drugs, analgesics, neuroleptics, anxiolytics, sedatives, mood stabilizers (lithium salts)

blocks.text: **General anesthesia (narcosis)** (Gr. narkosis — numbness) — a **reversible** state caused by drugs: loss of consciousness, loss of pain sensation (analgesia), reduction of reflexes and skeletal muscle tone, but **the activity of the vital centers (respiration and circulation) is preserved**.

parts.text: Components of modern general anesthesia: **hypnosis** (loss of consciousness), **analgesia**, **amnesia**, **muscle relaxation** and **suppression of unwanted autonomic reflexes**. No single drug can safely provide all of these, so **combined (balanced) anesthesia** is used.

blocks.text: **History.** On October 16, 1846, in Boston, W. Morton demonstrated the first public ether anesthesia. In 1847, J. Simpson used chloroform, and N.I. Pirogov used ether anesthesia in military field conditions.

blocks.label: Figure 7.1
blocks.caption: The first public demonstration of ether anesthesia, Boston, 1846 (D.A. Kharkevich, Pharmacology, 2010)

blocks.text: 2.1. Stages of anesthesia

The stages of anesthesia are well observed in classic ether anesthesia (according to Guedel). With modern agents they pass quickly and are not clearly seen, but they remain important in assessing the depth of anesthesia.

blocks.title: Table 7.2. Stages of anesthesia (using ether anesthesia as an example)
head: Step
Signs
Mechanism
rows: Consciousness preserved but confused; pain sensation reduced; reflexes and muscle tone preserved
Depression of the cerebral cortex and the reticular formation begins
Consciousness lost; speech and motor excitement, irregular breathing, tachycardia, rise in BP, vomiting, increased muscle tone, dilated pupils
The inhibitory influence of the cortex is lost and subcortical centers are “released” (disinhibition)
No consciousness or pain, reflexes gradually disappear, muscles relax, breathing is rhythmic; the pupils first constrict and then dilate as anesthesia deepens
The spinal cord is depressed; III1–III3 — surgery can be performed, III4 — excessively deep
In overdose — paralysis of the respiratory and vasomotor centers; the pupils are dilated and do not react to light

parts.text: The therapeutic range of anesthesia (the difference between the surgical stage and stage IV) is relatively narrow for inhalational anesthetics. The excitement stage is dangerous (aspiration of vomit, arrhythmias), so in modern anesthesia, anesthesia is started with fast-acting intravenous agents (**induction**), and stage II is hardly seen.

blocks.text: 2.2. Classification of general anesthetics

blocks.title: Table 7.3. Classification of general anesthetics
head: Group
Preparations
rows: Sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane; halothane (Fluothane), enflurane; ether (historically)
Propofol, thiopental sodium, ketamine, etomidate, sodium oxybate, midazolam; opioids (fentanyl) — in combination

blocks.text: 2.3. Inhalational anesthetics

The potency of an inhalational anesthetic is assessed by the **minimum alveolar concentration (MAC)**: the alveolar concentration at which 50% of patients lose the motor response to a skin incision. **The smaller the MAC, the more potent the anesthetic.** The speed of induction and awakening depends on the **solubility of the anesthetic in blood**: those poorly soluble in blood (desflurane, sevoflurane, nitrous oxide, xenon) act quickly and are quickly eliminated.

Weak anesthetic (does not produce deep anesthesia alone); expands gas in closed cavities (pneumothorax, intestinal obstruction); inactivates B~12~ with prolonged use; “diffusion hypoxia” — 100% oxygen must be given at the end

parts.text: **“Sevo is a child's friend”**: sevoflurane is pleasant and non-irritating, so it is the main agent for mask induction in children. **“Halothane is the enemy of the heart and liver”**: arrhythmias and hepatitis.

blocks.text: 2.4. Intravenous (non-inhalational) anesthetics

blocks.title: Table 7.5. Comparison of intravenous anesthetics
head: Preparation
Onset / duration of action
Main properties
Adverse effects
rows: The most commonly used induction agent; rapid and “clear-headed” awakening; antiemetic effect; maintenance of anesthesia by infusion (TIVA), sedation

parts.text: **Ketamine** is valuable in emergency medicine and in the field: in hemodynamically unstable patients (shock, blood loss) it does not lower BP, preserves breathing, can also be given intramuscularly, and is convenient in bronchial asthma. In small (subanesthetic) doses it is a strong analgesic and a fast-acting antidepressant (esketamine — nasal spray, treatment-resistant depression).

blocks.text: 2.5. Combined anesthesia and premedication
**Premedication** — preparation with drugs before surgery:

items: **anxiolytic and sedative** — benzodiazepines (midazolam);
**analgesic** — opioids (fentanyl, Promedol);
**vagolytic** (reducing salivary and bronchial secretion and reflex bradycardia) — atropine, glycopyrronium;
**antiemetic and antacid** (risk of aspiration) — ondansetron, dexamethasone, H~2~ blockers or proton pump inhibitors;
**antihistamine** (in an allergic history).

blocks.text: **Balanced anesthesia** scheme: induction (propofol) → analgesia (fentanyl) → muscle relaxation (rocuronium) and intubation → maintenance of anesthesia (sevoflurane or propofol infusion + fentanyl) → awakening (muscle relaxant antagonist). **Neuroleptanalgesia** — a combination of a neuroleptic (droperidol) + a potent opioid (fentanyl); the patient is conscious but indifferent and pain-free.

sections.title: 3. Laboratory class: studying the stages of anesthesia

blocks.text: This section corresponds to the 5th-semester class “Laboratory study of the stages of general anesthetics”.
Course of the experiment (in a mouse or rat):

items: The animal's baseline state is recorded: motor activity, respiratory rate, response to a painful stimulus (tail pinch), corneal and righting reflexes, muscle tone.
The animal is placed under a glass bell jar and a cotton ball soaked in the anesthetic (ether or sevoflurane) is placed inside.

Signs are recorded every 30–60 seconds: **stage I** — reduced activity, impaired coordination; **stage II** — motor excitement, irregular breathing; **stage III** — loss of the righting reflex, no response to pain, relaxed muscles, rhythmic and slow breathing.
If anesthesia deepens (breathing slows sharply), the animal is immediately taken out into fresh air and the order of awakening is observed.
The results are entered into a table and compared with an intravenous agent (thiopental): with it, stage II is hardly seen.

parts.text: Main criteria of the depth of anesthesia in the laboratory: the **righting reflex** (consciousness), **response to pain**, the **corneal reflex**, **muscle tone**, and **respiratory rate and pattern**. A sharp slowing of breathing is a sign of the danger of passing into stage IV.

blocks.text: **Neuroleptics** — drugs that eliminate **psychoses** (hallucinations, delusions, psychomotor agitation, thought disorders). They do not cause loss of consciousness and do not produce anesthesia even at large doses.
**History.** In 1952, in France, Delay and Deniker introduced chlorpromazine (aminazine) into psychiatry — the “psychopharmacological revolution” began.
4.1. Mechanism of action

According to the **dopamine theory** of psychoses, the positive symptoms of schizophrenia are associated with increased dopamine activity in the **mesolimbic** pathway. Neuroleptics **block D~2~ dopamine receptors**. Depending on which dopaminergic system is blocked, both therapeutic and adverse effects arise.

blocks.title: Table 7.6. Dopaminergic pathways and the effects of neuroleptics
head: Route
Function
Result of D~2~ blockade
rows: Worsening of negative symptoms and cognitive impairment
Extrapyramidal disorders (parkinsonism, dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia)
Chemoreceptor trigger zone of the vomiting center

parts.text: The 4 dopamine pathways — **“Limbic — Cortex — Substantia nigra — Pituitary”**: meso**limbic** (psychosis decreases), meso**cortical** (negative symptoms), nigrostriatal — **substantia nigra** (movement disorders), tuberoinfundibular — **pituitary** (prolactin increases). The therapeutic effect is only in the first; the others are a source of adverse effects.

blocks.text: Most neuroleptics also block other receptors, which determines additional effects: **alpha-1** (hypotension, orthostatic collapse), **M-cholinergic receptors** (dry mouth, constipation, tachycardia, urinary retention), **H~1~** (sedation, weight gain), **5-HT~2A~** (in atypical neuroleptics — reduces extrapyramidal disorders).
4.2. Classification of neuroleptics

Chemical group
Preparations
Property

Strongly antipsychotic, little sedation; the most extrapyramidal disorders; haloperidol decanoate — a depot preparation (once a month)
At small doses — antidepressant, at large doses — antipsychotic
Risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine, aripiprazole, ziprasidone, paliperidone, lurasidone
D~2~ + 5-HT~2A~ blockade (aripiprazole — a partial D~2~ agonist); few extrapyramidal disorders; also act on negative symptoms

blocks.text: 4.3. Pharmacological effects and uses

items: **Antipsychotic** — elimination of hallucinations and delusions;
**sedative**, stopping psychomotor agitation;
**antiemetic** (D~2~ blockade in the trigger zone; droperidol and metoclopramide also have this mechanism);
**potentiation** of the effects of anesthetics, analgesics and hypnotics;
**hypothermic** (depression of the thermoregulatory center);

**anti-hiccup** (chlorpromazine). **Uses:** schizophrenia, mania in bipolar disorder, acute psychoses (alcoholic delirium, organic psychoses), psychomotor agitation, delirium (haloperidol), vomiting, neuroleptanalgesia (droperidol), Tourette's syndrome, as an adjunct in treatment-resistant depression (atypical agents).

Involuntary movements of the face, lips, tongue and limbs; often irreversible
Change of neuroleptic (clozapine), VMAT2 inhibitors; anticholinergics make it worse

parts.text: **Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)** — a rare but life-threatening complication (mortality up to 10%): **high fever**, **“lead-pipe” muscle rigidity**, impaired consciousness, autonomic instability (tachycardia, fluctuating BP, sweating), a **sharp rise in blood creatine kinase**, leukocytosis, rhabdomyolysis and renal failure. **Treatment:** stop the neuroleptic immediately, intensive care, cooling, fluids, **dantrolene** and/or **bromocriptine** (a dopamine agonist), benzodiazepines.

blocks.text: Other adverse effects:

items: **metabolic syndrome** (weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia) — especially with olanzapine and clozapine;
**hyperprolactinemia** — with risperidone and typical agents;
**QT prolongation** and torsades de pointes arrhythmia — thioridazine, haloperidol (intravenous), ziprasidone;
**orthostatic hypotension** (alpha-1 blockade) — chlorpromazine, clozapine, quetiapine;
anticholinergic effects, sedation, lowering of the seizure threshold;
**agranulocytosis** — **clozapine** (up to 1%; regular monitoring of blood counts is mandatory), myocarditis;
skin photosensitization, cholestatic jaundice (chlorpromazine);
increased risk of stroke and death in elderly patients with dementia.

parts.text: **Clozapine** is the most effective neuroleptic in treatment-resistant schizophrenia and does not cause tardive dyskinesia, but because of the risk of agranulocytosis it is prescribed only with weekly (later monthly) monitoring of the white cell count.

blocks.text: **Anxiolytics** — drugs that reduce anxiety, fear and emotional tension. They do not eliminate psychoses.
5.1. Benzodiazepines

**Mechanism of action.** Benzodiazepines bind to a special **benzodiazepine (allosteric) binding site** of the **GABA-A receptor–chloride channel complex** and increase the affinity of GABA for the receptor. As a result, the **frequency of chloride channel opening** under the action of GABA increases, and the neuron is hyperpolarized — inhibition is enhanced. Benzodiazepines do not open the channel by themselves in the absence of GABA — that is why they are relatively safe when used alone.

blocks.label: Figure 7.2
blocks.caption: Action of benzodiazepines (BZ) and flumazenil on the GABA-A receptor: BZs bind to the allosteric site and enhance the action of GABA, flumazenil competitively blocks them (D.A. Kharkevich, Pharmacology, 2010)

parts.text: **Benzodiazepines** increase the **frequency** of chloride channel opening, while **barbiturates** increase its **duration**. At large doses, barbiturates open the channel even without GABA — that is why their therapeutic range is narrow and they can paralyze the respiratory center.

blocks.text: The five main effects of benzodiazepines:

items: **anxiolytic** (reducing anxiety);
**sedative and hypnotic**;
**muscle relaxant** (central, at the spinal cord level);
**anticonvulsant**;
**amnestic** (anterograde amnesia).

blocks.text: **Adverse effects:** drowsiness, lethargy, reduced reaction speed (dangerous for drivers), ataxia and **falls and hip fractures in the elderly**, anterograde amnesia, paradoxical excitement (in children and the elderly); **tolerance, psychological and physical dependence**; **withdrawal** on abrupt cessation (anxiety, insomnia, tremor, seizures); with alcohol, opioids and other CNS depressants — respiratory depression.

parts.text: Benzodiazepines are prescribed in **short courses** (not more than 2–4 weeks). In chronic anxiety disorders, the first choice is **antidepressants** (SSRIs) and psychotherapy. When long-term benzodiazepines are stopped, the dose must be reduced gradually over several weeks to months. **Combination with opioids** is one of the main causes of overdose deaths.

blocks.text: **Benzodiazepine poisoning:** drowsiness, ataxia, dysarthria, coma in severe cases; alone, respiratory depression is rare, but it is severe with alcohol and opioids. **Antidote — flumazenil** (a competitive antagonist of benzodiazepine receptors), 0.2 mg intravenously, up to 1 mg. The effect of flumazenil is short (≈ 1 hour), and resedation is possible; in chronic users and in mixed poisoning with tricyclic antidepressants, it may provoke **seizures**.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 30-year-old man injured in a road accident was brought to surgery with intra-abdominal bleeding. BP 75/40 mm Hg, HR 130/min. Induction of anesthesia is needed for emergency laparotomy.
cases.ask: 1) Which induction anesthetic is appropriate and why? 2) Which agent is dangerous?
cases.answer: 1) Ketamine (or etomidate): ketamine activates the sympathetic system and maintains or raises BP and heart rate; etomidate hardly affects hemodynamics. In parallel, blood and fluid replacement. 2) Propofol and thiopental, because of vasodilation and myocardial depression, can cause severe hypotension and cardiac arrest in a patient in hemorrhagic shock.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 22-year-old man was given haloperidol intramuscularly for an acute episode of schizophrenia. After 6 hours, the patient's head was pulled back and to the side, his eyes became fixed in an upward gaze, the tongue protruded, and speaking was difficult.
cases.ask: 1) What complication is this? 2) Its mechanism? 3) Treatment.
cases.answer: 1) Acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis, torticollis) — an extrapyramidal disorder. 2) Haloperidol blocks D~2~ receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway; the dopamine–acetylcholine balance is disturbed and cholinergic influence predominates. 3) Biperiden 2.5–5 mg or diphenhydramine 50 mg intramuscularly/intravenously (central M-cholinergic blockers restore the balance); then oral biperiden for several days; consider switching to an atypical neuroleptic with few extrapyramidal effects.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 75-year-old woman has taken phenazepam every day for 3 years for insomnia. In the last month she has fallen twice at night, and her forgetfulness has increased. Her daughter wants to stop the drug immediately.
cases.ask: 1) The link between the symptoms and the drug? 2) Is stopping the drug immediately correct? 3) Recommendations.
cases.answer: 1) A benzodiazepine with a long t½ accumulates in the elderly and causes ataxia, falls and cognitive impairment (a wrong choice for the elderly). 2) No — after 3 years of use there is physical dependence; abrupt cessation may cause a withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, insomnia, seizures, delirium). 3) Reduce the dose gradually over several weeks to months (by 10–25% every 2 weeks); cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, sleep hygiene; if there is depression or anxiety — an antidepressant; measures to reduce the risk of falls.

topics.title: Psychostimulants. Antidepressants

goals.text: Depression is one of the leading causes of disability in the world; it often hides behind somatic complaints (fatigue, insomnia, pain) at the GP's appointment. Antidepressants are among the most frequently prescribed drugs, but their delayed onset of action, serotonin syndrome and the risk of tricyclic antidepressant poisoning require sound knowledge. Psychostimulants are used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy, but they carry a high risk of abuse.
The student should know:

items: the classification of CNS stimulants;
the mechanism, effects, uses and adverse effects of psychostimulants (caffeine, amphetamine, methylphenidate, modafinil, mesocarb);
the monoamine theory of depression and the classification, mechanism, uses and adverse effects of antidepressants;
the clinical picture and treatment of serotonin syndrome and tricyclic antidepressant poisoning.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for preparations such as caffeine sodium benzoate, methylphenidate, amitriptyline, sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, venlafaxine and mirtazapine;
choose an antidepressant for a patient and explain the rules for taking it.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The effect of caffeine **depends on the initial state of the CNS**: it is strong in a tired person and weak in a rested one. Consuming more than 400 mg a day (about 4 cups of coffee) leads to anxiety, insomnia and tachycardia; when regular use is stopped abruptly, headache and lethargy (withdrawal) occur. Contraindications: anxiety disorders, insomnia, severe hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, glaucoma, gastric ulcer.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **TCA poisoning** — one of the most dangerous poisonings in suicide attempts (narrow therapeutic range: a 10–15-day supply can be fatal). Signs — **“3 C's”**: **C**oma, **C**onvulsions (seizures), **C**ardiotoxicity (wide QRS, arrhythmias, hypotension) + anticholinergic syndrome. **Treatment:** secure the airway, activated charcoal, intravenous **sodium bicarbonate** (if QRS > 100 ms — the sodium load and alkalinization reduce cardiotoxicity), benzodiazepines for seizures. Physostigmine and flumazenil are **contraindicated** (risk of seizures, asystole). A depressed patient should not be prescribed a large quantity of TCAs at one time.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **In children, adolescents and people under 25**, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior may increase in the first weeks of antidepressant treatment. The patient and relatives are warned, and frequent follow-up is arranged in the first month of treatment.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Distinguishing serotonin syndrome from NMS**: serotonin syndrome — **rapid** (hours), **clonus and hyperreflexia**, diarrhea, mydriasis (a serotonergic drug); NMS — **slow** (days), **“lead-pipe” rigidity**, hyporeflexia (a neuroleptic).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Basic rules of antidepressant treatment:** 1. The effect begins in **2–4 weeks**, the full effect in 6–8 weeks; the patient must be warned about this. 2. Start with a small dose and increase to the effective dose over 1–2 weeks. 3. If there is no effect after 4–6 weeks, increase the dose or switch to another group. 4. After remission, treatment is continued for at least **6–12 months** (in recurrent episodes — for years). 5. Withdrawal — **gradually** (over several weeks): abrupt cessation causes dizziness, “electric shock” sensations, nausea, anxiety and sleep disturbance. 6. Assess suicide risk; if there is a risk — refer to a psychiatrist.

blocks.text: **Psychostimulants** increase mental and physical activity, temporarily reduce fatigue and drowsiness, lift the mood and improve attention.
2.1. Caffeine and methylxanthines

**Caffeine** — an alkaloid of tea leaves, coffee beans, cocoa and the kola nut; a methylxanthine. With sodium benzoate, as **caffeine sodium benzoate**, it is readily soluble in water and suitable for injection.
Mechanism of action:

items: **Blockade of adenosine receptors (A~1~ and A~2A~)** — the main mechanism. Adenosine is an inhibitory modulator in the CNS; its blockade leads to excitation.
**Inhibition of phosphodiesterase** (at high concentrations) — accumulation of cAMP.
Enhanced release of Ca^2+^ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (at very high doses).

blocks.title: Table 8.2. Effects of caffeine
head: System
Effect
rows: Stimulates the cerebral cortex: alertness, reduced fatigue, increased mental performance; at large doses — restlessness, insomnia, tremor, seizures; stimulates the respiratory and vasomotor centers
The force and rate of contraction increase (tachycardia and arrhythmia at large doses)
Constricts cerebral vessels (reduces pain in migraine); directly dilates other vessels

blocks.text: **Uses:** mental and physical fatigue, drowsiness; in combination with analgesics for headache and migraine (Ascofen, Citramon, Cofetamin); hypotension; mild poisoning with CNS depressants; **apnea** in preterm infants (caffeine citrate — the first choice).

parts.text: The effect of caffeine **depends on the initial state of the CNS**: it is strong in a tired person and weak in a rested one. Consuming more than 400 mg a day (about 4 cups of coffee) leads to anxiety, insomnia and tachycardia; when regular use is stopped abruptly, headache and lethargy (withdrawal) occur. Contraindications: anxiety disorders, insomnia, severe hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, glaucoma, gastric ulcer.

blocks.text: 2.2. Amphetamine, methylphenidate and others

**Amphetamine** — a phenylalkylamine; an indirect sympathomimetic. It enhances the **release of dopamine and norepinephrine** from nerve endings and inhibits their reuptake. A strong psychostimulant; it reduces appetite and raises BP. It is under strict control as a **narcotic drug**; it causes dependence and psychoses.

**Methylphenidate** — blocks the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine. The main drug for treating **attention deficit hyperactivity disorder** (ADHD); paradoxically, it calms hyperactive children and improves attention. It is also used in narcolepsy.
**Modafinil** — reduces daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy and shift work disorder; the risk of dependence is lower than with amphetamine.
**Mesocarb (Sydnocarb)** — used in CIS countries for asthenic states; its effect develops gradually.
**Atomoxetine** — a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; not a psychostimulant, the second choice in ADHD, does not cause dependence.

rows: Take the drug in the first half of the day
Reduced appetite, weight loss, growth retardation in children

The body's resources are spent and no rest is given

parts.text: **Cocaine** — a local anesthetic and a strong psychostimulant: it blocks the reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin. Cocaine poisoning causes hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension, coronary spasm (**myocardial infarction in a young person**), seizures and psychosis. Treatment: **benzodiazepines** (the main treatment), cooling, nitrates and calcium antagonists; nonselective **beta-blockers are contraindicated** (unopposed alpha vasoconstriction).

blocks.text: 3.1. The monoamine theory of depression

**Depression** — a disease with a depressed mood or loss of interest (anhedonia) lasting at least 2 weeks, accompanied by disturbed sleep and appetite, fatigue, feelings of guilt, reduced concentration and thoughts of death.

According to the **monoamine theory**, depression is associated with a deficiency of **serotonin** and **norepinephrine** (and also dopamine) in the CNS. Antidepressants increase the amount of these mediators in the synapse. However, although mediator concentrations rise within a few hours, the clinical effect appears only **after 2–4 weeks** — this is explained by adaptation of receptor sensitivity (down-regulation), neuroplasticity and increased production of BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor).

blocks.text: 3.3. Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)

**Amitriptyline** — the most commonly used TCA; it has a strong **sedative and anxiolytic** component (H~1~ blockade). **Imipramine** — has a stimulating component. **Clomipramine** — serotonergic, effective in obsessive-compulsive disorder.

**Uses:** depression (now more often as second line), **chronic pain syndromes** — neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, tension-type headache and migraine prophylaxis (in small doses), nocturnal enuresis in children (imipramine), insomnia.

parts.text: **TCA poisoning** — one of the most dangerous poisonings in suicide attempts (narrow therapeutic range: a 10–15-day supply can be fatal). Signs — **“3 C's”**: **C**oma, **C**onvulsions (seizures), **C**ardiotoxicity (wide QRS, arrhythmias, hypotension) + anticholinergic syndrome. **Treatment:** secure the airway, activated charcoal, intravenous **sodium bicarbonate** (if QRS > 100 ms — the sodium load and alkalinization reduce cardiotoxicity), benzodiazepines for seizures. Physostigmine and flumazenil are **contraindicated** (risk of seizures, asystole). A depressed patient should not be prescribed a large quantity of TCAs at one time.

blocks.text: 3.4. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

SSRIs are **first-line** drugs for depression, anxiety disorders, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder, bulimia and premenstrual dysphoria. They are safer: they hardly act on M, H~1~ and alpha-1 receptors and are of low toxicity in overdose.

blocks.title: Table 8.6. Properties of SSRI preparations

Property

blocks.text: **Adverse effects of SSRIs:** nausea and dyspepsia (in the first weeks), headache, insomnia or drowsiness, **sexual dysfunction** (libido and orgasm), increased anxiety in the first weeks, hyponatremia (in the elderly), increased risk of bleeding (platelet serotonin decreases — especially with NSAIDs and anticoagulants), QT prolongation (citalopram, escitalopram), withdrawal syndrome.

parts.text: **In children, adolescents and people under 25**, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior may increase in the first weeks of antidepressant treatment. The patient and relatives are warned, and frequent follow-up is arranged in the first month of treatment.

blocks.text: 3.5. Serotonin syndrome

**Serotonin syndrome** — an excessive increase of serotonin in the CNS. Causes: combinations of serotonergic drugs — SSRIs/SNRIs + **MAO inhibitors** (the most dangerous), tramadol, triptans, linezolid, methylene blue, lithium, St John's wort, MDMA (ecstasy).

blocks.title: Table 8.7. Signs of serotonin syndrome (triad)
head: Group
Signs
rows: Hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating, mydriasis, diarrhea, fluctuating BP
Clonus (especially in the legs, ocular clonus), hyperreflexia, tremor, muscle rigidity

blocks.text: **Treatment:** stop the serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines (for agitation and muscle hyperactivity), cooling, fluids; in severe cases **cyproheptadine** (a 5-HT~2A~ antagonist), intensive care.

parts.text: **Distinguishing serotonin syndrome from NMS**: serotonin syndrome — **rapid** (hours), **clonus and hyperreflexia**, diarrhea, mydriasis (a serotonergic drug); NMS — **slow** (days), **“lead-pipe” rigidity**, hyporeflexia (a neuroleptic).

blocks.text: 3.6. SNRIs, MAO inhibitors and atypical antidepressants

**SNRIs** (venlafaxine, duloxetine) — severe depression, anxiety; **duloxetine** — also for the pain of diabetic neuropathy and fibromyalgia. Adverse effects: rise in BP (venlafaxine, at high doses), nausea, sweating, strong withdrawal syndrome.

**MAO inhibitors.** Irreversible nonselective agents (phenelzine) are now used only in treatment-resistant cases. While taking them, eating **tyramine-rich foods** (aged cheese, smoked fish and meat, red wine, beer, soy sauce) causes a **hypertensive crisis** (“cheese reaction”). A **2-week** break is needed before switching to an SSRI (5 weeks when switching from fluoxetine to an MAOI). **Moclobemide** (reversible, MAO-A) — low risk of the “cheese reaction”.

**Mirtazapine** — sedative, increases appetite, little effect on sexual function; convenient in depression with insomnia and weight loss and in the elderly. **Bupropion** — does not affect sexual function, causes no weight gain, also used for smoking cessation; lowers the seizure threshold. **Trazodone** — in small doses for insomnia; rarely priapism. **Agomelatine** — restores the circadian rhythm; liver enzymes must be monitored.
3.7. Principles of antidepressant treatment

parts.text: **Basic rules of antidepressant treatment:** 1. The effect begins in **2–4 weeks**, the full effect in 6–8 weeks; the patient must be warned about this. 2. Start with a small dose and increase to the effective dose over 1–2 weeks. 3. If there is no effect after 4–6 weeks, increase the dose or switch to another group. 4. After remission, treatment is continued for at least **6–12 months** (in recurrent episodes — for years). 5. Withdrawal — **gradually** (over several weeks): abrupt cessation causes dizziness, “electric shock” sensations, nausea, anxiety and sleep disturbance. 6. Assess suicide risk; if there is a risk — refer to a psychiatrist.

blocks.text: In **bipolar disorder**, antidepressants are given only together with mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate, lamotrigine) — otherwise there is a risk of switching to **mania**.

parts.text: Screening for the GP: the **PHQ-2** questions — “Over the last 2 weeks, have you been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?” and “Have you lost interest or pleasure in doing things?”. A “yes” to both requires a more thorough assessment (PHQ-9).

skills.title: Skill 1. Instructions given to the patient when prescribing an antidepressant

items: The drug does not improve the mood immediately — the effect begins in 2–4 weeks.
Nausea and headache in the first days usually pass within 1–2 weeks.
Do not stop the drug yourself, even if you feel better — it is continued for at least 6–12 months.
Avoid alcoholic drinks.
Take other drugs (tramadol, migraine drugs, St John's wort) only after agreeing with the physician.
If your condition worsens or thoughts of harming yourself appear — seek help immediately.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 19-year-old female student was brought in by her relatives: 2 hours ago she took 30 of her mother's amitriptyline tablets. The patient is drowsy, her speech is slurred, the pupils are dilated, the skin is dry and hot, HR 135/min, BP 90/55 mm Hg. The ECG shows QRS 130 ms. She had one seizure during transport.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Mechanism of the signs? 3) Treatment.
cases.answer: 1) Acute poisoning with a tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline). 2) Mydriasis, dry hot skin, tachycardia — anticholinergic effect; hypotension — alpha-1 blockade; QRS widening — sodium channel blockade (cardiotoxicity); seizures and drowsiness — CNS effect. 3) Secure the airway (intubation if necessary), activated charcoal; sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1–2 mmol/kg intravenously (until the QRS narrows, blood pH 7.45–7.55); for seizures — benzodiazepines; for hypotension — fluids and norepinephrine; ECG monitoring; physostigmine and flumazenil are contraindicated. After recovery — psychiatric consultation (suicide attempt).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 45-year-old woman has taken sertraline for depression for 3 months. An orthopedic trauma surgeon prescribed tramadol for low back pain. Two days later the patient developed restlessness, profuse sweating, tremor, diarrhea, a temperature of 38.8 °C, HR 118/min, and clonus and hyperreflexia in the legs.
cases.ask: 1) Your diagnosis? 2) The cause? 3) Treatment.
cases.answer: 1) Serotonin syndrome. 2) Sertraline (an SSRI) and tramadol (an opioid + inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake) — a combination of two serotonergic agents. 3) Stop both drugs, benzodiazepines (for agitation and muscle hyperactivity), cooling, fluids; cyproheptadine for marked signs; in severe hyperthermia — intensive care. Later, choose a non-serotonergic analgesic for the pain (paracetamol, NSAIDs).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 70-year-old man (history of prostatic adenoma, angle-closure glaucoma, ischemic heart disease) presented with signs of depression: insomnia, loss of appetite, a weight loss of 6 kg in 3 months.
cases.ask: Which antidepressant would you choose, and which should be avoided?
cases.answer: Mirtazapine (improves sleep, increases appetite, has no anticholinergic effect, relatively safe for the heart) or sertraline. TCAs (amitriptyline) are absolutely not recommended: the anticholinergic effect causes urinary retention in prostatic adenoma, an attack of glaucoma and delirium in the elderly; sodium channel blockade — arrhythmia in IHD; alpha-1 blockade — falls. Paroxetine is also inappropriate because of its anticholinergic effect. In an elderly patient, the sodium level should be monitored (SSRIs — hyponatremia).

topics.title: Drugs acting on the respiratory system

goals.text: Cough, sputum and bronchial obstruction are among the most common complaints at the GP's appointment. Bronchial asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) affect millions of people, and correctly chosen inhalation therapy radically changes their quality of life. At the same time, errors such as using antitussives together with expectorants, or treating asthma only with a “reliever”, are widespread. This topic covers respiratory pharmacology on the basis of modern clinical guidelines.
The student should know:

items: the classification of drugs acting on the respiratory system;
respiratory stimulants (analeptics) and their current place;
the mechanism and uses of antitussive (central and peripheral), expectorant and mucolytic agents;
bronchodilators (beta-2 adrenomimetics, M-cholinergic blockers, methylxanthines) and anti-inflammatory agents used in bronchial asthma;
the principles of stepwise treatment of bronchial asthma and COPD, and the treatment of pulmonary edema.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for preparations such as salbutamol, budesonide/formoterol, tiotropium, aminophylline (Euphylline), acetylcysteine, ambroxol, codeine, butamirate and montelukast;
provide emergency care in an attack of bronchial asthma;
choose a drug according to the type of cough.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks recommended analeptics for restoring breathing in poisoning with anesthetics, hypnotics and alcohol. In modern practice, respiratory failure is treated by **securing the airway, oxygen and mechanical ventilation**. The effect of analeptics is short and their therapeutic range is narrow; in a severely depressed CNS they are ineffective, and at large doses they cause **seizures** and increase oxygen demand. Doxapram is used by specialists in some cases (respiratory depression after anesthesia, hypercapnia in COPD); the specific antidote in opioid poisoning is **naloxone**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Antitussives and expectorants (mucolytics) must not be given together**: the mucolytic thins the sputum and increases its volume, while the antitussive suppresses the reflex that expels it — sputum accumulates in the bronchi (**“bogging”**), and the risk of pneumonia and obstruction increases.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **In bronchial asthma, using a LABA as monotherapy without an ICS is forbidden** — the risk of death from asthma increases (the inflammation is not treated and the symptoms are masked). In addition, current GINA recommendations (since 2019) **do not recommend treating asthma with a SABA (salbutamol) alone** in adults and adolescents; every patient should receive ICS-containing treatment.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Theophylline has a **narrow therapeutic range** (effective blood concentration 5–15 mg/l, above 20 mg/l — toxic): nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, **arrhythmias**, **seizures**. It is metabolized by CYP1A2: **ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin and fluvoxamine** increase its concentration; smoking and rifampicin decrease it. Aminophylline (Euphylline) must be given intravenously **very slowly** (over at least 10–20 minutes). In modern recommendations, methylxanthines are only reserve drugs in asthma and COPD.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The main rule of asthma control**: “Every asthmatic should receive an ICS”. Budesonide/formoterol in a single inhaler serves both as maintenance anti-inflammatory therapy and as a fast-acting bronchodilator — this reduces severe attacks and hospitalizations. Alternative approach: ICS (or ICS-LABA) maintenance therapy + salbutamol for attacks.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Treatment approaches are constantly being updated: older textbooks recommended starting asthma treatment with salbutamol and using aminophylline and cromones as maintenance drugs. Rely on the current GINA reports (updated every year) and the national clinical protocols of Uzbekistan.

blocks.text: **Analeptics** stimulate the respiratory center in the medulla oblongata directly (bemegride, nikethamide, caffeine, doxapram) or reflexly through the chemoreceptors of the carotid bodies (lobeline, cytisine; doxapram as well).
**Carbogen** (a mixture of 5–7% CO~2~ and 93–95% O~2~) — a physiological stimulant of the respiratory center.

parts.text: Older textbooks recommended analeptics for restoring breathing in poisoning with anesthetics, hypnotics and alcohol. In modern practice, respiratory failure is treated by **securing the airway, oxygen and mechanical ventilation**. The effect of analeptics is short and their therapeutic range is narrow; in a severely depressed CNS they are ineffective, and at large doses they cause **seizures** and increase oxygen demand. Doxapram is used by specialists in some cases (respiratory depression after anesthesia, hypercapnia in COPD); the specific antidote in opioid poisoning is **naloxone**.

blocks.text: **Cough** is a protective reflex that clears the airways. Therefore suppressing cough is appropriate only for a **dry, unproductive, troublesome** cough (when the cough disturbs sleep and quality of life).

parts.text: **Antitussives and expectorants (mucolytics) must not be given together**: the mucolytic thins the sputum and increases its volume, while the antitussive suppresses the reflex that expels it — sputum accumulates in the bronchi (**“bogging”**), and the risk of pneumonia and obstruction increases.

blocks.text: 4.1. Expectorants

**Reflex-acting** agents irritate receptors in the gastric mucosa and, through the vagus nerve, reflexly enhance bronchial gland secretion and the activity of the ciliated epithelium (gastropulmonary reflex). At large doses they cause **vomiting** (proximity to the vomiting center). Preparations: thermopsis herb, polygala root, marshmallow root (also provides mucilage), licorice root, ivy leaf extract, terpin hydrate.

**Directly (resorptively) acting** agents, after absorption, are excreted through the bronchial glands, increase secretion and thin the sputum: potassium and sodium iodide (contraindicated in thyrotoxicosis and iodine allergy), sodium bicarbonate (inhalation), ammonium chloride.
4.2. Mucolytics

blocks.title: Table 9.3. Mucolytics
head: Preparation
Mechanism
Features
rows: Free SH groups break the disulfide bonds of mucoproteins; a precursor of glutathione
Oral, inhalation, injection; antidote for paracetamol poisoning; may cause bronchospasm (by inhalation)
Increases serous gland secretion, depolymerizes mucopolysaccharides; converted to ambroxol in the body
The active metabolite of bromhexine; increases surfactant synthesis, improves mucociliary clearance
Recombinant DNase; breaks down neutrophil DNA in purulent sputum

parts.text: In cough due to acute bronchitis and viral infections, the effectiveness of mucolytics and expectorants is limited; **adequate fluid intake** and air humidity are important. In children under 2 years, mucolytics may increase sputum accumulation in the bronchi — they are used with caution.

blocks.label: Figure 9.2
blocks.caption: Mechanism of action of bronchodilators: beta-2 adrenomimetics increase cAMP, M-cholinergic blockers reduce cGMP formation and the spasmogenic effect (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: 5.1. Beta-2 adrenomimetics

They stimulate beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle: G~s~ → adenylate cyclase → **cAMP ↑** → relaxation of the muscle through protein kinase A; in addition, they reduce mediator release from mast cells and improve mucociliary clearance.

blocks.title: Table 9.4. Beta-2 adrenomimetics
head: Group
Preparations
Onset / duration of action
Role
rows: Relief of attacks, prevention before exercise
In maintenance therapy — only together with an ICS
Maintenance therapy + relief of attacks (together with budesonide)

parts.text: **In bronchial asthma, using a LABA as monotherapy without an ICS is forbidden** — the risk of death from asthma increases (the inflammation is not treated and the symptoms are masked). In addition, current GINA recommendations (since 2019) **do not recommend treating asthma with a SABA (salbutamol) alone** in adults and adolescents; every patient should receive ICS-containing treatment.

blocks.text: 5.2. M-cholinergic blockers

Ipratropium (short-acting, 6–8 hours) and tiotropium, glycopyrronium and umeclidinium (long-acting, 24 hours) block M~3~ receptors in the bronchi and reduce the bronchoconstrictor tone of the vagus nerve. In COPD, parasympathetic tone is the main reversible component of bronchial obstruction, so **long-acting M-cholinergic blockers (LAMAs) are the main bronchodilators in COPD**. In asthma — an add-on drug in severe cases. Adverse effects: dry mouth, rarely urinary retention, glaucoma (if it gets into the eye through a nebulizer mask).
5.3. Methylxanthines

**Theophylline** and **aminophylline** (**Euphylline**; theophylline + ethylenediamine, readily soluble in water): inhibit phosphodiesterase (cAMP ↑), block adenosine receptors and improve diaphragmatic contractility.

parts.text: Theophylline has a **narrow therapeutic range** (effective blood concentration 5–15 mg/l, above 20 mg/l — toxic): nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, **arrhythmias**, **seizures**. It is metabolized by CYP1A2: **ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin and fluvoxamine** increase its concentration; smoking and rifampicin decrease it. Aminophylline (Euphylline) must be given intravenously **very slowly** (over at least 10–20 minutes). In modern recommendations, methylxanthines are only reserve drugs in asthma and COPD.

sections.title: 6. Anti-inflammatory agents used in bronchial asthma

blocks.text: 6.1. Inhaled glucocorticoids (ICS)

**ICS are the most effective maintenance therapy for bronchial asthma.** They reduce allergic inflammation in the bronchial wall (eosinophils, mast cells, T lymphocytes, cytokines), reduce bronchial hyperreactivity and restore the sensitivity of beta-2 receptors. Their effect develops gradually (days to weeks) — **they do not stop an attack**.

Preparations: budesonide, fluticasone propionate and furoate, beclometasone dipropionate, mometasone, ciclesonide. Combinations: **budesonide/formoterol**, beclometasone/formoterol, fluticasone/salmeterol, fluticasone furoate/vilanterol.

**Adverse effects: oral and pharyngeal candidiasis**, hoarseness (dysphonia) — prevention: rinsing the mouth after inhalation, a spacer; with prolonged use at high doses — systemic effects (slight growth retardation in children, osteoporosis, cataract), risk of pneumonia in COPD.
6.2. Other anti-inflammatory agents

items: **Montelukast** — a cysteinyl leukotriene (CysLT1) receptor antagonist; one tablet a day. Aspirin-induced asthma, exercise-induced asthma, asthma with allergic rhinitis. Adverse effects: neuropsychiatric disorders (sleep, mood, suicidal thoughts) — warning.
**Cromones** (sodium cromoglicate, nedocromil) — stabilize the mast cell membrane and prevent degranulation; prophylactic only; rarely used now.
**Systemic glucocorticoids** (oral prednisolone, intravenous methylprednisolone) — a short course (5–7 days) in severe attacks.
**Biologics** — in severe uncontrolled asthma: omalizumab (allergic), mepolizumab, benralizumab (eosinophilic), dupilumab, tezepelumab.

parts.text: **The main rule of asthma control**: “Every asthmatic should receive an ICS”. Budesonide/formoterol in a single inhaler serves both as maintenance anti-inflammatory therapy and as a fast-acting bronchodilator — this reduces severe attacks and hospitalizations. Alternative approach: ICS (or ICS-LABA) maintenance therapy + salbutamol for attacks.

Treatment approaches are constantly being updated: older textbooks recommended starting asthma treatment with salbutamol and using aminophylline and cromones as maintenance drugs. Rely on the current GINA reports (updated every year) and the national clinical protocols of Uzbekistan.

blocks.text: 7.2. Emergency care in an attack of bronchial asthma

items: **Salbutamol** 2.5–5 mg via a nebulizer or 4–10 puffs (100 mcg) through a **spacer**, every 20 minutes in the first hour.
**Oxygen** (maintain SpO~2~ at 93–95%).
In a severe attack — **ipratropium** (together with salbutamol in a nebulizer).
**Systemic glucocorticoid** — prednisolone 40–50 mg orally (or methylprednisolone/hydrocortisone intravenously), for 5–7 days.
In a life-threatening attack — **magnesium sulfate** intravenously (2 g over 20 minutes), intensive care, intubation and mechanical ventilation.
**Sedatives are contraindicated** (they depress the respiratory center); beta-blockers are contraindicated.

blocks.text: 7.3. COPD

In COPD, the main bronchodilators are **LAMAs (tiotropium)** and **LABAs**, often a **LAMA + LABA** combination. An ICS is added only in frequently exacerbating COPD with high blood eosinophils. **Stopping smoking** is the only effective measure that slows the progression of the disease. In exacerbations — a SABA + a short-acting M-cholinergic blocker, a systemic glucocorticoid (5 days), and an antibiotic if there are signs of bacterial infection.
**Cardiogenic pulmonary edema** (left ventricular failure) is an emergency.

Mechanism

Correction of hypoxemia, reduction of fluid leakage into the alveoli
Nitroglycerin (sublingual, intravenous) — if BP > 110 mm Hg
Dilates the veins and reduces the load on the heart
Morphine (in a small dose, with caution)
Reduces anxiety and dyspnea, venodilation; but depresses breathing — routine use is now not recommended
Antifoaming agents (oxygen through 30–40% ethyl alcohol vapor, Antifomsilan)
Reduce the surface tension of the foam (mainly a historical method)

blocks.text: In pulmonary edema against a background of arterial hypertension, rapid lowering of BP is also used (ganglionic blockers — historically; now nitrates).

parts.text: **ACE inhibitors** (enalapril, lisinopril) cause a **dry cough** in 5–20% of patients (accumulation of bradykinin). Such a cough is not treated with antitussives — the ACE inhibitor is replaced with an angiotensin receptor blocker (losartan).
