cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 24-year-old woman has had bronchial asthma for 2 years. She uses only a salbutamol inhaler — in the last month 4–5 times a week, and she woke up choking at night twice. She used up 2 inhalers in one month.
cases.ask: 1) Is her asthma controlled? 2) What is the error in treatment? 3) Recommendations.
cases.answer: 1) Uncontrolled asthma (symptoms more than twice a week, night awakenings, frequent need for salbutamol). 2) Treatment with a SABA alone — the inflammation is not treated; heavy SABA use is associated with a risk of severe attacks and death. 3) Low-dose budesonide/formoterol in the MART regimen (one inhaler for maintenance and attacks) or ICS maintenance therapy; check inhaler technique, eliminate triggers, a written action plan; follow-up after 2–3 months.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 58-year-old man with COPD uses tiotropium once a day. Because of an exacerbation of bronchitis, the doctor prescribed ciprofloxacin; at home he has also been taking aminophylline (Euphylline) tablets for a long time. After 3 days he developed nausea, vomiting, palpitations and hand tremor.
cases.ask: 1) The cause of the symptoms? 2) Management?
cases.answer: 1) Theophylline toxicity: ciprofloxacin inhibited CYP1A2, slowed theophylline metabolism, and its blood concentration reached a toxic level (narrow therapeutic range). 2) Stop aminophylline, measure blood theophylline and potassium, ECG monitoring; in severe cases activated charcoal (repeated doses), treatment of arrhythmias and seizures. Replace the antibiotic with a drug that does not affect CYP1A2 (amoxicillin/clavulanate); optimize COPD maintenance therapy with a LAMA + LABA.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 3-year-old child has a dry cough during an ARVI. The mother bought a codeine cough syrup and an ambroxol syrup at the pharmacy at the same time.
cases.ask: Explain the mother's mistakes and give the correct advice.
cases.answer: 1) Codeine is not allowed in children under 12 — in CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers a lot of morphine is formed and there is a risk of respiratory arrest. 2) Giving an antitussive and a mucolytic together — sputum accumulation (“swamping” of the bronchi). 3) Advice: plenty of warm fluids, humidifying the room air, rinsing the nasal passages with saline; for a dry troublesome cough — an age-appropriate non-opioid agent (butamirate drops) on a pediatrician's advice; mucolytics with caution in children under 2; if there is shortness of breath or prolonged fever — a pediatrician's examination.

In asthma only with an ICS
The main maintenance therapy of asthma; rinse the mouth

topics.title: Antiarrhythmic drugs. Antianginal drugs

goals.text: Cardiac arrhythmias and ischemic heart disease (IHD) are the main forms of cardiovascular disease, which ranks first among causes of death. Atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, an attack of angina and acute coronary syndrome are conditions that GPs and emergency physicians face every day. Paradoxically, antiarrhythmic drugs can themselves cause arrhythmias (proarrhythmic effect), so choosing them requires a deep knowledge of their mechanisms. In line with the 6th-semester laboratory class, this topic also covers **cardiotonic drugs (cardiac glycosides)**.
The student should know:

items: the phases of the action potential of cardiac cells and the mechanisms of arrhythmias;
the classification of antiarrhythmic drugs (Vaughan Williams), the mechanism, uses and adverse effects of each class;
the pathogenesis of angina and the mechanism of antianginal drugs (nitrates, beta-blockers, calcium antagonists, others);
the mechanism and uses of cardiac glycosides and non-glycoside cardiotonics, and glycoside toxicity.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as amiodarone, verapamil, adenosine, lidocaine, nitroglycerin, isosorbide mononitrate, amlodipine, ivabradine and digoxin;
provide emergency care in an attack of angina and in supraventricular tachycardia;
recognize glycoside toxicity and draw up a plan of care.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Antiarrhythmics stop re-entry in two ways: **converting a unidirectional block into a bidirectional one** (slowing conduction even further — class I) or **prolonging the effective refractory period** (when the impulse returns, the tissue is still unexcitable — class III).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Vaughan Williams classes — **“Sodium, Beta, Potassium, Calcium”** (1, 2, 3, 4). To remember IA, IB, IC: **“IA — Affects both QRS and QT (prolongs both); IB — Best in ischemia; IC — Causes marked QRS widening”**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **The CAST trial** (1989): in patients with ventricular extrasystoles after myocardial infarction, flecainide and encainide reduced the extrasystoles but **increased mortality** (proarrhythmic effect). Since then class IC drugs **are contraindicated in IHD, after infarction and in heart failure**. This trial is the classic proof of the principle “treat the patient, not the ECG”.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The adverse effects of amiodarone — **“Thyroid, lungs, liver, eyes, skin”** — all the “fatty” organs where it accumulates. Amiodarone increases the concentrations of warfarin and digoxin — their doses must be reduced.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Verapamil and diltiazem: 1) **contraindicated** in atrial fibrillation with **WPW syndrome** — by blocking the AV node they “direct” impulses to the ventricles through the accessory pathway and may cause ventricular fibrillation; 2) contraindicated in **wide-QRS tachycardia** (it may be ventricular tachycardia); 3) not given **intravenously together with beta-blockers** (risk of asystole); 4) heart failure (reduced ejection fraction) — a contraindication.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Tolerance to nitrates** — with continuous use the effect decreases within 24–48 hours (depletion of sulfhydryl groups, neurohormonal activation). Prevention — **an 8–12-hour “nitrate-free interval” each day** (for example, sustained-release isosorbide mononitrate once a day in the morning; a patch is removed at night).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Nitrates + phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil)** — absolutely contraindicated: both increase cGMP and **life-threatening hypotension** develops. No nitrate is given for 24 hours after sildenafil or 48 hours after tadalafil. Other contraindications: hypotension (systolic BP < 90), right ventricular infarction, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, raised intracranial pressure.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Short-acting nifedipine** (ordinary capsules) **increases the risk of death** in acute coronary syndrome because of abrupt vasodilation and reflex sympathetic activation; giving it sublingually in a hypertensive crisis is also not recommended. In angina and hypertension only long-acting forms (amlodipine, nifedipine GITS) are used.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The higher the **lipophilicity** (nonpolarity) of glycosides, the stronger their intestinal absorption, protein binding, hepatic metabolism and **cumulation**: **digitoxin > digoxin > strophanthin**. Because digoxin is excreted by the kidneys, **its dose is reduced in renal failure**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks presented cardiac glycosides as the main drugs for treating heart failure and recommended “digitalization” (loading) schemes. In modern recommendations, the main treatment of heart failure is ACE inhibitors/ARNIs, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors (Topic 11); digoxin is an add-on drug used at low doses (blood concentration 0.5–0.9 ng/ml).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In glycoside toxicity **calcium preparations are contraindicated** (they worsen arrhythmias and cardiac arrest), and electrical cardioversion is avoided as far as possible (risk of ventricular fibrillation). Intravenous calcium preparations must not be given to a patient taking glycosides.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Conclusions of the experiment: cardiac glycosides have a **positive inotropic, negative chronotropic and dromotropic** effect; at toxic doses — arrhythmias and systolic arrest; **hypokalemia increases toxicity**. Verapamil is antiarrhythmic but negatively inotropic.

blocks.text: In the sinus and AV nodes, phase 0 depends on the **calcium** current — that is why beta-blockers and calcium antagonists slow conduction in them.
Mechanisms of arrhythmias:

items: **Disturbed impulse formation** — enhanced automaticity (ischemia, catecholamines, hypokalemia) and **triggered activity** (early and delayed afterdepolarizations; glycoside toxicity, long QT).
**Disturbed impulse conduction** — **re-entry**: with a unidirectional block and slow conduction, the impulse circulates and re-excites the tissue. The main mechanism of most tachyarrhythmias.

parts.text: Antiarrhythmics stop re-entry in two ways: **converting a unidirectional block into a bidirectional one** (slowing conduction even further — class I) or **prolonging the effective refractory period** (when the impulse returns, the tissue is still unexcitable — class III).

parts.text: Vaughan Williams classes — **“Sodium, Beta, Potassium, Calcium”** (1, 2, 3, 4). To remember IA, IB, IC: **“IA — Affects both QRS and QT (prolongs both); IB — Best in ischemia; IC — Causes marked QRS widening”**.

blocks.text: 2.2. Class I — sodium channel blockers

**Quinidine** — an alkaloid of the cinchona tree (an isomer of quinine). The classic IA antiarrhythmic; now hardly used: M-cholinergic blocking action (it may speed up AV conduction and increase the ventricular rate in atrial flutter), **QT prolongation and torsades de pointes** (quinidine syncope), diarrhea, cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, visual disturbances), thrombocytopenia; it increases digoxin concentration.

**Procainamide (Novocainamide)** — given intravenously to restore sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation and in ventricular tachycardia. Adverse effects: hypotension, QT prolongation, with prolonged use a **lupus-like syndrome** (especially in slow acetylators), agranulocytosis.

**Lidocaine** — selectively blocks sodium channels in ischemically damaged (depolarized) ventricular myocardium; it has almost no effect on the atria. Only **intravenously** (strong first-pass effect). Uses: **ventricular arrhythmias** (especially in acute ischemia), defibrillation-resistant ventricular fibrillation when amiodarone is not available. Toxicity — CNS signs (Topic 3).
**Class IC** (flecainide, propafenone) — for restoring rhythm in atrial fibrillation and preventing it (the **“pill-in-the-pocket”** approach), in patients **without** structural heart disease.

parts.text: **The CAST trial** (1989): in patients with ventricular extrasystoles after myocardial infarction, flecainide and encainide reduced the extrasystoles but **increased mortality** (proarrhythmic effect). Since then class IC drugs **are contraindicated in IHD, after infarction and in heart failure**. This trial is the classic proof of the principle “treat the patient, not the ECG”.

blocks.text: 2.3. Class II — beta-blockers

By reducing sympathetic stimulation, they slow sinus node automaticity and AV conduction. They are proven antiarrhythmics **that reduce the risk of sudden death after myocardial infarction**. Uses: sinus tachycardia, rate control in atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardias, catecholamine-dependent ventricular arrhythmias, long QT syndrome. **Esmolol** — ultrashort-acting, intravenous.
2.4. Class III — potassium channel blockers

**Amiodarone** — the most effective and broad-spectrum antiarrhythmic; it has properties of all four classes (blockade of K^+^, Na^+^ and Ca^2+^ channels and beta receptors). It may also be used in structural heart disease and heart failure.

items: **Pharmacokinetics:** highly lipophilic, a very large volume of distribution; **t½ — 40–60 days**; the effect develops over weeks — treatment is started with a **loading dose**.
**Uses:** atrial fibrillation (restoring and maintaining rhythm), ventricular tachycardia, defibrillation-resistant ventricular fibrillation **in cardiac arrest** (300 mg intravenously, then 150 mg).

blocks.title: Table 10.3. Adverse effects of amiodarone (it contains iodine and accumulates in tissues)
head: Organ
Adverse effect
Monitoring
rows: Interstitial pneumonitis, pulmonary fibrosis (the most dangerous)
Corneal microdeposits (in almost all patients), optic neuropathy
Bradycardia, AV block, QT prolongation (torsades is rare)

parts.text: The adverse effects of amiodarone — **“Thyroid, lungs, liver, eyes, skin”** — all the “fatty” organs where it accumulates. Amiodarone increases the concentrations of warfarin and digoxin — their doses must be reduced.

blocks.text: **Sotalol** — a beta-blocker + class III; prolongs QT, with a risk of torsades (reduce the dose in renal failure). **Dronedarone** — an iodine-free analog of amiodarone; contraindicated in severe heart failure.
2.5. Class IV — calcium channel blockers

**Verapamil** and **diltiazem** block the calcium current in the sinus and AV nodes and slow AV conduction. Uses: **supraventricular tachycardias** involving the AV node (if adenosine is ineffective), rate control in atrial fibrillation and flutter.

parts.text: Verapamil and diltiazem: 1) **contraindicated** in atrial fibrillation with **WPW syndrome** — by blocking the AV node they “direct” impulses to the ventricles through the accessory pathway and may cause ventricular fibrillation; 2) contraindicated in **wide-QRS tachycardia** (it may be ventricular tachycardia); 3) not given **intravenously together with beta-blockers** (risk of asystole); 4) heart failure (reduced ejection fraction) — a contraindication.

blocks.text: 2.6. Other antiarrhythmics

items: **Adenosine** — via A~1~ receptors briefly (for seconds) stops conduction in the AV node; t½ < 10 seconds. **The drug of choice for terminating AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia**: 6 mg intravenously as a **rapid bolus** (into a proximal vein, immediately “flushed” with 20 ml of saline); if there is no effect — 12 mg. Adverse effects (brief): chest discomfort, facial flushing, dyspnea, brief asystole. Contraindicated in **bronchial asthma**; theophylline reduces its effect, dipyridamole enhances it.
**Magnesium sulfate** — the drug of choice for **torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia** (long QT) (2 g intravenously); hypomagnesemia, glycoside arrhythmias.
**Digoxin** — slows AV conduction by increasing vagal tone; rate control in atrial fibrillation combined with heart failure (Section 6).
**Atropine** — in sinus bradycardia and AV blocks (Topic 4).

blocks.text: 2.7. Proarrhythmic effect of antiarrhythmics

Almost all antiarrhythmics can themselves cause new or more severe arrhythmias: classes IA and III — QT prolongation and **torsades de pointes**; IC — ventricular tachycardia (especially in ischemia); classes II and IV, digoxin — bradycardia and AV block. Factors that increase the risk of proarrhythmia: **hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia**, bradycardia, other QT-prolonging drugs (macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, ondansetron), renal failure, female sex.

parts.text: **Stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation** is more important than the choice of antiarrhythmic. According to the CHA~2~DS~2~-VASc score (≥ 2 points in men, ≥ 3 in women), an **oral anticoagulant** (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran or warfarin) is prescribed (Topic 14). Aspirin is ineffective for this purpose.

blocks.text: 3.1. Pathogenesis of angina

**Angina** is retrosternal pain caused by a mismatch between the myocardial oxygen **demand** and its **supply** through coronary blood flow. Causes: atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries (exertional angina), coronary spasm (vasospastic — Prinzmetal angina), thrombus (acute coronary syndrome).
Antianginal drugs work in two ways:

items: **reducing the myocardial oxygen demand** — lowering the heart rate, contractile force, preload (venous return) and afterload (BP);
**increasing the oxygen supply** to the myocardium — dilating the coronary vessels, relieving spasm, prolonging diastole (coronary perfusion takes place in diastole).

Dihydropyridines: amlodipine, nifedipine (sustained-release), felodipine; non-dihydropyridines: verapamil, diltiazem

blocks.text: 3.2. Organic nitrates

**Mechanism.** In the body, nitrates release **nitric oxide (NO)**. In smooth muscle cells NO activates guanylate cyclase → **cGMP** ↑ → myosin light chains are dephosphorylated → the vessel wall relaxes.
Hemodynamic effects:

items: at small doses they dilate mainly **veins** — venous return and the preload of the heart (diastolic volume and wall tension) decrease → **the myocardial oxygen demand decreases** (the main mechanism);
at large doses they also dilate arteries — BP (afterload) falls;
they dilate the large epicardial coronary arteries and **relieve spasm**, improve collateral blood flow and redistribute blood to the subendocardial layers.

Use

parts.text: **Tolerance to nitrates** — with continuous use the effect decreases within 24–48 hours (depletion of sulfhydryl groups, neurohormonal activation). Prevention — **an 8–12-hour “nitrate-free interval” each day** (for example, sustained-release isosorbide mononitrate once a day in the morning; a patch is removed at night).

blocks.text: **Adverse effects: headache** (dilation of cerebral vessels; the most common, usually decreasing over time), facial flushing, dizziness, **orthostatic hypotension** and fainting, reflex tachycardia, methemoglobinemia (at large doses), rebound on abrupt withdrawal of nitrates.

parts.text: **Nitrates + phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil)** — absolutely contraindicated: both increase cGMP and **life-threatening hypotension** develops. No nitrate is given for 24 hours after sildenafil or 48 hours after tadalafil. Other contraindications: hypotension (systolic BP < 90), right ventricular infarction, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, raised intracranial pressure.

blocks.text: 3.3. Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers

**Beta-blockers** (Topic 6) — **first-line** drugs for stable exertional angina: by lowering the heart rate they reduce oxygen demand, and by prolonging diastole they improve coronary perfusion. Target resting heart rate — 55–60 beats/min. In **vasospastic angina**, nonselective beta-blockers may worsen spasm.
**Calcium channel blockers** block L-type calcium channels and reduce Ca^2+^ entry into smooth muscle and cardiomyocytes.

parts.text: **Short-acting nifedipine** (ordinary capsules) **increases the risk of death** in acute coronary syndrome because of abrupt vasodilation and reflex sympathetic activation; giving it sublingually in a hypertensive crisis is also not recommended. In angina and hypertension only long-acting forms (amlodipine, nifedipine GITS) are used.

blocks.text: 3.4. Other antianginal drugs

items: **Ivabradine** — by selectively inhibiting the If current in the sinus node, it **reduces only the heart rate**; it does not affect contractility or BP. Effective only **in sinus rhythm** (not in atrial fibrillation). Used when a beta-blocker cannot be used or is insufficient. Adverse effects: **phosphenes** (flashes of light in vision), bradycardia.
**Trimetazidine** — reduces beta-oxidation of fatty acids and shifts metabolism to glucose oxidation (saves oxygen). An add-on drug; it may cause parkinsonism and movement disorders.
**Ranolazine** — inhibits the late sodium current and improves diastolic relaxation; slightly prolongs QT.
**Nicorandil** — a potassium channel opener and NO donor; may cause oral and intestinal ulcers.

blocks.text: 3.5. Prognosis-improving treatment
The treatment of angina has two goals: **reducing symptoms** (the antianginal drugs above) and **preventing myocardial infarction and death**:

items: **antiplatelet agents** — acetylsalicylic acid 75–100 mg/day (or clopidogrel);
**statins** — high-intensity (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin), to the target level of LDL cholesterol;
**ACE inhibitors** (or ARBs) — with concomitant hypertension, diabetes or heart failure;
**beta-blockers** — after infarction and in heart failure;
elimination of risk factors: stopping smoking, controlling BP and glucose, physical activity.

parts.text: **Care in an attack of angina**: stop physical activity, sit down; **nitroglycerin** 0.5 mg sublingually (or 1 spray dose); if the pain does not pass in 5 minutes — a second dose and **call an ambulance**; up to 3 doses in total. If the pain lasts more than 15–20 minutes — acute coronary syndrome is suspected: chew aspirin 150–300 mg (if there is no allergy), ECG, urgent hospitalization.

sections.title: 4. Cardiotonic drugs (cardiac glycosides and non-glycoside inotropes)

blocks.text: This section corresponds to the 6th-semester class “Laboratory study of the effects of antiarrhythmic and cardiotonic drugs on the heart”.
4.1. Cardiac glycosides

**Cardiac glycosides** are substances obtained from plants, whose molecule consists of an **aglycone (genin)** — a steroid nucleus and a lactone ring — and a **sugar** part. Sources: foxglove (Digitalis lanata — digoxin, Digitalis purpurea — digitoxin), strophanthus (strophanthin), lily of the valley (Corglycon), spring adonis.

**Mechanism of action.** Glycosides inhibit **Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase** in the cardiomyocyte membrane → Na^+^ increases inside the cell → Ca^2+^ efflux via the Na^+^/Ca^2+^ exchanger decreases → **Ca^2+^ increases** in the sarcoplasmic reticulum and cytoplasm → contraction is strengthened.

parts.text: The higher the **lipophilicity** (nonpolarity) of glycosides, the stronger their intestinal absorption, protein binding, hepatic metabolism and **cumulation**: **digitoxin > digoxin > strophanthin**. Because digoxin is excreted by the kidneys, **its dose is reduced in renal failure**.

blocks.text: Uses (modern):

items: **atrial fibrillation** — control of the ventricular rate (especially in heart failure and in patients with low mobility);
**chronic heart failure** (reduced ejection fraction) — when symptoms persist on the main drugs; it reduces hospitalizations but **does not reduce mortality**.

parts.text: Older textbooks presented cardiac glycosides as the main drugs for treating heart failure and recommended “digitalization” (loading) schemes. In modern recommendations, the main treatment of heart failure is ACE inhibitors/ARNIs, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors (Topic 11); digoxin is an add-on drug used at low doses (blood concentration 0.5–0.9 ng/ml).

blocks.text: 4.2. Glycoside toxicity

The therapeutic range is very narrow (the toxic dose is only 2–3 times the therapeutic dose). Factors that increase toxicity: **hypokalemia** (diuretics!), hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, old age, **renal failure**, hypothyroidism, hypoxia, drugs (**amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine and clarithromycin** increase digoxin concentration).

blocks.title: Table 10.10. Signs of glycoside toxicity
head: System
Signs
rows: Ventricular extrasystoles (bigeminy), ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, AV blocks, bradycardia, atrial tachycardia with block; “trough-shaped” (scooped) ST depression on the ECG (this also occurs at therapeutic doses)
Loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting (the first signs), abdominal pain, diarrhea
Headache, weakness, confusion (in the elderly), visual disturbances — objects appear yellow-green (xanthopsia), spots before the eyes

blocks.text: Treatment:

items: Stop the glycoside; measure the blood digoxin concentration and **potassium** level, ECG monitoring.
**Correction of hypokalemia** — potassium preparations (potassium chloride, Panangin) — only in the absence of AV block and hyperkalemia.
**Digoxin-specific antibody Fab fragments** — in life-threatening arrhythmias, hyperkalemia (> 5 mmol/l), severe toxicity.
In ventricular arrhythmias — **lidocaine**, phenytoin; magnesium sulfate; in bradycardia and AV block — atropine, temporary pacing.
**Unithiol** (a donor of SH groups) — reactivates Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase (used in CIS countries).
In acute poisoning — activated charcoal.

parts.text: In glycoside toxicity **calcium preparations are contraindicated** (they worsen arrhythmias and cardiac arrest), and electrical cardioversion is avoided as far as possible (risk of ventricular fibrillation). Intravenous calcium preparations must not be given to a patient taking glycosides.

blocks.text: 4.4. Laboratory class: effects of drugs on the isolated heart
Experiment (frog heart, Straub method, or isolated heart):

items: The frog heart is connected to a cannula and perfused with Ringer's solution; contractions are recorded with a kymograph or a sensor.
Normal contractions are recorded; then a **“heart failure model”** is created (for example, with a low-calcium solution — the contractions weaken).
**Strophanthin** or **digoxin** is added to the solution: the **contraction amplitude increases** (positive inotropy), systole is strong and short, diastole is prolonged, the rhythm slows.

When the glycoside dose is increased, a **toxic effect** is seen: arrhythmias, incomplete contractions and **arrest of the heart in systole**. If K^+^ in the solution is reduced, the toxic effect appears sooner.

**Studying the antiarrhythmic effect**: against the background of an arrhythmia (induced with calcium chloride or epinephrine), lidocaine or verapamil is added and restoration of the rhythm is observed; verapamil also reduces the force of contraction (negative inotropy).

parts.text: Conclusions of the experiment: cardiac glycosides have a **positive inotropic, negative chronotropic and dromotropic** effect; at toxic doses — arrhythmias and systolic arrest; **hypokalemia increases toxicity**. Verapamil is antiarrhythmic but negatively inotropic.

skills.title: Skill 1. Care in supraventricular (AV nodal) tachycardia

items: Record an ECG (narrow QRS, regular rhythm, 150–250 beats/min) and assess the hemodynamics.
Unstable (hypotension, shock, acute heart failure) — synchronized electrical cardioversion.
Stable — **the modified Valsalva maneuver** (straining, then lying the patient down and raising the legs); carotid sinus massage (not in the elderly or with a carotid bruit).
If ineffective — **adenosine 6 mg** as a rapid intravenous bolus + 20 ml of saline; if there is no effect in 1–2 minutes — 12 mg.
If adenosine cannot be used (asthma) or is ineffective — verapamil 5 mg intravenously slowly.
After the rhythm is restored, refer to a cardiologist (ablation).

blocks.text: **PRESCRIPTION 10.1. AMIODARONE (TABLETS)** Rp.: Amiodaroni 0.2
D.t.d. N. 30 in tabulettis S. Loading dose: 1 tablet 3 times a day for 1 week, then 1 tablet 2 times a day for 1 week, then 1 tablet a day.
**PRESCRIPTION 10.2. AMIODARONE (AMPOULES)** Rp.: Solutionis Amiodaroni 5% — 3 ml
D.t.d. N. 10 in ampullis S. 300 mg (2 ampoules) in 20 ml of 5% glucose intravenously (in cardiac arrest — as a bolus).

D.t.d. N. 6 in ampullis S. 6 mg as a rapid intravenous bolus, immediately flushed with 20 ml of 0.9% NaCl; if there is no effect, 12 mg.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 72-year-old woman takes digoxin 0.25 mg/day and furosemide for chronic heart failure and atrial fibrillation. In recent days she has lost her appetite, feels nauseous and vomits, and “everything looks yellowish”. The ECG shows ventricular bigeminy, HR 48 beats/min. Blood potassium is 3.0 mmol/l, creatinine is raised.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Aggravating factors? 3) Treatment.
cases.answer: 1) Glycoside (digoxin) toxicity. 2) Hypokalemia (furosemide), reduced renal function (digoxin is excreted by the kidneys), old age, a relatively large dose. 3) Stop digoxin and furosemide; measure the blood digoxin level; ECG monitoring; potassium preparations intravenously slowly (if there is no AV block); in severe arrhythmias — digoxin-specific Fab fragments, lidocaine; atropine for bradycardia. Calcium preparations are contraindicated. Later the digoxin dose is reduced according to creatinine clearance (0.0625–0.125 mg).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 55-year-old man has had exertional angina for 2 years and takes isosorbide mononitrate and bisoprolol. On a friend's advice he took sildenafil for erectile dysfunction; an hour later he had an attack of angina and also put a nitroglycerin tablet under his tongue. He lost consciousness, BP 60/30 mm Hg.
cases.ask: 1) The cause of the condition? 2) Care.
cases.answer: 1) The combination of a nitrate and a PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil) — both increase cGMP, causing strong vasodilation and life-threatening hypotension. 2) Lay the patient down and raise the legs, oxygen, rapid intravenous crystalloids; if ineffective — vasopressors (phenylephrine or norepinephrine); ECG monitoring (myocardial ischemia). Do not give nitrates. Later explain to the patient that nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors must not be taken together, and resolve the question of erectile dysfunction with a cardiologist.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman suddenly developed palpitations. ECG: narrow QRS, regular tachycardia of 190 beats/min, P waves not visible. BP 115/75 mm Hg, general condition satisfactory. She has a history of bronchial asthma.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Algorithm of care and choice of drug.
cases.answer: 1) Paroxysmal supraventricular (AV nodal re-entrant) tachycardia, hemodynamically stable. 2) First vagal maneuvers (modified Valsalva). Adenosine is usually the drug of choice, but in bronchial asthma adenosine may cause bronchospasm — so verapamil 5 mg intravenously slowly (over 2–3 minutes) is preferred. If unstable — electrical cardioversion. Then a cardiologist's consultation; radiofrequency ablation for recurrent attacks.

topics.title: Antihypertensive drugs. Hypertensive drugs

goals.text: Arterial hypertension (AH) occurs in about one third of adults and is the main risk factor for stroke, myocardial infarction, and heart and kidney failure. Lowering BP to the target level significantly reduces these complications. GPs choose and combine antihypertensive drugs and monitor their adverse effects every day. Emergency care in hypertensive crisis and in hypotensive states (collapse, shock) is also every doctor's duty. At the end of the topic, the modern pharmacotherapy of chronic heart failure is also briefly covered, because its main drugs are the same as the antihypertensives.
The student should know:

items: the systems that regulate BP and the sites of action of antihypertensive drugs;
the classification of antihypertensive drugs, and the mechanism, uses and adverse effects of the first-line drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium antagonists, diuretics) and the additional groups;
the principles of treating AH, rational combinations, and the choice of drugs in particular groups of patients;
the treatment of hypertensive crisis and hypertension in pregnancy;
hypertensive (BP-raising) drugs and their uses.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as enalapril, lisinopril, losartan, amlodipine, indapamide, hydrochlorothiazide, moxonidine, methyldopa and spironolactone;
draw up an antihypertensive treatment plan for a patient and choose a combination;
provide emergency care in hypertensive crisis.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The 5 groups of first-line (main) drugs in AH**: **ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium antagonists, thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics** and (when there are specific indications) **beta-blockers**. They have been proven to reduce cardiovascular complications and mortality.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Adverse effects of ACE inhibitors — **“CAPTOPRIL”**: **C**ough (dry, irritating), **A**ngioedema, **P**roteinuria (rare, captopril), **T**aste disturbance, **O**rthostatic (first-dose) hypotension, **P**regnancy — contraindicated, **R**enal artery stenosis — contraindicated, **I**ncreased potassium (hyperkalemia), **L**eukopenia (neutropenia).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The combination **ACE inhibitor + ARB** (or either of them + aliskiren) — “dual RAAS blockade” — **is not recommended**: it gives no additional benefit and increases the risk of hyperkalemia, hypotension and acute kidney injury.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Clonidine used to be one of the main drugs for AH in CIS countries. Modern recommendations **do not recommend it for regular treatment** (rebound, sedation, no proven organ-protective effect). Clonidine is also under strict control because it can be used for criminal purposes (combined with alcohol).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: For most patients the target BP is **below 130/80 mm Hg** (individualized in those over 65 and in frail elderly people, usually systolic 130–139 mm Hg). In most patients, treatment is recommended to start with **a fixed low-dose combination of two drugs (in a single tablet)**; in low-risk grade 1 AH and in frail elderly people — with monotherapy.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In a hypertensive crisis, giving **short-acting nifedipine sublingually**, and lowering BP very quickly and sharply, is dangerous: cerebral, cardiac and renal ischemia (stroke, infarction) may develop. In an uncomplicated crisis, urgent hospitalization is usually not required — a calm environment, an oral drug and follow-up within 24–48 hours are enough.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **In acute hypotension, the cause must be identified first**: hypovolemia (blood loss, dehydration) — fluids; anaphylaxis — epinephrine; septic shock — fluids + norepinephrine; cardiogenic shock — inotropes; bradycardia — atropine; adrenal insufficiency — hydrocortisone. Vasopressors are ineffective and harmful in hypovolemia without adequate fluid replacement.

sections.title: 1. Regulation of blood pressure and classification of antihypertensive drugs

blocks.text: BP = **cardiac output (minute volume)** × **total peripheral vascular resistance**. The main systems that regulate it:

items: **the sympathetic nervous system** (vasomotor center, baroreceptors, alpha and beta receptors);

**the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)**: renin → angiotensin I from angiotensinogen → ACE → **angiotensin II** (via AT~1~ receptors — strong vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sympathetic activation, remodeling of the heart and vessels);
excretion of sodium and water by the **kidneys** (circulating volume);
local factors: NO, endothelin, prostacyclin, bradykinin, natriuretic peptides.

parts.text: **The 5 groups of first-line (main) drugs in AH**: **ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium antagonists, thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics** and (when there are specific indications) **beta-blockers**. They have been proven to reduce cardiovascular complications and mortality.

sections.title: 2. Drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

blocks.text: 2.1. ACE inhibitors
**Mechanism.** They inhibit angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, kininase II):

items: **angiotensin II formation decreases** → vasodilation, reduced aldosterone release (sodium and water are excreted, potassium is retained), reduced sympathetic activity;

**bradykinin breakdown decreases** → bradykinin accumulates → release of NO and prostacyclin increases (additional vasodilation) — but **dry cough** and **angioedema** are also related to this. **Organ-protective effects:** reduction of left ventricular hypertrophy and vascular remodeling; **kidney protection** — by dilating the efferent arteriole they reduce intraglomerular pressure and **reduce proteinuria** (diabetic nephropathy).

blocks.title: Table 11.2. Features of ACE inhibitors
head: Preparation
Property
Duration of action
rows: Active form (not a prodrug), contains an SH group; rapid action
Short (2–3 times a day) — sublingually in hypertensive crisis
Prodrug → enalaprilat (in the liver); enalaprilat intravenously
Active, not metabolized in the liver, excreted by the kidneys

blocks.text: **Uses:** arterial hypertension (especially with diabetes, proteinuria, left ventricular hypertrophy), **chronic heart failure** (reduced ejection fraction — reduces mortality), after myocardial infarction, diabetic and nondiabetic nephropathy.

blocks.title: Table 11.3. Adverse effects of ACE inhibitors
head: Adverse effect
Mechanism / note
rows: Bradykinin accumulation; switch to an ARB
Bradykinin; more common in Black patients; never prescribed again
Reduced aldosterone; especially with renal failure, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs
In bilateral renal artery stenosis — the efferent arteriole dilates and the filtration pressure falls sharply
Impaired fetal kidney development, oligohydramnios — absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy

parts.text: Adverse effects of ACE inhibitors — **“CAPTOPRIL”**: **C**ough (dry, irritating), **A**ngioedema, **P**roteinuria (rare, captopril), **T**aste disturbance, **O**rthostatic (first-dose) hypotension, **P**regnancy — contraindicated, **R**enal artery stenosis — contraindicated, **I**ncreased potassium (hyperkalemia), **L**eukopenia (neutropenia).

blocks.text: 2.2. Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs, sartans)

**Mechanism. Selective blockade of AT~1~ receptors** — all the harmful effects of angiotensin II are abolished (including angiotensin II formed by pathways other than ACE). They do not affect bradykinin breakdown — so they **do not cause cough**, and angioedema is very rare.

**Uses:** the same as ACE inhibitors (AH, heart failure, diabetic nephropathy); in patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors. **Losartan** increases uric acid excretion (AH with gout). **Telmisartan** is long-acting.
**Adverse effects and contraindications** are similar to those of ACE inhibitors: hyperkalemia, worsening of renal function (in renal artery stenosis), **contraindicated in pregnancy**.

parts.text: The combination **ACE inhibitor + ARB** (or either of them + aliskiren) — “dual RAAS blockade” — **is not recommended**: it gives no additional benefit and increases the risk of hyperkalemia, hypotension and acute kidney injury.

blocks.text: 2.3. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and the renin inhibitor

**Spironolactone** and **eplerenone** block aldosterone receptors (in detail in Topic 13). Uses: **resistant AH** (BP still high on three drugs — the fourth drug), primary hyperaldosteronism, chronic heart failure (reduces mortality), ascites in liver cirrhosis. Adverse effects: **hyperkalemia**; with spironolactone — **gynecomastia**, menstrual disorders (antiandrogenic effect); eplerenone is more selective.
**Aliskiren** inhibits renin directly; now rarely used.

Their mechanism and classification were covered in Topic 10. In AH, mainly **long-acting dihydropyridines** (amlodipine, lercanidipine, nifedipine GITS) are used: they dilate arterioles and reduce peripheral resistance.

items: **Advantages:** metabolically neutral, effective in the elderly and in isolated systolic AH, good effect in Black patients, effective in stroke prevention, allowed in pregnancy (nifedipine).
**Adverse effects: ankle edema** (not reduced by a diuretic, reduced by an ACE inhibitor/ARB), headache, facial flushing, gingival hyperplasia; with verapamil — constipation and bradycardia.

blocks.text: Their mechanism is covered in detail in Topic 13. In AH, mainly **thiazide and thiazide-like** diuretics are used: at first they reduce the circulating volume, and later they lower peripheral resistance through a decrease in sodium in the vessel wall.

items: **Indapamide** and **chlorthalidone** (thiazide-like) — long-acting, with few metabolic adverse effects; proven to reduce cardiovascular complications.
**Hydrochlorothiazide** — often in combination tablets (12.5–25 mg).

**Loop diuretics** (furosemide, torasemide) are used in AH only with **renal failure** (GFR < 30 ml/min) and in heart failure with edema. **Metabolic adverse effects of thiazides:** hypokalemia, hyponatremia, **hyperuricemia** (gout attack), hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, hypercalcemia — mainly at high doses.

parts.text: Clonidine used to be one of the main drugs for AH in CIS countries. Modern recommendations **do not recommend it for regular treatment** (rebound, sedation, no proven organ-protective effect). Clonidine is also under strict control because it can be used for criminal purposes (combined with alcohol).

blocks.text: 5.2. Beta- and alpha-blockers

**Beta-blockers** (Topic 6) are first-line in AH in the following cases: IHD, after infarction, heart failure, tachyarrhythmias, planning pregnancy, sympathetic hyperactivity in young patients. In the elderly they are slightly weaker than other groups in preventing stroke. **Preferred drugs**: bisoprolol, nebivolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (not atenolol).
**Alpha-1 blockers** (doxazosin) — an add-on drug in resistant AH, especially together with **prostatic hyperplasia**.

items: **Hydralazine** dilates arterioles directly; strong reflex tachycardia and fluid retention (given with a beta-blocker and a diuretic); with prolonged use — **drug-induced lupus** (in slow acetylators). Given intravenously in severe AH of pregnancy; in Black patients with heart failure — together with isosorbide dinitrate.
**Minoxidil** opens KATP channels; very potent; used in resistant AH; **hypertrichosis** — that is why its topical solution is used for alopecia.

**Sodium nitroprusside** — an NO donor; dilates arteries and veins; the effect begins immediately and ends 1–2 minutes after the infusion is stopped. Given **as an intravenous drip** through a light-protected line (it decomposes in light) in **hypertensive crisis** and aortic dissection (with a beta-blocker). With prolonged use — **cyanide toxicity** (antidote — sodium thiosulfate, hydroxocobalamin).
**Bendazol (Dibazol)** — a weak myotropic antispasmodic; used in CIS countries with papaverine for mild crises; its effectiveness does not meet modern standards.
**Magnesium sulfate** — **prevention of seizures in preeclampsia and eclampsia** (the main indication); its antihypertensive effect is weak.

blocks.text: 7.1. Target BP and initial treatment

parts.text: For most patients the target BP is **below 130/80 mm Hg** (individualized in those over 65 and in frail elderly people, usually systolic 130–139 mm Hg). In most patients, treatment is recommended to start with **a fixed low-dose combination of two drugs (in a single tablet)**; in low-risk grade 1 AH and in frail elderly people — with monotherapy.

blocks.text: **Lifestyle changes** at every step: less than 5 g of table salt a day, weight loss, regular physical activity, limiting alcohol, stopping smoking, a diet rich in vegetables and fruit.

parts.text: If a woman planning pregnancy or already pregnant is taking an ACE inhibitor or ARB, it is **immediately** replaced with methyldopa, labetalol or nifedipine. When prescribing these drugs to women of reproductive age, advice on contraception must be given.

blocks.text: 7.3. Hypertensive crisis
**Hypertensive crisis** is a sharp rise in BP (usually > 180/120 mm Hg). Two types are distinguished:

items: **complicated (emergency) crisis** — with acute target-organ damage: hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary edema, aortic dissection, eclampsia, acute kidney injury. BP is lowered **stepwise** with **intravenous** drugs (in the first hour mean BP by no more than 25%; in aortic dissection — rapidly, to systolic < 120);
**uncomplicated crisis** — without organ damage; BP is lowered gradually over 24–48 hours with **oral** drugs.

Esmolol or labetalol + nitroprusside or nitroglycerin
Intravenous labetalol or hydralazine, oral nifedipine + magnesium sulfate (seizure prevention)
Benzodiazepines, nitrates, phentolamine; beta-blockers are contraindicated

parts.text: In a hypertensive crisis, giving **short-acting nifedipine sublingually**, and lowering BP very quickly and sharply, is dangerous: cerebral, cardiac and renal ischemia (stroke, infarction) may develop. In an uncomplicated crisis, urgent hospitalization is usually not required — a calm environment, an oral drug and follow-up within 24–48 hours are enough.

skills.title: Skill 1. Drawing up a treatment plan for a patient newly diagnosed with AH

items: Measure BP correctly (repeatedly, on both arms) and teach home measurement.
Assess cardiovascular risk and target-organ damage (ECG, creatinine, GFR, potassium, glucose, lipids, urine albumin).
Give advice on lifestyle changes.
Choose a drug taking comorbidities into account (Table 11.7).
In most patients, start with a fixed combination of an ACE inhibitor/ARB + a calcium antagonist or a diuretic.
Check creatinine and potassium 1–2 weeks after starting an ACE inhibitor/ARB.
Follow-up at 4 weeks; if the target is not reached — a combination of three drugs.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, BP 158/96 mm Hg, raised urine albumin/creatinine ratio, normal creatinine, potassium 4.3 mmol/l. Previously untreated.
cases.ask: 1) Which drug(s) would you start with? 2) What monitoring is needed? 3) Target BP?
cases.answer: 1) An ACE inhibitor or ARB (nephroprotective — reduces albuminuria) + a calcium antagonist (amlodipine) or a thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide) — in a fixed combination; consider adding an SGLT2 inhibitor for diabetes and kidney protection. 2) Creatinine and potassium after 1–2 weeks (if GFR falls by more than 30% or potassium is > 5.5 — reconsider the dose), home BP monitoring. 3) < 130/80 mm Hg.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 32-year-old woman has been taking enalapril for AH for 2 years. She has found out that she is 10 weeks pregnant.
cases.ask: 1) Management? 2) Which drugs can she be switched to?
cases.answer: 1) Stop enalapril immediately — ACE inhibitors (especially in the 2nd–3rd trimesters) impair fetal kidney development and may lead to oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia and fetal death. When taken in the 1st trimester, the risk is relatively low, but the fetus must be monitored by ultrasound. 2) Methyldopa, labetalol or sustained-release nifedipine; follow-up jointly by an obstetrician-gynecologist and an internist; monitoring for signs of preeclampsia (proteinuria, edema, headache).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 60-year-old patient was brought in with BP 200/120 mm Hg, severe headache, nausea, blurred vision and confusion. No focal neurological signs. Papilledema on the fundus.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Treatment approach and rate of BP lowering.
cases.answer: 1) Complicated hypertensive crisis — hypertensive encephalopathy. 2) Admission to the intensive care unit, BP monitoring; titratable intravenous drugs — labetalol, nicardipine or sodium nitroprusside; in the first hour lower mean BP by no more than 20–25%, over the next 2–6 hours to 160/100, then gradually to normal over 24–48 hours. Abrupt lowering causes cerebral ischemia. Short-acting nifedipine sublingually is contraindicated.

topics.title: Drugs acting on the digestive system

goals.text: Gastrointestinal diseases are among the most common reasons for visiting a GP: dyspepsia, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), gastric and duodenal ulcer, constipation, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, biliary tract and liver diseases. Proton pump inhibitors are among the most prescribed drugs in the world, but they are often used without reason and for too long. Eradication of Helicobacter pylori has radically changed the treatment of peptic ulcer disease. This topic covers the main groups of digestive system pharmacology based on modern recommendations.
The student should know:

items: the classification of drugs acting on the digestive system;
the regulation of gastric secretion and the mechanism of antisecretory drugs (PPIs, H~2~ blockers), antacids and gastroprotectors;
H. pylori eradication regimens;
emetic and antiemetic drugs, prokinetics, laxatives and antidiarrheals;
choleretic and cholagogue drugs, hepatoprotectors, pancreatic enzymes and probiotics.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as omeprazole, famotidine, Almagel, De-Nol, ondansetron, metoclopramide, domperidone, loperamide, lactulose, bisacodyl, ursodeoxycholic acid and pancreatin;
draw up an H. pylori eradication regimen;
give instructions on treating dehydration in diarrhea and vomiting.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: PPIs block only **actively working** pumps. Therefore they are taken **30–60 minutes before meals** (usually before breakfast) — when food activates the pumps, the drug is at its peak blood concentration. The full effect develops in 3–5 days; a PPI is not a quick “switch-off” (symptomatic, as-needed) drug.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Antacids reduce the absorption of many drugs (**tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones**, iron preparations, digoxin, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates). Other drugs are taken **at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after** an antacid.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The effectiveness of eradication is checked **at least 4 weeks** after it (and 2 weeks after stopping the PPI) with a **urea breath test** or a stool antigen test. A serological test (antibodies) is unsuitable for assessing the result of eradication — antibodies persist for months.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The drug according to the cause of vomiting: **“Chemo — Ondansetron, Sea — Dimenhydrinate and scopolamine, Slow stomach — Metoclopramide/domperidone, Delayed chemo — Aprepitant”**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Laxatives are **contraindicated** in **intestinal obstruction**, an acute abdomen (suspected appendicitis), and abdominal pain of unknown cause. In treating constipation, diet (fiber), fluids and physical activity come first; of the drugs — bulk-forming and osmotic laxatives. Regular long-term use of contact (stimulant) laxatives is not recommended.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Choleretic drugs (especially cholekinetics) are contraindicated in **gallstone disease** — a stone may become lodged in the bile duct and lead to obstructive jaundice and pancreatitis. They are also not used in acute cholecystitis, acute hepatitis and pancreatitis. The effectiveness of most herbal choleretics has not been proven in modern studies.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Hepatoprotectors are very widely prescribed in CIS countries, but the effectiveness of most of them (silymarin, essential phospholipids) **has not been proven** in high-quality clinical trials and they are not included in international recommendations. In liver diseases the main focus is on **treating the cause**: antiviral therapy in viral hepatitis, abstinence from alcohol in alcoholic disease, weight loss in fatty liver disease, **N-acetylcysteine** in paracetamol poisoning.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The diagnosis of **“dysbacteriosis”** and prescribing probiotics to treat it on the basis of stool analysis is widespread in CIS countries, but international medicine does not recognize it as a separate disease.

blocks.text: 2.1. Regulation of gastric acid secretion
The **parietal cells** of the stomach produce hydrochloric acid. Their secretion is regulated by three main stimulants:

items: **acetylcholine** (vagus nerve) — via M~3~ receptors;
**gastrin** (antral G cells) — via CCK~2~ receptors and by releasing histamine from enterochromaffin-like cells;

**histamine** (enterochromaffin-like cells) — via **H~2~ receptors** (cAMP ↑) — the main final stimulant. All pathways converge on **H^+^/K^+^-ATPase (the proton pump)** — the **final common step** of acid secretion.

blocks.label: Figure 12.1
blocks.caption: Production of hydrochloric acid in the stomach and the sites of action of drugs that reduce it: M~1~-cholinergic blockers, H~2~ blockers, gastrin antagonists, prostaglandins, proton pump inhibitors (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: 2.2. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)
**Preparations:** omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole.

**Mechanism.** PPIs are **prodrugs**, unstable in acid, so they are produced in **enteric-coated** capsules or tablets. After absorption from the intestine they reach the parietal cell via the blood; in the acidic environment of the secretory canaliculi they are converted into the active **sulfenamide**, which binds **irreversibly and covalently** to the SH groups of H^+^/K^+^-ATPase. Acid secretion falls by more than 90%; the effect lasts until new pumps are synthesized (more than 24 hours), although t½ is only 1–2 hours.

parts.text: PPIs block only **actively working** pumps. Therefore they are taken **30–60 minutes before meals** (usually before breakfast) — when food activates the pumps, the drug is at its peak blood concentration. The full effect develops in 3–5 days; a PPI is not a quick “switch-off” (symptomatic, as-needed) drug.

blocks.text: **Uses:** GERD and reflux esophagitis, gastric and duodenal ulcer, **H. pylori eradication** (with antibiotics), prevention and treatment of NSAID gastropathy, Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, ulcer bleeding (intravenously), functional dyspepsia.

**Adverse effects (with long-term use):** headache, diarrhea or constipation; increased risk of **Clostridioides difficile infection** and pneumonia; reduced absorption of **vitamin B~12~, magnesium, iron and calcium** (hypomagnesemia, osteoporosis, bone fractures), interstitial nephritis; hypergastrinemia; **rebound acid hypersecretion** on abrupt withdrawal.

parts.text: **Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19** and may reduce the conversion of **clopidogrel** into its active metabolite. If a patient taking clopidogrel needs gastroprotection, **pantoprazole** is preferred. In every patient taking a PPI long term, the indication should be reviewed regularly and, where possible, the dose reduced or the drug stopped (“deprescribing”).

blocks.text: 2.3. H~2~-histamine receptor blockers
**Preparations:** famotidine (the main one), ranitidine (withdrawn from the market in many countries in 2020 because of N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA) contamination), cimetidine (outdated).

By competitively blocking the H~2~ receptors of parietal cells, they reduce basal secretion, especially at **night**. They are weaker than PPIs, and tolerance develops quickly. Uses: mild GERD, dyspepsia, an add-on to a PPI (nocturnal acid “breakthrough”). **Cimetidine** — a CYP450 inhibitor (many interactions), antiandrogenic effect (gynecomastia) — no longer used.
2.4. Antacids

**Antacids** **chemically neutralize** hydrochloric acid in the stomach. The effect begins quickly (minutes) but is short (30–60 minutes on an empty stomach; up to 3 hours if taken 1 hour after a meal).

parts.text: Antacids reduce the absorption of many drugs (**tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones**, iron preparations, digoxin, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates). Other drugs are taken **at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after** an antacid.

blocks.text: 2.5. Gastroprotectors

items: **Bismuth tripotassium dicitrate (De-Nol)** — forms a protective **film** on the ulcer surface in an acidic environment, increases the synthesis of prostaglandins and bicarbonate, and **acts against H. pylori** (in quadruple regimens). Adverse effect: **darkening of the stool and tongue** (harmless); with long-term use at large doses — encephalopathy (contraindicated in renal failure).
**Sucralfate** — forms a sticky paste in an acidic environment and coats the ulcer base. Constipation; reduces the absorption of other drugs.

**Misoprostol** — a prostaglandin E~1~ analog: reduces acid secretion and increases the production of mucus and bicarbonate. **Prevention of NSAID gastropathy**. Adverse effects: diarrhea; **uterine contractions — absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy** (it causes abortion; it is used for this purpose in obstetrics).

blocks.text: 2.6. Eradication of Helicobacter pylori
H. pylori is the main cause of gastric and duodenal ulcer, chronic gastritis, gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma. Eradication sharply reduces ulcer recurrence.

parts.text: The effectiveness of eradication is checked **at least 4 weeks** after it (and 2 weeks after stopping the PPI) with a **urea breath test** or a stool antigen test. A serological test (antibodies) is unsuitable for assessing the result of eradication — antibodies persist for months.

blocks.text: 3.1. Mechanism of vomiting
The vomiting center is located in the medulla oblongata and receives impulses from:

items: **the chemoreceptor trigger zone** (in the floor of the fourth ventricle, outside the blood-brain barrier; D~2~, 5-HT~3~ and NK~1~ receptors) — circulating toxins, drugs (cytostatics, opioids, glycosides), metabolites;
**the gastrointestinal tract** — vagal afferents (5-HT~3~; cytostatics release serotonin from enterochromaffin cells);
**the vestibular apparatus** (M~1~, H~1~ receptors) — motion sickness;
the cerebral cortex (fear, smells, “anticipatory vomiting”).

blocks.label: Figure 12.2
blocks.caption: Pathways of vomiting and the sites of action of antiemetics: chemoreceptor trigger zone, vomiting center, afferent fibers (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: 3.2. Emetics

**Apomorphine** stimulates D~2~ receptors in the trigger zone; given subcutaneously. **Ipecacuanha** irritates the stomach reflexly. They were formerly used in poisoning; now **not recommended** (risk of aspiration, unproven effectiveness) — gastric lavage and activated charcoal are preferred in poisoning. Apomorphine is now used in Parkinson's disease.

blocks.text: 4.1. Prokinetics

**Metoclopramide** (D~2~ blocker + 5-HT~4~ agonist), **domperidone** (peripheral D~2~ blocker), **itopride** (D~2~ blocker + anticholinesterase) — speed up gastric emptying and increase the tone of the lower esophageal sphincter. Uses: gastroparesis (diabetic), functional dyspepsia, reflux (as an add-on). **Erythromycin** at a small dose stimulates motilin receptors (in gastric bleeding before endoscopy).
4.2. Antispasmodics

items: **Myotropic**: drotaverine (No-Spa), papaverine — phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitors (cAMP ↑) that relax smooth muscle directly; **mebeverine** (Na^+^ channel blockade) and otilonium bromide — selective for the intestine, in **irritable bowel syndrome**.
**Neurotropic**: hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan), platyphylline (Topic 4).
**Peppermint oil** capsules — in irritable bowel syndrome.

parts.text: Laxatives are **contraindicated** in **intestinal obstruction**, an acute abdomen (suspected appendicitis), and abdominal pain of unknown cause. In treating constipation, diet (fiber), fluids and physical activity come first; of the drugs — bulk-forming and osmotic laxatives. Regular long-term use of contact (stimulant) laxatives is not recommended.

blocks.text: 4.4. Antidiarrheal drugs

**The main treatment of acute diarrhea is rehydration.** Oral rehydration solution (the WHO low-osmolarity ORS: sodium chloride, potassium chloride, sodium citrate, glucose) sharply reduces dehydration and death: glucose enhances the absorption of sodium and water in the intestine (sodium-glucose cotransport, SGLT1). In children, **zinc** preparations (10–14 days) are recommended together with ORS.

items: **Loperamide** — a peripheral mu-opioid agonist that hardly crosses the BBB; it slows peristalsis and increases anal sphincter tone. Symptomatic in acute nonspecific diarrhea in adults. **Contraindicated in bloody diarrhea, high fever** (dysentery, invasive infection), C. difficile colitis and **in children under 2** (toxic megacolon, ileus). At large doses — cardiotoxicity (QT prolongation).
**Adsorbents** — diosmectite (Smecta), activated charcoal (Topic 3).
**Racecadotril** — an enkephalinase inhibitor; antisecretory effect.
**Probiotics** (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Saccharomyces boulardii) — slightly shorten the duration of acute diarrhea in children; prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

parts.text: In acute diarrhea, **antibiotics** are used only when indicated: dysentery (bloody stool + fever), cholera, severe travelers' diarrhea, immunodeficiency. Most acute diarrheas (viral) do not require antibiotics.

sections.title: 5. Drugs affecting liver and biliary function

blocks.text: 5.1. Choleretics and cholagogues

items: **Choleretics** enhance bile formation in the liver: those containing bile acids (Allochol, Cholenzym), synthetic (hymecromone, osalmid), herbal (corn silk, immortelle, rose hip — Cholosas).
**Cholekinetics** enhance gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi: magnesium sulfate, sorbitol, xylitol, cholecystokinin.
**Cholespasmolytics** relax biliary spasm: drotaverine, papaverine, hymecromone, M-cholinergic blockers.

parts.text: Choleretic drugs (especially cholekinetics) are contraindicated in **gallstone disease** — a stone may become lodged in the bile duct and lead to obstructive jaundice and pancreatitis. They are also not used in acute cholecystitis, acute hepatitis and pancreatitis. The effectiveness of most herbal choleretics has not been proven in modern studies.

blocks.text: 5.2. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)

**UDCA** is a hydrophilic bile acid. Mechanism: it reduces cholesterol saturation of bile (**dissolves cholesterol stones**), displaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids and protects hepatocytes and cholangiocytes, choleresis and immunomodulation.

**Uses: primary biliary cholangitis** (the main drug), small (< 15 mm) radiolucent cholesterol stones (with preserved gallbladder function), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, cholestatic liver diseases, prevention of stone formation after bariatric surgery.
5.3. Hepatoprotectors

Hepatoprotectors are a heterogeneous group intended to protect liver cells from harmful influences: **ademetionine** (Heptral), **silymarin** (milk thistle — Karsil), **essential phospholipids** (Essentiale), ornithine aspartate (Hepa-Merz — reduces ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy).

parts.text: Hepatoprotectors are very widely prescribed in CIS countries, but the effectiveness of most of them (silymarin, essential phospholipids) **has not been proven** in high-quality clinical trials and they are not included in international recommendations. In liver diseases the main focus is on **treating the cause**: antiviral therapy in viral hepatitis, abstinence from alcohol in alcoholic disease, weight loss in fatty liver disease, **N-acetylcysteine** in paracetamol poisoning.

sections.title: 6. Drugs acting on the pancreas and the intestinal microflora

blocks.text: **Pancreatin** — a mixture of **lipase, amylase and protease** obtained from the porcine pancreas. Uses: **exocrine pancreatic insufficiency** (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, after pancreatectomy). The dose is set in **lipase units** (25,000–50,000 units per main meal) and taken **with food**. Enteric-coated microsphere capsules (Creon) are preferred. In cystic fibrosis, very large doses may cause fibrosing colonopathy.

**Probiotics** are live microorganisms that confer a benefit when taken in adequate amounts (lactobacilli, bifidobacteria, Saccharomyces boulardii). **Prebiotics** are nondigestible substances that stimulate the growth of beneficial microflora (inulin, lactulose, oligosaccharides). Their effectiveness depends on the strain; proven indications are limited (antibiotic-associated diarrhea, acute gastroenteritis in children).

parts.text: The diagnosis of **“dysbacteriosis”** and prescribing probiotics to treat it on the basis of stool analysis is widespread in CIS countries, but international medicine does not recognize it as a separate disease.

skills.title: Skill 1. Teaching oral rehydration at home

items: Dissolve a ready-made ORS sachet in the stated volume (usually 1 liter or 200–500 ml) of clean, boiled, cooled water.
Give the child after each loose stool: under 2 years — 50–100 ml, 2–10 years — 100–200 ml, adults — as much as they want.
If the child is vomiting — give 1 teaspoon every 1–2 minutes; pause for 10 minutes and continue.
Do not stop breastfeeding or normal feeding.
Warning signs: repeated vomiting, bloody stool, lethargy, reduced urine output, fever — see a doctor immediately.
The prepared solution is discarded after 24 hours.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 42-year-old man complains of epigastric pain that worsens on an empty stomach and at night. Upper GI endoscopy shows an 8 mm ulcer in the duodenal bulb; the urease test is positive. He has taken clarithromycin before. Clarithromycin resistance in the area is high.
cases.ask: 1) Draw up a treatment regimen. 2) When and how is eradication checked?
cases.answer: 1) Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days: a PPI (for example, esomeprazole 20 mg or omeprazole 20 mg 2 times a day) + bismuth tripotassium dicitrate 240 mg 2 times a day + tetracycline 500 mg 4 times a day + metronidazole 500 mg 3 times a day. Because of his previous clarithromycin use and the local resistance, a clarithromycin regimen is not appropriate. After eradication, the PPI is continued until the ulcer heals (4–8 weeks). 2) At least 4 weeks after the end of treatment, with the PPI stopped for 2 weeks — a urea breath test or a stool antigen test.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 65-year-old woman has been taking omeprazole 20 mg “to protect the stomach” for 5 years; endoscopy shows no pathology, and she does not take NSAIDs. Recently she has had muscle cramps, weakness and numbness in the legs. Blood magnesium is low, B~12~ is low, and densitometry shows osteopenia.
cases.ask: 1) Are the symptoms related to the PPI? 2) Management?
cases.answer: 1) Long-term PPI use is associated with hypomagnesemia (muscle cramps), vitamin B~12~ deficiency (neuropathy, numbness) and reduced calcium absorption (osteopenia, fracture risk). 2) There is no indication — stop the PPI gradually (reduce the dose over 2–4 weeks or switch to as-needed use to reduce rebound hypersecretion; temporarily an antacid or famotidine for symptoms); replace magnesium and B~12~; treat the osteopenia.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 2-year-old child (12 kg) is brought in with watery diarrhea for 2 days (6–8 times a day) and several episodes of vomiting. The child is thirsty and restless, the eyes are slightly sunken, and a skin pinch goes back slowly. No blood in the stool, temperature 37.8 °C. The mother has bought loperamide at the pharmacy.
cases.ask: 1) Assess the condition. 2) Can loperamide be given? 3) Treatment.
cases.answer: 1) Acute gastroenteritis (probably viral), moderate dehydration. 2) No — loperamide is contraindicated in children under 2 (risk of intestinal obstruction, toxic megacolon, CNS depression). 3) Oral rehydration: low-osmolarity ORS, about 75 ml/kg over 4 hours (≈ 900 ml), in small, frequent portions; if vomiting is frequent — a single dose of ondansetron (age-appropriate) to make oral rehydration easier; zinc 20 mg/day for 10–14 days (in children over 6 months); continue breastfeeding and feeding; no antibiotics are needed. If the condition worsens or the child refuses to drink — intravenous rehydration.

topics.cards_title: Table 12.7. Drugs acting on the digestive system — summary

topics.title: Diuretics

goals.text: Diuretics are among the most commonly used drugs in cardiology, nephrology and intensive care. They relieve edema and pulmonary congestion in heart failure, reduce complications in arterial hypertension, and are used to treat ascites in liver cirrhosis, cerebral edema and glaucoma. At the same time, diuretics significantly change the electrolyte balance: hypokalemia can lead to glycoside toxicity and arrhythmias, and hyperkalemia to cardiac arrest. Knowing which part of the nephron each diuretic acts on is the key to understanding its effectiveness and adverse effects logically.
The student should know:

items: the main mechanisms of sodium and water reabsorption in the nephron;
the classification of diuretics (by site of action, potency and mechanism);
the mechanism of each group, its effect on electrolyte metabolism, its uses and adverse effects;
the principles of rational combination of diuretics and of overcoming diuretic resistance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as furosemide, torasemide, hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, spironolactone, acetazolamide and mannitol;
choose a diuretic according to the clinical situation;
recognize and correct electrolyte disturbances during diuretic therapy.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The **potency** of a diuretic depends on how much sodium is reabsorbed in the segment it acts on: loop diuretics (25%) — **strong**, thiazides (5–8%) — **moderate**, potassium-sparing agents (2–3%) — **weak**. Agents acting on the proximal tubule are also weak, because the later segments “catch” the sodium.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Giving furosemide intravenously **slowly** (at no more than 4 mg per minute) reduces the risk of ototoxicity. Giving it together with aminoglycosides, vancomycin or cisplatin increases **ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity**. NSAIDs reduce the effect of loop diuretics.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The “opposite relationship” with calcium: **“Loops Lose calcium, Thiazides Take it back”**. That is why loop diuretics are useful in hypercalcemia, and thiazides in calcium kidney stones and a tendency to osteoporosis.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Risk of hyperkalemia**: potassium-sparing diuretics must be used with caution or not at all together with **potassium preparations, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, trimethoprim and heparin**, and **in renal failure** (GFR < 30). If potassium exceeds 5.5 mmol/l — risk of cardiac arrhythmias and arrest. Regular monitoring of blood potassium and creatinine is mandatory.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Mannitol is **absolutely contraindicated in heart failure and pulmonary edema**: it first increases the circulating volume and worsens pulmonary edema. It is also not used in anuria (no urine output), severe dehydration and the active phase of intracerebral hemorrhage.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Diuretics that cause acidosis — A, K, and Stop”**: **A**cetazolamide, **K**-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride, triamterene) — **S**top, that's all. The other diuretics (loop, thiazide) cause **alkalosis**.

sections.title: 1. Nephron physiology and the sites of action of diuretics

blocks.text: About **180 liters** of primary urine are filtered in the glomeruli each day, but only 1–1.5 liters are excreted — **more than 99%** of filtered sodium is reabsorbed. Diuretics inhibit sodium reabsorption; water leaves together with sodium.

blocks.label: Figure 13.1
blocks.caption: Sites of action of diuretics in the nephron: I — processes involved in urine formation; II — segments on which diuretics act (1 — glomerulus, 2 — proximal tubule, 3–4 — loop of Henle, 5 — distal tubule, 6–7 — collecting duct) (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

parts.text: The **potency** of a diuretic depends on how much sodium is reabsorbed in the segment it acts on: loop diuretics (25%) — **strong**, thiazides (5–8%) — **moderate**, potassium-sparing agents (2–3%) — **weak**. Agents acting on the proximal tubule are also weak, because the later segments “catch” the sodium.

blocks.text: **The general mechanism of potassium loss.** All diuretics acting before the collecting duct (loop, thiazide, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, osmotic) deliver more sodium and water to the collecting duct → here more sodium is reabsorbed through aldosterone-dependent channels and, in exchange, **more potassium and hydrogen ions are secreted** → **hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis**. In addition, hypovolemia activates the RAAS and increases aldosterone.

blocks.title: Table 13.2. Classification of diuretics

Preparations
Potency
Onset / duration of action (oral)

blocks.text: **Mechanism.** In the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle they block the **Na^+^-K^+^-2Cl– cotransporter** from the luminal side. Up to 25% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed here — that is why they are the **most potent** diuretics. In addition:

items: the **hyperosmolarity** of the renal medulla is disrupted — the ability to concentrate urine decreases;
paracellular reabsorption of Ca^2+^ and Mg^2+^ in this segment also decreases — **calcium and magnesium excretion increases** (unlike thiazides!);

by increasing prostaglandin synthesis in the kidney they increase renal blood flow; **when given intravenously — venodilation before diuresis** (immediate relief in pulmonary edema) — NSAIDs reduce this effect.

blocks.text: Uses:

items: **acute left ventricular failure and pulmonary edema** (intravenously);
edema and congestion in chronic heart failure (torasemide acts longer and has higher bioavailability);
edema in liver cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome (with spironolactone);
edema and AH **in renal failure** (GFR < 30 ml/min — thiazides are ineffective);
**hypercalcemia** (after fluid replacement);
forced diuresis (in poisoning; now rarely), hyperkalemia.
