head: Adverse effect
Comment
rows: Strong diuresis; especially in the elderly
With rapid intravenous injection of large doses, together with aminoglycosides; more common with ethacrynic acid
Furosemide, torasemide and bumetanide have a sulfonamide structure; ethacrynic acid does not (an alternative in sulfonamide allergy)

parts.text: Giving furosemide intravenously **slowly** (at no more than 4 mg per minute) reduces the risk of ototoxicity. Giving it together with aminoglycosides, vancomycin or cisplatin increases **ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity**. NSAIDs reduce the effect of loop diuretics.

blocks.text: **Mechanism.** They block the **Na^+^-Cl– cotransporter** in the distal convoluted tubule. In addition, they **increase calcium reabsorption** (urinary calcium decreases) — the opposite of loop diuretics.
Uses:

items: **arterial hypertension** — first-line drugs (indapamide and chlorthalidone are preferred; Topic 11);
mild and moderate edema (heart failure);
**prevention of kidney stones** — idiopathic hypercalciuria (calcium stones);
**nephrogenic diabetes insipidus** (paradoxically reduces urine volume — by increasing proximal reabsorption);
in severe resistant edema, combined with loop diuretics (metolazone — “sequential nephron blockade”).

parts.text: The “opposite relationship” with calcium: **“Loops Lose calcium, Thiazides Take it back”**. That is why loop diuretics are useful in hypercalcemia, and thiazides in calcium kidney stones and a tendency to osteoporosis.

blocks.text: **Adverse effects (mainly at high doses):** hypokalemia, **hyponatremia** (especially in elderly women — thiazides more than loop diuretics), hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, **hyperuricemia and gout**, **hyperglycemia** (reduced insulin secretion), dyslipidemia, **hypercalcemia**, photosensitivity, erectile dysfunction, sulfonamide allergy; they increase **lithium** concentration.

parts.text: When **GFR is below 30 ml/min**, thiazides are usually **ineffective** (chlorthalidone is a partial exception) — loop diuretics are used in such patients. There is evidence that long-term, high-dose hydrochlorothiazide slightly increases the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer (especially squamous cell) — sun protection is recommended.

blocks.text: 5.1. Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid receptor) antagonists

**Spironolactone** is a **competitive antagonist** of aldosterone: by blocking mineralocorticoid receptors in collecting duct cells, it reduces the synthesis of Na^+^ channels and Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase. Sodium excretion increases slightly, and **potassium and hydrogen secretion decreases**. Its effect develops slowly (over 2–3 days) and it is **the more effective the higher the aldosterone level**.
Uses:

items: **chronic heart failure** (reduced ejection fraction) — reduces mortality;
**ascites in liver cirrhosis** (secondary hyperaldosteronism) — the diuretic of first choice;
**primary hyperaldosteronism** (Conn syndrome);
resistant arterial hypertension;
with thiazide or loop diuretics — prevention of hypokalemia;

hyperandrogenism in women (hirsutism, acne) — because of its antiandrogenic effect. **Adverse effects: hyperkalemia** (especially with renal failure, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, potassium preparations, NSAIDs), metabolic acidosis; **antiandrogenic and progestogenic effects** — **gynecomastia** and impotence in men, menstrual disorders and breast pain in women.

blocks.text: **Eplerenone** is more selective for mineralocorticoid receptors; it does not cause gynecomastia. **Finerenone** is a nonsteroidal antagonist; used in diabetic kidney disease.
5.2. Sodium channel blockers

**Amiloride** and **triamterene** block the epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) of the collecting duct **directly** — their effect does not depend on aldosterone. Mainly in combination with thiazides to prevent hypokalemia (Triampur — triamterene + hydrochlorothiazide). Amiloride — in **Liddle syndrome** and lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Adverse effects: hyperkalemia; triamterene — kidney stones, folic acid antagonism.

parts.text: **Risk of hyperkalemia**: potassium-sparing diuretics must be used with caution or not at all together with **potassium preparations, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, trimethoprim and heparin**, and **in renal failure** (GFR < 30). If potassium exceeds 5.5 mmol/l — risk of cardiac arrhythmias and arrest. Regular monitoring of blood potassium and creatinine is mandatory.

blocks.text: 6.1. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

**Acetazolamide (Diacarb)** inhibits **carbonic anhydrase** in the proximal tubule → H^+^ formation and Na^+^/H^+^ exchange decrease → excretion of **bicarbonate**, sodium and potassium increases, the urine becomes alkaline, and **metabolic acidosis** develops. The diuretic effect is weak and decreases within 2–3 days as acidosis develops (self-limiting).

**Uses** (mainly non-diuretic): **glaucoma** (reduces the production of aqueous humor; in an attack of angle-closure glaucoma — orally or intravenously; topical analogs — dorzolamide and brinzolamide drops), **prevention of mountain (altitude) sickness**, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, as an add-on in epilepsy, correction of metabolic alkalosis, alkalinization of urine (in uric acid and cystine stones).

**Adverse effects:** metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias (numbness of the hands and feet), **calcium phosphate stones**, sulfonamide allergy; in liver cirrhosis — ammonia accumulation (hepatic encephalopathy).
6.2. Osmotic diuretics

**Mannitol** is filtered but not reabsorbed; by increasing the osmotic pressure in the tubules, it stops **water** reabsorption (mainly in the proximal tubule and the thin limb of the loop of Henle). By also increasing osmotic pressure in the blood, it **draws water from the tissues into the vessels**.

**Uses** (intravenous only): **cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure**, **an acute attack of angle-closure glaucoma** (rapid lowering of intraocular pressure), prevention of acute kidney injury with oliguria (rhabdomyolysis — historically).

parts.text: Mannitol is **absolutely contraindicated in heart failure and pulmonary edema**: it first increases the circulating volume and worsens pulmonary edema. It is also not used in anuria (no urine output), severe dehydration and the active phase of intracerebral hemorrhage.

blocks.text: 6.3. SGLT2 inhibitors and aquaretics

**SGLT2 inhibitors** (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) block the sodium-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule and cause glucosuria and moderate natriuresis. Although they are not strong diuretics, they reduce hospitalizations and mortality in **heart failure** (regardless of ejection fraction) and **chronic kidney disease** (Topics 11 and 15).

**Vaptans** (tolvaptan) block vasopressin V~2~ receptors in the collecting duct and increase the excretion of **free water** (aquaresis). Uses: **hypervolemic and euvolemic hyponatremia** (syndrome of inappropriate vasopressin secretion — SIADH, heart failure), autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Raising sodium too quickly (> 10 mmol/l/day) carries a risk of **osmotic demyelination**; hepatotoxicity.

blocks.text: 8.1. Choice of diuretic

Choice

blocks.text: 8.2. Diuretic resistance

**Causes:** high salt intake, taking NSAIDs, low perfusion (hypotension), hypoalbuminemia (furosemide reaches the tubule bound to protein), impaired intestinal absorption (bowel edema), adaptive hypertrophy of the distal nephron (the “braking” phenomenon).

**Ways to overcome it:** salt restriction; stopping NSAIDs; giving the diuretic intravenously or switching to a continuous infusion; increasing the dose; **sequential nephron blockade** — adding a thiazide (metolazone) or acetazolamide to a loop diuretic; with albumin in hypoalbuminemia.

parts.text: **Daily weight monitoring** during diuretic therapy is the simplest and most reliable method: a 1 kg decrease in weight corresponds to a loss of about 1 liter of fluid. Patients with heart failure are taught to see a doctor (or to increase the diuretic dose themselves) if their weight increases by more than 2 kg in 2–3 days.

skills.title: Skill 1. Monitoring electrolytes during diuretic therapy

items: Before starting treatment: sodium, potassium, creatinine (GFR), glucose, uric acid.
When starting loop and thiazide diuretics or increasing the dose — potassium and creatinine after 1–2 weeks.
When starting spironolactone — potassium and creatinine at 3 days and 1 week, then at 1, 2, 3 and 6 months.
Hypokalemia (< 3.5 mmol/l) — add potassium preparations or a potassium-sparing diuretic; especially important in a patient taking glycosides.
Hyperkalemia (> 5.5 mmol/l) — reduce the dose of the potassium-sparing diuretic or stop it; > 6.0 — urgent treatment (calcium gluconate, insulin + glucose, salbutamol).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 68-year-old man takes furosemide 80 mg/day, digoxin and enalapril for chronic heart failure and atrial fibrillation. In recent days he has felt weakness, muscle cramps, nausea and an irregular heartbeat. Potassium 2.9 mmol/l, magnesium low.
cases.ask: 1) The cause of the electrolyte disturbance? 2) Why is it especially dangerous for this patient? 3) Correction.
cases.answer: 1) The loop diuretic (furosemide) causes large losses of potassium and magnesium (increased Na^+^ delivery to the collecting duct, secondary hyperaldosteronism). 2) Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia increase digoxin toxicity and the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. 3) Potassium and magnesium preparations (slowly intravenously if needed), adding spironolactone (it also reduces mortality in HF and retains potassium), reducing the furosemide dose to the lowest effective dose; monitoring of the digoxin level and ECG; recheck electrolytes in 1 week.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 55-year-old woman takes hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg/day for AH. She has developed acute pain, redness and swelling in the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe. Blood uric acid is raised. In addition, glucose is at a borderline level.
cases.ask: 1) Are these conditions related to the diuretic? 2) How should the antihypertensive treatment be changed?
cases.answer: 1) Thiazides (especially at high doses) cause hyperuricemia (competition for tubular secretion of uric acid and increased reabsorption with hypovolemia) and hyperglycemia — an attack of gout has developed. 2) Stop hydrochlorothiazide; for AH choose losartan (it has a uricosuric effect) and/or amlodipine; treat the gout attack (colchicine or an NSAID or a glucocorticoid); later, allopurinol if needed.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 30-year-old mountaineer is planning to climb to an altitude of 4,500 m. On his previous trip he had headache, nausea and insomnia.
cases.ask: Which diuretic would you recommend for prevention, and by what mechanism?
cases.answer: Acetazolamide (125 mg 2 times a day, starting 1 day before the ascent and continuing for 2 days after reaching the highest point). Mechanism: by excreting bicarbonate it causes metabolic acidosis — this stimulates the respiratory center, increases ventilation and speeds up acclimatization (the hypoxic ventilatory response). Adverse effects: paresthesias, altered taste of carbonated drinks, frequent urination; contraindicated in sulfonamide allergy. The main prevention is a gradual ascent.

topics.title: Drugs acting on the blood system. Antiplatelet agents. Anticoagulants. Fibrinolytic agents

goals.text: Thromboses are the main cause of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Antithrombotic drugs (antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, fibrinolytics) save millions of lives, but they are also among the drugs that cause the most serious adverse effects (bleeding). Anemia — especially iron deficiency anemia — is also widespread among women and children in Uzbekistan. This topic covers drugs that affect blood coagulation, hemostasis and hematopoiesis.
The student should know:

items: the stages of hemostasis: vascular-platelet hemostasis, the coagulation cascade and fibrinolysis;
the mechanism and uses of antiplatelet agents (acetylsalicylic acid, P2Y~12~ blockers, GP IIb/IIIa blockers);
direct (heparins, Xa and thrombin inhibitors) and indirect (warfarin) anticoagulants, their monitoring and antidotes;
fibrinolytics, antifibrinolytics and hemostatics;
drugs that stimulate hematopoiesis (iron, B~12~, folic acid, erythropoietin).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as acetylsalicylic acid, clopidogrel, heparin, enoxaparin, warfarin, rivaroxaban, apixaban, alteplase, tranexamic acid and iron preparations;
adjust the warfarin dose according to the INR and provide care in anticoagulant-related bleeding;
draw up a treatment plan for iron deficiency anemia.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors** — **II, VII, IX, X** (and proteins C and S). To remember them: **“1972”** — 10, 9, 7, 2. Warfarin disrupts the synthesis of exactly these factors.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Arterial and venous thrombi: in arteries (high velocity) — a **platelet-rich “white” thrombus** → **antiplatelet agents** (prevention of infarction and stroke); in veins (slow flow) — a **fibrin- and red cell-rich “red” thrombus** → **anticoagulants** (deep vein thrombosis, PE, atrial fibrillation).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The antiplatelet dose of aspirin is 75–100 mg/day** (low dose). At high doses (> 300 mg), prostacyclin synthesis in the endothelium is also inhibited and gastrointestinal adverse effects rise sharply, while the antiplatelet effect does not increase. In acute coronary syndrome and stroke, a **loading dose** of 150–300 mg is chewed.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The antidote to heparin is protamine sulfate**: a strongly basic protein that binds heparin directly and inactivates it (chemical antagonism). **1 mg of protamine neutralizes 100 units of heparin** (the amount of heparin given in the last 2–3 hours is taken into account). It neutralizes LMWH only partly (≈ 60%).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Warfarin has very many interactions** (narrow therapeutic range, metabolism via CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, 99% protein binding): **enhance its effect (bleeding risk)**: amiodarone, fluconazole and other azoles, metronidazole, many antibiotics (co-trimoxazole, fluoroquinolones, macrolides — they also reduce the intestinal flora), NSAIDs and aspirin (pharmacodynamic), SSRIs, acute alcohol intake, liver diseases; **reduce its effect**: rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort, foods rich in vitamin K (spinach, cabbage, broccoli, green tea — intake should be kept stable). Whenever a new drug is prescribed, the INR should be checked frequently.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Absolute contraindications to thrombolysis**: a history of intracerebral hemorrhage at any time; ischemic stroke in the last 3–6 months (other than the acute stroke); a brain tumor or vascular malformation; active internal bleeding (except menstruation); suspected aortic dissection; severe trauma, head injury or major surgery in the last month; uncontrolled AH (> 185/110 mm Hg). The main complication is **bleeding, especially intracerebral hemorrhage**; antidote — tranexamic acid, cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Acute iron poisoning** is one of the common causes of fatal poisoning in children (sweet tablets!): vomiting (with blood), diarrhea, then a “false improvement”, followed by shock, metabolic acidosis and liver failure. **Antidote — deferoxamine** (intravenously). Activated charcoal does not bind iron.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In B~12~ deficiency, giving **folic acid** alone improves the anemia but **worsens the neurological disorders**. In megaloblastic anemia, the B~12~ level should be measured first, or both should be given together.

blocks.text: **Hemostasis** is the system that stops bleeding when a vessel is damaged and keeps the blood fluid. It consists of three stages:

items: **Vascular-platelet hemostasis.** Collagen and von Willebrand factor under the damaged endothelium cause platelet **adhesion**. Activated platelets release **thromboxane A~2~** (TXA~2~), **ADP** and serotonin and recruit other platelets. The final common pathway is activation of the **GP IIb/IIIa** receptors on the platelet membrane, which link platelets to each other through fibrinogen (**aggregation**) — a white thrombus forms.

**Coagulation hemostasis.** The cascade of plasma clotting factors: tissue factor (with factor VII) → **factor Xa** → prothrombin (II) → **thrombin** (IIa) → fibrinogen → **fibrin** → factor XIIIa stabilizes the fibrin — a red thrombus.
**Fibrinolysis.** Under the influence of tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA), plasminogen is converted into **plasmin**, which breaks down fibrin.

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: The prostacyclin–thromboxane system and platelet aggregation: thromboxane A~2~ enhances aggregation and vasoconstriction, prostacyclin (in the endothelium) reduces them (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: **Natural anticoagulants:** antithrombin III (inactivates thrombin and Xa; heparin enhances its action), proteins C and S (vitamin K-dependent), tissue factor pathway inhibitor.

parts.text: **Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors** — **II, VII, IX, X** (and proteins C and S). To remember them: **“1972”** — 10, 9, 7, 2. Warfarin disrupts the synthesis of exactly these factors.

Arterial and venous thrombi: in arteries (high velocity) — a **platelet-rich “white” thrombus** → **antiplatelet agents** (prevention of infarction and stroke); in veins (slow flow) — a **fibrin- and red cell-rich “red” thrombus** → **anticoagulants** (deep vein thrombosis, PE, atrial fibrillation).

blocks.caption: Directions of action of drugs affecting blood coagulation and fibrinolysis (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: 2.1. Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin)

**Mechanism.** It **irreversibly acetylates** **cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1)** in platelets → TXA~2~ synthesis stops. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot synthesize new enzyme, so the effect lasts for **the whole life of the platelet** (7–10 days). Endothelial cells, in contrast, resynthesize COX and restore prostacyclin production.

parts.text: **The antiplatelet dose of aspirin is 75–100 mg/day** (low dose). At high doses (> 300 mg), prostacyclin synthesis in the endothelium is also inhibited and gastrointestinal adverse effects rise sharply, while the antiplatelet effect does not increase. In acute coronary syndrome and stroke, a **loading dose** of 150–300 mg is chewed.

blocks.text: **Uses:** acute coronary syndrome, stable IHD, ischemic stroke and TIA, peripheral artery disease — **secondary prevention**; after coronary stenting (with a P2Y~12~ blocker — dual antiplatelet therapy); prevention of preeclampsia (in high-risk pregnant women). In **primary prevention** (in people without cardiovascular disease), the risk of bleeding may outweigh the benefit — it is now **not routinely recommended**.

**Adverse effects:** gastrointestinal erosions and ulcers, **bleeding**, bronchospasm (**“aspirin-induced asthma”** — NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease), **Reye syndrome** in children (during a viral infection — liver and brain damage; contraindicated for fever under 16 years).
2.2. P2Y~12~ receptor blockers
By blocking **ADP receptors (P2Y~12~)** on platelets, they stop GP IIb/IIIa activation.

head: Preparation
Features
Recovery
rows: A prodrug — activated in the liver via CYP2C19; slow action, large individual variation (genetic “poor metabolizers”); interaction with omeprazole
A prodrug, but activated quickly and reliably; more potent
An active drug, binds reversibly; 2 times a day; dyspnea (related to adenosine)

blocks.text: **Uses:** **together with aspirin** in acute coronary syndrome and after coronary stenting (dual antiplatelet therapy, usually for 12 months), in aspirin allergy or intolerance, in ischemic stroke and peripheral artery disease (clopidogrel).
2.3. Other antiplatelet agents

items: **GP IIb/IIIa blockers** (eptifibatide, tirofiban) — intravenous only, during coronary interventions with a large angiographic thrombus burden; the most potent antiplatelet agents; bleeding and thrombocytopenia.
**Dipyridamole** — a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that also inhibits adenosine uptake; with aspirin for secondary prevention of stroke; the “steal” phenomenon (may worsen angina in IHD).
**Cilostazol** — a PDE-3 inhibitor; in peripheral artery disease (claudication); contraindicated in heart failure.
**Pentoxifylline** — improves red cell deformability; limited effectiveness.

blocks.text: 3.1. Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
**Heparin** is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan formed in mast cells; a natural anticoagulant. The preparation is obtained from porcine intestinal mucosa.

**Mechanism.** Heparin binds to **antithrombin III** and increases its activity **1,000-fold**. The complex inactivates **thrombin (IIa)** and **factor Xa** (as well as IXa, XIa and XIIa). To inactivate thrombin, the heparin molecule must be long (18 or more saccharides) — it binds antithrombin and thrombin simultaneously like a “bridge”.

items: It acts **in vitro and in vivo**; the effect begins **immediately** (intravenously).
It is not absorbed from the intestine — only **intravenously** or **subcutaneously** (intramuscular injection is contraindicated because of the risk of hematoma).
Short action (t½ ≈ 1–1.5 hours); nonlinear pharmacokinetics, variable individual response.

**Laboratory monitoring: activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)** — prolonged to 1.5–2.5 times normal. **Uses:** acute coronary syndrome, PE, deep vein thrombosis, cardiopulmonary bypass, hemodialysis, the hypercoagulable phase of DIC, anticoagulation **in severe renal failure** (instead of LMWH), situations requiring rapid reversal.

blocks.text: Adverse effects:

items: **bleeding**;

**heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)** — immune (antibodies to the heparin-PF4 complex), on days 5–14; platelets fall by more than 50% and **paradoxical thrombosis** (arterial and venous) develops. Treatment: stop all heparins, switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux);
with long-term use — **osteoporosis**, alopecia, hyperkalemia (inhibition of aldosterone synthesis), allergic reactions.

parts.text: **The antidote to heparin is protamine sulfate**: a strongly basic protein that binds heparin directly and inactivates it (chemical antagonism). **1 mg of protamine neutralizes 100 units of heparin** (the amount of heparin given in the last 2–3 hours is taken into account). It neutralizes LMWH only partly (≈ 60%).

blocks.text: 3.2. Low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH)
**Enoxaparin, nadroparin, dalteparin** — short-chain fractions of heparin. They inactivate mainly **factor Xa** (less effect on thrombin).

blocks.text: **Uses:** **prevention** (surgery, prolonged bed rest, oncology) and treatment of venous thromboembolism, acute coronary syndrome, **anticoagulation in pregnancy** (does not cross the placenta — the drug of choice).
**Fondaparinux** — a synthetic pentasaccharide; through antithrombin it inactivates only Xa; it does not cause HIT.
3.3. Indirect anticoagulants — warfarin

**Mechanism.** Warfarin inhibits **vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1)** → the active (reduced) form of vitamin K is not regenerated → gamma-carboxylation of factors **II, VII, IX and X** in the liver is disrupted → inactive factors are formed.

items: It acts **only in vivo** (not in vitro).

The effect begins **with a delay** — 3–5 days (the existing factors must be broken down; t½ of factor VII is 6 hours, of factor II 60 hours). Therefore, **in acute thrombosis, warfarin is started together with heparin (LMWH)**, and the heparin is stopped when the INR has been in the target range on 2 consecutive days.
In the first days of treatment, **protein C** (short t½) falls quickly — a temporary **hypercoagulable** state, rarely **warfarin skin necrosis** (in protein C deficiency).

**Laboratory monitoring: prothrombin time and INR** (international normalized ratio). For most indications the target INR is **2.0–3.0**; with a mechanical mitral valve — 2.5–3.5. **Uses:** atrial fibrillation (especially with mitral stenosis and **mechanical heart valves** — in these cases direct oral anticoagulants are **contraindicated**), deep vein thrombosis and PE (treatment and secondary prevention), antiphospholipid syndrome.

parts.text: **Warfarin has very many interactions** (narrow therapeutic range, metabolism via CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, 99% protein binding):

items: **enhance its effect (bleeding risk)**: amiodarone, fluconazole and other azoles, metronidazole, many antibiotics (co-trimoxazole, fluoroquinolones, macrolides — they also reduce the intestinal flora), NSAIDs and aspirin (pharmacodynamic), SSRIs, acute alcohol intake, liver diseases;
**reduce its effect**: rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort, foods rich in vitamin K (spinach, cabbage, broccoli, green tea — intake should be kept stable).

parts.text: Whenever a new drug is prescribed, the INR should be checked frequently.

blocks.text: **Adverse effects: bleeding** (the most important), skin necrosis, “purple toe” syndrome, **teratogenicity** (in the 1st trimester warfarin embryopathy — hypoplasia of the nose and bones; in the 3rd trimester — fetal bleeding) — **contraindicated in pregnancy**.

Management

Stop warfarin temporarily; if the bleeding risk is high — vitamin K 1–2.5 mg orally
Stop warfarin; prothrombin complex concentrate (or fresh frozen plasma) + vitamin K 5–10 mg intravenously slowly

blocks.text: 3.4. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs)
**Rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban** — direct inhibitors of **factor Xa**; **dabigatran** — a direct inhibitor of **thrombin** (the prodrug dabigatran etexilate).

**Advantages (over warfarin):** fixed doses, **no routine laboratory monitoring needed**, rapid onset and offset of action (hours), no food interactions, few drug interactions, **lower risk of intracerebral hemorrhage**.
Disadvantages and limitations:

items: **contraindicated with mechanical heart valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis** (warfarin is used);
dependent on renal function (especially dabigatran — 80% renal): dose adjustment by GFR, not used in severe renal failure;
contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding;
interactions with strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitors/inducers;

a missed dose means rapid loss of protection (adherence is important). **Antidotes:** dabigatran — **idarucizumab** (a monoclonal antibody fragment); Xa inhibitors — **andexanet alfa** (if unavailable — prothrombin complex concentrate).

blocks.text: **Uses:** stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis and PE (treatment and prevention), prevention after orthopedic surgery; low-dose rivaroxaban — with aspirin in IHD and peripheral artery disease.

parts.text: **Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation**: according to the CHA~2~DS~2~-VASc score (HF — 1, AH — 1, age ≥ 75 — 2, diabetes — 1, stroke/TIA — 2, vascular disease — 1, age 65–74 — 1, female sex — 1), an oral anticoagulant **is recommended** at ≥ 2 points in men and ≥ 3 in women. In nonvalvular fibrillation **DOACs are preferred to warfarin**. The bleeding risk is assessed with the HAS-BLED score — a high score is not a reason to withhold the anticoagulant but a basis for correcting modifiable risk factors (AH, NSAIDs, alcohol).

blocks.text: **Mechanism. They convert plasminogen into plasmin**; plasmin breaks down the fibrin in the thrombus (dissolves the thrombus).

blocks.caption: Mechanism of action of fibrinolytic drugs: conversion of profibrinolysin (plasminogen) into fibrinolysin (plasmin) in the blood plasma and inside the thrombus (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: Uses:

items: **ST-elevation myocardial infarction** — if percutaneous coronary intervention (stenting) is not possible within 120 minutes; up to **12 hours** from symptom onset (most effective in the first 3 hours — **“time is muscle”**);
**ischemic stroke** — up to **4.5 hours** from symptom onset (alteplase, tenecteplase), after hemorrhage has been excluded on CT (**“time is brain”**);
hemodynamically unstable (massive) **PE**;
thrombosis of catheters and shunts.

parts.text: **Absolute contraindications to thrombolysis**: a history of intracerebral hemorrhage at any time; ischemic stroke in the last 3–6 months (other than the acute stroke); a brain tumor or vascular malformation; active internal bleeding (except menstruation); suspected aortic dissection; severe trauma, head injury or major surgery in the last month; uncontrolled AH (> 185/110 mm Hg). The main complication is **bleeding, especially intracerebral hemorrhage**; antidote — tranexamic acid, cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen).

blocks.text: 5.1. Antifibrinolytics
**Tranexamic acid** and **aminocaproic acid** are lysine analogs; they block the binding of plasminogen to fibrin and inhibit fibrinolysis.

**Uses of tranexamic acid: massive bleeding in trauma** (within the first 3 hours — reduces mortality), **postpartum hemorrhage**, menorrhagia, dental procedures (in hemophilia), orthopedic and cardiac surgery, overdose of fibrinolytics. Contraindications: active thrombosis, DIC (hypercoagulable phase); seizures at high doses.
5.2. Coagulants

items: **Vitamin K** — **phytomenadione** (K~1~, natural, fat-soluble; oral and slow intravenous) and **menadione (Vikasol, K~3~, synthetic)**. Uses: warfarin overdose, vitamin K deficiency (biliary obstruction, obstructive jaundice, prolonged antibiotic therapy, malabsorption), **prevention of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn** (phytomenadione 1 mg intramuscularly after birth). The effect begins in 6–24 hours (the factors must be synthesized). Rapid intravenous injection of phytomenadione causes anaphylactoid reactions. Vikasol may cause hemolysis and jaundice in newborns — phytomenadione is preferred.
**Prothrombin complex concentrate** (factors II, VII, IX, X) — rapid treatment of severe warfarin-related bleeding.

**Clotting factor concentrates**: factor VIII (hemophilia A), factor IX (hemophilia B), von Willebrand factor; **desmopressin** increases the release of factor VIII and von Willebrand factor in mild hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease.
**Local hemostatics**: hemostatic collagen sponge, thrombin, hydrogen peroxide, calcium alginate, epinephrine (topical).
**Etamsylate** reduces capillary permeability and increases platelet adhesion; widely used in CIS countries, with a limited evidence base.

blocks.text: 6.1. Iron preparations
**Iron deficiency anemia** is the most common anemia (pregnant women, women with heavy periods, children, chronic blood loss).

blocks.label: Figure 14.4
blocks.caption: Absorption, distribution, storage and excretion of iron (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

blocks.text: Iron is absorbed mainly in **the duodenum and the upper jejunum**, in the divalent (**Fe^2+^**) form; ascorbic acid improves absorption; antacids, PPIs, tetracyclines, calcium and tea (tannins) reduce it. In the blood it is carried by transferrin and stored as ferritin and hemosiderin.

items: **Oral preparations** (first choice): iron(II) sulfate, fumarate, gluconate; iron(III) hydroxide polymaltose complex. The dose is based on **elemental iron**: 100–200 mg a day for adults (or 60–100 mg every other day — better absorption, fewer adverse effects). After hemoglobin normalizes, treatment continues for another **3 months** to replenish stores.
**Adverse effects**: nausea, epigastric pain, constipation or diarrhea, **black discoloration of the stool** (must be distinguished from bleeding); liquid preparations stain tooth enamel.

**Parenteral (intravenous) preparations** — ferric carboxymaltose, iron sucrose, ferric derisomaltose: when oral preparations are not tolerated or are ineffective, in malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, the 2nd–3rd trimesters of pregnancy. Anaphylactic reactions are possible — give where resuscitation is available.

parts.text: **Acute iron poisoning** is one of the common causes of fatal poisoning in children (sweet tablets!): vomiting (with blood), diarrhea, then a “false improvement”, followed by shock, metabolic acidosis and liver failure. **Antidote — deferoxamine** (intravenously). Activated charcoal does not bind iron.

blocks.text: 6.2. Vitamin B~12~ and folic acid

items: **Cyanocobalamin, hydroxocobalamin (B~12~)** — in **megaloblastic (pernicious) anemia**, especially with intrinsic factor deficiency (atrophic gastritis, gastric resection), and with long-term metformin and PPI use; only parenterally or orally at high doses. B~12~ deficiency causes **neurological disorders** (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord).

**Folic acid** — folate deficiency anemia; **when planning pregnancy** (400 mcg/day from 1–3 months before pregnancy and in the 1st trimester) — **prevention of neural tube defects**; during treatment with methotrexate.

parts.text: In B~12~ deficiency, giving **folic acid** alone improves the anemia but **worsens the neurological disorders**. In megaloblastic anemia, the B~12~ level should be measured first, or both should be given together.

blocks.text: 6.3. Stimulants of erythropoiesis and leukopoiesis

items: **Erythropoietins** (epoetin alfa and beta, darbepoetin) — anemia of **chronic kidney disease**, chemotherapy-induced anemia. Hemoglobin is not raised above 120 g/l (risk of thrombosis, stroke, AH); iron stores must be adequate.
**Granulocyte colony-stimulating factors** (filgrastim, pegfilgrastim) — neutropenia after chemotherapy.

head: Situation
Treatment
rows: Aspirin 150–300 mg chewed + a P2Y~12~ blocker (ticagrelor or clopidogrel) + heparin; primary coronary intervention or thrombolysis (alteplase, tenecteplase)
LMWH or a DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban); for at least 3 months
LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg SC once a day) or a DOAC

parts.text: **Stopping antithrombotic drugs before surgery**: aspirin — often continued (in patients with high cardiovascular risk); clopidogrel — 5 days before; warfarin — 5 days before (with LMWH “bridging” at high thrombotic risk); apixaban and rivaroxaban — 24–48 hours (depending on renal function); dabigatran — 48–96 hours. The decision is made jointly with the surgeon, anesthesiologist and cardiologist.

skills.title: Skill 1. Starting and monitoring warfarin treatment

items: Determine the baseline INR, complete blood count, and liver and kidney function.
Start warfarin at 2.5–5 mg a day (2.5 mg in the elderly, in liver disease and with low body weight).
In acute thrombosis, give it together with LMWH for at least 5 days, until the INR is above 2.0 on 2 consecutive days.
Check the INR on days 3–5, then every 2–3 days, and once stable — every 4 weeks.

Explain to the patient: take the drug at the same time every day, eat foods rich in vitamin K in stable amounts, tell the doctor about new drugs, signs of bleeding (blood in the urine, black stool, bleeding gums, bruising).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 72-year-old woman takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation (stable at INR 2.4). She was prescribed co-trimoxazole for a urinary tract infection and fluconazole for foot candidiasis. After 6 days she developed nosebleeds and many bruises under the skin; INR 7.8.
cases.ask: 1) The cause of the INR rise? 2) Management? 3) What should be done in the future?
cases.answer: 1) Co-trimoxazole and fluconazole inhibited CYP2C9 and slowed warfarin metabolism (co-trimoxazole also displaces it from proteins and reduces the intestinal flora) — the anticoagulant effect increased sharply. 2) Stop warfarin temporarily; INR 4.5–10 with minor bleeding — vitamin K 1–2.5 mg orally; local control of the nosebleed; recheck the INR after 24 hours; if there is major bleeding — prothrombin complex concentrate + intravenous vitamin K. 3) Choose antibiotics with few interactions (nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin); monitor the INR frequently when a new drug is prescribed; consider switching to a DOAC (apixaban) in nonvalvular fibrillation.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 60-year-old man is receiving enoxaparin after knee replacement surgery. On day 8 his platelets fell from 250 to 90 × 10^9^/l, and deep vein thrombosis of the left leg was found.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Management.
cases.answer: 1) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — an immune mechanism (antibodies to the heparin-PF4 complex), a platelet fall of more than 50%, on days 5–14 and with paradoxical thrombosis. 2) Stop all heparins immediately (including heparin solutions for flushing catheters); a non-heparin anticoagulant — intravenous argatroban or bivalirudin, or fondaparinux; once platelets recover, a DOAC or warfarin (warfarin only when platelets are > 150, otherwise there is a risk of skin necrosis and venous gangrene); platelet transfusion is not recommended; antibody testing; record heparin allergy in the medical records.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman complains of weakness, dizziness, brittle nails and a craving to eat chalk. Her periods are heavy and prolonged. Hemoglobin 88 g/l, MCV 68 fl, ferritin 6 ng/ml. She is planning a pregnancy.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Treatment plan? 3) Additional advice about planning pregnancy.
cases.answer: 1) Iron deficiency anemia (microcytic, low ferritin) caused by menorrhagia. 2) An oral iron(II) preparation — elemental iron 100 mg once a day or every other day, on an empty stomach, with ascorbic acid, without tea or milk; the effect is assessed by a rise in hemoglobin after 2–4 weeks; after hemoglobin normalizes, continue for another 3 months (to replenish stores); warn about dark stools; a gynecologist's consultation to find the cause of the menorrhagia (tranexamic acid if needed). If oral iron is not tolerated — intravenous ferric carboxymaltose. 3) Start folic acid 400 mcg/day 1–3 months before pregnancy (prevention of neural tube defects) and restore iron stores before pregnancy.

topics.cards_title: Table 14.8. Drugs acting on the blood system — summary

topics.title: Hormonal preparations of protein and polypeptide structure. Anti-inflammatory drugs

goals.text: This topic brings together two large and practically very important sections. Among **protein and polypeptide hormones**, the most important is **insulin**: diabetes mellitus affects about 10% of the population, and insulin and other glucose-lowering drugs are part of a GP's daily practice. Hypothalamic and pituitary hormones, and thyroid and parathyroid hormones are used in endocrinology, obstetrics and pediatrics. **Anti-inflammatory drugs** — nonsteroidal (NSAIDs) and steroidal (glucocorticoids) — are among the most consumed drugs in the world, and their adverse effects (gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury, corticosteroid complications) are also very common.
The student should know:

items: the classification of hormonal preparations and the preparations of hypothalamic-pituitary hormones;
thyroid hormones and antithyroid drugs;
the classification of insulin preparations, the principles of insulin therapy and the management of hypoglycemia;
the mechanism and uses of oral and other glucose-lowering drugs (metformin, sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors);
inflammatory mediators, and the classification, mechanism, uses and adverse effects of NSAIDs;
the mechanism, effects, uses and adverse effects of glucocorticoids and the rules for withdrawing them.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as insulin, metformin, gliclazide, levothyroxine, thiamazole, oxytocin, ibuprofen, diclofenac, paracetamol, prednisolone and dexamethasone;
provide emergency care in hypoglycemia;
assess the patient's gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk when choosing an NSAID.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Protein and polypeptide hormones **are broken down in the gastrointestinal tract** — so they are given mainly **parenterally** (injection, intranasally). Exceptions: desmopressin (nasal spray, sublingual and oral tablets), the oral form of semaglutide (with a special absorption enhancer).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: During treatment with **desmopressin** (especially in the elderly and in children with enuresis) there is a risk of **hyponatremia** and water intoxication: fluid intake in the evening must be restricted.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Using levothyroxine **for weight loss** is dangerous and prohibited.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Treatment of thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy: **in the 1st trimester — propylthiouracil** (thiamazole is teratogenic), **in the 2nd–3rd trimesters — thiamazole** (PTU is hepatotoxic). During treatment with thionamides, the patient must be warned about **signs of agranulocytosis** (fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers), and in such cases the drug must be stopped immediately and the white cell count checked.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Only short-acting (regular, soluble) insulin can be given intravenously**; NPH and premixed insulins are suspensions — not for intravenous use. In diabetic ketoacidosis: **fluids (0.9% NaCl)** → **intravenous infusion of short-acting insulin** (0.1 U/kg/hour) → **potassium** (insulin shifts potassium into cells and causes hypokalemia) → glucose is added when blood glucose falls to 14 mmol/l.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Care in hypoglycemia (the “rule of 15”)**: if conscious — **15–20 g of rapidly absorbed carbohydrate** (3–4 glucose tablets, 150–200 ml of sweet juice), recheck glucose after 15 minutes, repeat if needed, then a meal with complex carbohydrates. If **unconscious** — **40% glucose 20–40 ml intravenously** (or 10% glucose) or **glucagon 1 mg** intramuscularly or subcutaneously (nasal powder 3 mg) — relatives can also give it at home. Fluids must not be poured into the mouth of an unconscious patient (aspiration).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks presented sulfonylureas (especially glibenclamide) and biguanides such as buformin and phenformin as the main drugs. **Phenformin and buformin were withdrawn from the market because of lactic acidosis**; glibenclamide is not recommended in the elderly because it causes prolonged hypoglycemia — **gliclazide MR** or glimepiride is preferred.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Paracetamol poisoning** — hepatotoxicity. At therapeutic doses, paracetamol is conjugated mainly with glucuronide and sulfate; a small part is converted by CYP2E1 into the toxic **NAPQI**, which is detoxified by **glutathione**. In overdose glutathione is depleted → NAPQI destroys hepatocytes → **liver necrosis** (on days 2–4; almost no signs on the first day!). **Antidote — N-acetylcysteine** (restores glutathione stores), most effective within 8 hours; measure the blood paracetamol concentration (using the nomogram). Risk factors: alcoholism, starvation, CYP inducers. Many combined “cold” remedies contain paracetamol — risk of **hidden overdose**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Equivalent doses: **“20 – 5 – 4 – 0.75”** — hydrocortisone 20 mg = prednisolone 5 mg = methylprednisolone 4 mg = dexamethasone 0.75 mg. Dexamethasone is chosen for fetal lung maturation and in cerebral edema (no mineralocorticoid effect, potent, crosses the placenta).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The rule for withdrawing glucocorticoids**: if systemic glucocorticoids have been taken **for more than 3 weeks** (or > 20 mg/day of prednisolone equivalent for more than 1 week), they **must not be stopped abruptly** — the dose is reduced gradually (to allow the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis to recover). Abrupt withdrawal causes **acute adrenal insufficiency** (severe weakness, hypotension, shock, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia) and relapse of the disease. In such patients the dose must be increased during **stress** (surgery, severe infection, trauma) (“stress dose”, intravenous hydrocortisone).

parts.text: **Oxytocin** stimulates oxytocin receptors of the uterine myometrium and strengthens rhythmic contractions; the sensitivity of the myometrium rises sharply toward the end of pregnancy. Its use carries a risk of **uterine hyperstimulation** (fetal hypoxia, uterine rupture) and, at large doses, of an antidiuretic effect (**water intoxication**, hyponatremia); it is given only with an infusion pump under CTG monitoring. Other drugs acting on the myometrium are studied in 5th-semester independent study.

During treatment with **desmopressin** (especially in the elderly and in children with enuresis) there is a risk of **hyponatremia** and water intoxication: fluid intake in the evening must be restricted.

blocks.text: 3.1. Thyroid hormones

The thyroid gland produces **thyroxine (T~4~)** and **triiodothyronine (T~3~)**. T~4~ is converted in the periphery into the more active T~3~. Through nuclear receptors they regulate basal metabolism, heat production, growth and development (especially of the CNS), and cardiac function.

**Levothyroxine** (L-thyroxine) is the drug of choice for treating **hypothyroidism** (replacement therapy). T½ ≈ 7 days — once a day; the dose is titrated according to **TSH** (every 6–8 weeks). The full replacement dose in adults is ≈ 1.6 mcg/kg/day; **in the elderly and in IHD it is started at a small dose** (12.5–25 mcg) so as not to provoke myocardial ischemia. It is taken **on an empty stomach**, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, separately from other drugs (calcium, iron, PPIs, antacids). The dose requirement increases in pregnancy.
Other uses: congenital hypothyroidism (in newborns — early start is crucial for mental development), after thyroidectomy, TSH suppression in thyroid cancer.
**Adverse effects (in overdose)** — drug-induced thyrotoxicosis: tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, angina, weight loss, tremor, osteoporosis.

parts.text: Using levothyroxine **for weight loss** is dangerous and prohibited.

3.3. Hormones regulating calcium metabolism

The **parathyroid hormone** analog **teriparatide** (in severe osteoporosis, stimulates bone formation, daily SC). **Calcitonin** inhibits osteoclasts (hypercalcemia, Paget disease; now rarely). Drugs for treating osteoporosis (bisphosphonates, denosumab, vitamin D) are studied in 5th-semester independent study.
4.1. Physiology of insulin

**Insulin** is the hormone of the pancreatic **beta cells**; it consists of A and B chains (51 amino acids). Glucose enters the beta cell and generates ATP → **ATP-dependent K^+^ channels close** → depolarization → Ca^2+^ enters → insulin is released.
Insulin acts through a **tyrosine kinase receptor**:

items: it increases glucose entry into muscle and fat cells (GLUT4 transporters move to the membrane);
it enhances glycogen synthesis in the liver and inhibits **gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis**;
it inhibits lipolysis and enhances fat synthesis (stops the formation of **ketone bodies**);
it increases protein synthesis;
it shifts **potassium into cells** (activation of Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase).

blocks.text: 4.2. Insulin preparations
Modern preparations are **recombinant human insulin** and its **analogs** (with a modified amino acid sequence and improved pharmacokinetics). The concentration is usually **100 U/ml** (U-100).

parts.text: **Only short-acting (regular, soluble) insulin can be given intravenously**; NPH and premixed insulins are suspensions — not for intravenous use. In diabetic ketoacidosis: **fluids (0.9% NaCl)** → **intravenous infusion of short-acting insulin** (0.1 U/kg/hour) → **potassium** (insulin shifts potassium into cells and causes hypokalemia) → glucose is added when blood glucose falls to 14 mmol/l.

blocks.text: Insulin therapy regimens:

items: **basal-bolus (intensive)** — the standard in type 1 diabetes: a long-acting insulin (basal, ≈ 50% of the daily dose) + a short- or ultra-short-acting insulin before each meal (bolus); or an insulin pump;

**in type 2 diabetes** — adding an evening basal insulin to oral agents (starting with 10 U or 0.1–0.2 U/kg, titrated by fasting morning glucose). **Uses:** type 1 diabetes mellitus (vital), type 2 diabetes when other agents are ineffective or in decompensation, **gestational diabetes** (the drug of choice in pregnancy), diabetic ketoacidosis and the hyperosmolar state, surgery and severe illness, **hyperkalemia** (with glucose).

blocks.text: **Adverse effects: hypoglycemia** (the most common and dangerous), weight gain, **lipodystrophy** at the injection site (sites must be rotated), hypokalemia, allergic reactions (rare).
4.3. Hypoglycemia

**Hypoglycemia** is glucose **below 3.9 mmol/l** (clinically significant — below 3.0). Causes: an excessive dose of insulin or a sulfonylurea, a missed meal, physical exertion, alcohol, renal failure.

**Signs:** adrenergic — sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety; neuroglycopenic — headache, confusion, unusual behavior, visual disturbances, seizures, coma. **Beta-blockers mask the adrenergic signs.**

parts.text: **Care in hypoglycemia (the “rule of 15”)**: if conscious — **15–20 g of rapidly absorbed carbohydrate** (3–4 glucose tablets, 150–200 ml of sweet juice), recheck glucose after 15 minutes, repeat if needed, then a meal with complex carbohydrates. If **unconscious** — **40% glucose 20–40 ml intravenously** (or 10% glucose) or **glucagon 1 mg** intramuscularly or subcutaneously (nasal powder 3 mg) — relatives can also give it at home. Fluids must not be poured into the mouth of an unconscious patient (aspiration).

parts.text: **The modern principle of treating type 2 diabetes mellitus**: first line — lifestyle changes + **metformin** (unless contraindicated). If the patient has **atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease**, an **SGLT2 inhibitor** and/or a **GLP-1 agonist** is added regardless of the glucose level (organ-protective effect). GLP-1 agonists are preferred in obesity. The target HbA~1c~ for most patients is **< 7%** (individualized in the elderly and frail, avoiding hypoglycemia).

Older textbooks presented sulfonylureas (especially glibenclamide) and biguanides such as buformin and phenformin as the main drugs. **Phenformin and buformin were withdrawn from the market because of lactic acidosis**; glibenclamide is not recommended in the elderly because it causes prolonged hypoglycemia — **gliclazide MR** or glimepiride is preferred.

blocks.text: 5.1. Inflammatory mediators and the arachidonic acid cascade
**Arachidonic acid** is released from cell membrane phospholipids by **phospholipase A~2~**. It is metabolized by two pathways:

items: **the cyclooxygenase (COX)** pathway → prostaglandin G~2~/H~2~ → **prostaglandins** (PGE~2~ — pain, fever, inflammation, gastric protection, renal blood flow; PGI~2~ — prostacyclin), **thromboxane A~2~**;
**the lipoxygenase** pathway → **leukotrienes** (LTB~4~ — chemotaxis; LTC~4~, D~4~, E~4~ — bronchospasm, vascular permeability).

blocks.text: 5.2. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
**Mechanism.** By inhibiting COX, they reduce prostaglandin synthesis. As a result:

items: **anti-inflammatory** effect (vascular permeability and edema decrease);
**analgesic** effect — peripheral (fewer PGs that sensitize nociceptors to bradykinin and histamine) and central;
**antipyretic** effect — PGE~2~ synthesis in the hypothalamus decreases (normal temperature is not lowered);
**antiplatelet** effect — TXA~2~ in platelets decreases (aspirin — irreversibly).

blocks.label: Figure 15.4
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the analgesic action of acetylsalicylic acid: by reducing prostaglandin E synthesis it lowers the sensitivity of nociceptors to bradykinin (teaching material of the TMA Department of Pharmacology)

parts.text: Prescribing NSAIDs **to patients at high gastrointestinal risk**: paracetamol or a topical NSAID (gel) where possible; if necessary — the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, **together with a PPI**, or a selective COX-2 inhibitor + a PPI. In patients at high cardiovascular risk — **naproxen** or low-dose ibuprofen; avoid coxibs and diclofenac. Ibuprofen may interfere with the cardioprotective antiplatelet effect of aspirin — aspirin is taken at least 30 minutes before ibuprofen.

blocks.text: 5.3. Paracetamol

**Paracetamol (acetaminophen)** is an analgesic and antipyretic; its anti-inflammatory effect is very weak. Its mechanism is not fully clear: it inhibits COX mainly in the CNS (in the periphery, the high peroxide levels in the inflammatory focus inactivate it) and acts on the serotonergic and cannabinoid systems. It has almost no effect on the gastric mucosa, platelets or kidneys — it is the **first-choice** analgesic-antipyretic **in children, pregnant women and the elderly** and in gastric diseases.

**Dose:** 500–1000 mg for adults, **no more than 4 g a day** (2–3 g with liver disease, alcoholism, starvation, low body weight); **10–15 mg/kg** for children, every 4–6 hours, no more than 60 mg/kg a day.

parts.text: **Paracetamol poisoning** — hepatotoxicity. At therapeutic doses, paracetamol is conjugated mainly with glucuronide and sulfate; a small part is converted by CYP2E1 into the toxic **NAPQI**, which is detoxified by **glutathione**. In overdose glutathione is depleted → NAPQI destroys hepatocytes → **liver necrosis** (on days 2–4; almost no signs on the first day!). **Antidote — N-acetylcysteine** (restores glutathione stores), most effective within 8 hours; measure the blood paracetamol concentration (using the nomogram). Risk factors: alcoholism, starvation, CYP inducers. Many combined “cold” remedies contain paracetamol — risk of **hidden overdose**.

blocks.text: 5.4. Metamizole (Analgin)

A strong analgesic and antipyretic, antispasmodic. Because of **agranulocytosis** (rare but potentially fatal), it is banned or restricted in many countries; it is widely used in CIS countries. Rapid intravenous injection causes hypotension and anaphylaxis.
6.1. Mechanism

**Glucocorticoids** (cortisol and its synthetic analogs), being lipophilic molecules, enter the cell and bind to the cytoplasmic **glucocorticoid receptor**; the complex moves into the nucleus and changes gene transcription:

items: **transrepression** — suppresses the expression of inflammatory genes (via NF-kappaB, AP-1): cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha), COX-2, iNOS and adhesion molecules decrease;

**transactivation** — increases the synthesis of anti-inflammatory proteins (**lipocortin-1 (annexin-1)**, which inhibits phospholipase A~2~ — as a result **both prostaglandins and leukotrienes** decrease); the metabolic adverse effects also arise mainly through this pathway.

blocks.text: Topical preparations: **inhaled** (budesonide, fluticasone — Topic 9), **nasal sprays** (mometasone), **for the skin** (hydrocortisone 1% — weak, betamethasone, clobetasol — very potent), **eye drops**, intra-articular (triamcinolone, depot betamethasone).
6.4. Uses

items: **replacement therapy** — adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease — hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone), congenital adrenal hyperplasia;
**rheumatic and autoimmune diseases** — rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis, polymyalgia;
**allergic conditions** — anaphylaxis (after epinephrine, as an add-on), angioedema, severe dermatitis, allergic rhinitis (topical);
**bronchial asthma and COPD** (inhaled maintenance therapy; systemic in exacerbations);
**kidney diseases** (nephrotic syndrome), **bowel** (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis), **liver** (autoimmune hepatitis);
**hematology and oncology** — leukemias, lymphomas (in chemotherapy regimens), chemotherapy-induced vomiting;
**transplantation** — prevention of rejection of the transplanted organ;
**cerebral edema** (peritumoral — dexamethasone), bacterial meningitis (dexamethasone), severe COVID-19 and pneumonia (dexamethasone);
**fetal lung maturation** — at risk of preterm birth (dexamethasone, betamethasone);
**shock** — septic shock (resistant to vasopressors), adrenal crisis.

parts.text: **The rule for withdrawing glucocorticoids**: if systemic glucocorticoids have been taken **for more than 3 weeks** (or > 20 mg/day of prednisolone equivalent for more than 1 week), they **must not be stopped abruptly** — the dose is reduced gradually (to allow the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis to recover). Abrupt withdrawal causes **acute adrenal insufficiency** (severe weakness, hypotension, shock, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia) and relapse of the disease. In such patients the dose must be increased during **stress** (surgery, severe infection, trauma) (“stress dose”, intravenous hydrocortisone).

**Prevention during long-term glucocorticoid treatment**: take once in the morning (in line with the circadian rhythm); the lowest effective dose; **calcium and vitamin D**, and a bisphosphonate if the risk is high (osteoporosis); a PPI if combined with an NSAID; monitoring of glucose, BP and intraocular pressure; screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before treatment; live vaccines are contraindicated.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA~1c~ 8.4%), a myocardial infarction 2 years ago, obesity (BMI 34), GFR 65 ml/min. He currently takes only glibenclamide; in the last month he has had two episodes of nocturnal hypoglycemia.
cases.ask: 1) Shortcomings of the current treatment? 2) Optimal treatment plan.
cases.answer: 1) Glibenclamide is the sulfonylurea with the highest risk of hypoglycemia, it leads to weight gain and does not reduce cardiovascular complications. 2) Stop glibenclamide; metformin (allowed at GFR 65); because of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and obesity, a GLP-1 agonist (semaglutide) and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) regardless of glucose — they reduce cardiovascular complications, lower weight and do not cause hypoglycemia; statin, aspirin, BP control; target HbA~1c~ < 7%.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 19-year-old female student has type 1 diabetes. On the day of an exam she skipped breakfast but injected her usual insulin dose. Two hours later she developed tremor, heavy sweating and confusion, and then lost consciousness. The glucometer shows 1.9 mmol/l.
cases.ask: 1) Condition? 2) Emergency care?
cases.answer: 1) Severe hypoglycemia (hypoglycemic coma). 2) Do not pour anything into her mouth (aspiration); glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly or subcutaneously (or 3 mg intranasally) — bystanders can give it; a health worker — 40% glucose 40–60 ml as an intravenous push, then an infusion of 5–10% glucose; once conscious — a carbohydrate meal; analyze the cause and teach the patient not to inject insulin without eating; she should always carry a glucagon kit.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 45-year-old woman has been taking prednisolone 15 mg/day for 6 months for rheumatoid arthritis. Because she felt better, she stopped the drug abruptly on her own. Three days later she developed severe weakness, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, BP 80/50 mm Hg, glucose 3.2 mmol/l, sodium 128 mmol/l.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Pathogenesis? 3) Treatment and prevention.
cases.answer: 1) Acute adrenal insufficiency (glucocorticoid withdrawal syndrome, secondary). 2) Long-term exogenous glucocorticoid intake suppressed the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (ACTH secretion decreased, the adrenal cortex atrophied); when the drug was stopped, her own cortisol production was insufficient. 3) Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously immediately, then 200 mg/day as an infusion or every 6 hours; infusion of 0.9% NaCl and glucose; once stable, switch to oral prednisolone and reduce the dose gradually (over several weeks to months). Explain to the patient that glucocorticoids must not be stopped abruptly and that the dose must be increased in stressful situations; give her a “steroid card”.

topics.title: Antiseptic and disinfectant agents. Synthetic antibacterial agents

goals.text: The fight against infections is waged in two directions: destroying microorganisms in the environment and on the skin surface (**antisepsis and disinfection**) and treating infection inside the body (**chemotherapy**). Proper hand disinfection is considered the most effective measure for preventing hospital-acquired infections. Synthetic antibacterial agents (fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, nitrofurans, nitroimidazoles) are widely used to treat urinary tract, intestinal and anaerobic infections. Antibiotic **resistance** is a global health problem of the 21st century; that is why knowing the principles of rational use of antimicrobials is mandatory for every doctor.
The student should know:

items: the concepts of antisepsis, disinfection and sterilization and the classification of antiseptics;
the mechanism, spectrum of activity and uses of the main groups of antiseptics;
the general principles of chemotherapy, the targets of antimicrobial drugs and the mechanisms of resistance;
the mechanism, uses and adverse effects of sulfonamides, co-trimoxazole, quinolones and fluoroquinolones, nitrofurans, nitroimidazoles, oxazolidinones and 8-hydroxyquinolines.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as ethyl alcohol, chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate, brilliant green, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, co-trimoxazole, nitrofurantoin and metronidazole;
perform the technique of hygienic hand disinfection;
choose a synthetic antibacterial agent for a urinary tract infection.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The main difference between antiseptic and chemotherapeutic agents is **selective action (selectivity)**. Antiseptics are protoplasmic poisons: they act on microbial and human cells **nonselectively**, so they are used only on surfaces. Chemotherapeutic agents act on targets specific to microbes and cause little harm to the macroorganism — they are used systemically.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Common incorrect practices: 1) applying iodine and brilliant green **into an open wound** — this damages tissue and slows healing (only around the wound); 2) using boric acid in children — it is absorbed through the skin and may cause severe poisoning; 3) pouring alcohol onto an open wound. The most important thing in cleaning minor wounds is **irrigation with plenty of clean water or saline**.

summary.label: Remember

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Antimicrobial resistance** is a global threat that causes millions of deaths a year. Factors that worsen it: unjustified use of antibiotics in viral infections (ARVI, influenza), over-the-counter sales, wrong dose and duration, antibiotics in animal farming. The WHO **AWaRe** classification divides antibiotics into “Access” (can be widely used), “Watch” (use with caution) and “Reserve” groups.

summary.text: Sources of PABA reduce the effect of sulfonamides: **pus and necrotic tissue** (much PABA) and drugs that form PABA — **procaine (Novocaine), benzocaine (Anesthesin)**. That is why sulfonamides are ineffective when used together with procaine or in a purulent wound.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Because of **serious adverse effects of fluoroquinolones** (FDA and EMA warnings), they are **not recommended as first choice** in uncomplicated cystitis, acute bronchitis and mild sinusitis: **tendinitis and tendon (Achilles) rupture** — especially in people over 60 and together with **glucocorticoids**; peripheral neuropathy (may be irreversible), CNS disorders (dizziness, insomnia, psychosis, **seizures** — especially with NSAIDs); **QT prolongation** and arrhythmias; aortic aneurysm and dissection; dysglycemia (hypo- and hyperglycemia), photosensitivity, C. difficile colitis; contraindicated **in children and adolescents** (damage to growing joint cartilage) and **in pregnancy and breastfeeding** (except for special indications).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The spectrum of metronidazole — **“GET GAP on the Metro”**: **G**iardia, **E**ntamoeba, **T**richomonas, **G**ardnerella, **A**naerobes, **P** — H. pylori. In short: **“Anaerobes and protozoa — metronidazole”**.

items: **Antisepsis** — destroying microorganisms on the skin, mucous membranes and wound surfaces or stopping their multiplication.
**Disinfection** — destroying pathogenic microorganisms on objects in the environment (instruments, rooms, waste, clothing).
**Sterilization** — complete destruction of all microorganisms, including spores (autoclave, dry heat, ethylene oxide, glutaraldehyde).
**Chemotherapeutic agents** — agents that act selectively inside the body on microorganisms, parasites or tumor cells.

parts.text: The main difference between antiseptic and chemotherapeutic agents is **selective action (selectivity)**. Antiseptics are protoplasmic poisons: they act on microbial and human cells **nonselectively**, so they are used only on surfaces. Chemotherapeutic agents act on targets specific to microbes and cause little harm to the macroorganism — they are used systemically.

blocks.text: Types of antimicrobial action: **bacteriostatic** (stops multiplication) and **bactericidal** (kills). The type of action depends on concentration, the type of microbe and the conditions of the environment.
2.1. Requirements for antiseptics and factors affecting their activity

An ideal antiseptic should be broad-spectrum, fast-acting, not lose its activity in the presence of organic matter (blood, pus), not damage tissue, not be absorbed, not cause allergy, and be inexpensive and stable. No such substance exists — each group has its own advantages and disadvantages.

Factors affecting activity: **concentration** and contact time, temperature, the pH of the environment, **organic matter** (blood, pus and proteins inactivate most antiseptics), the type of microbe (spores, mycobacteria and non-enveloped viruses are the most resistant).
2.2. Classification of antiseptics

blocks.text: 2.3. Features of the main antiseptics

**Ethyl alcohol** — the **70%** concentration is the most effective: 96% alcohol rapidly coagulates the proteins on the cell surface, forms a protective layer and does not penetrate inside; at 70%, the presence of water improves denaturation. It acts on bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses; **it does not act on spores**. It is not used on open wounds (pain, tissue necrosis). Alcohol-based antiseptics with added glycerin do not dry the skin of the hands.

**Iodine preparations.** Alcoholic iodine solution — on the skin and around wounds; irritating, allergenic, and with long-term use — **iodism** (rhinitis, rash, increased salivation) and thyroid dysfunction. **Povidone-iodine** (an iodophor — a complex of iodine with polyvinylpyrrolidone) releases iodine slowly, irritates little, has a broad spectrum (including spores) and is widely used for surgical field antisepsis. It is not applied to large areas in newborns and pregnant women (iodine absorption — hypothyroidism).

**Chlorhexidine** — a potent antiseptic with a long (residual) effect; it “sticks” well to the skin. The **chlorhexidine + alcohol** combination is **the most effective** for antisepsis of the surgical field and the central venous catheter site. Its activity decreases with organic matter and soap. It must not come into contact with the eye, the middle ear or the meninges (it damages them); with prolonged use as a mouthwash it stains the teeth.

**Hydrogen peroxide 3%** — under the action of tissue catalase it releases oxygen, forms **foam** and cleans the wound mechanically; its antiseptic effect is weak and short. It helps stop capillary bleeding. Injecting it into deep closed cavities is dangerous (gas embolism).

**Potassium permanganate** — a strong oxidizing agent; depending on the concentration it is antiseptic (0.01–0.1%), astringent and caustic (2–5%). In some poisonings (alkaloids, phosphorus) a 0.02–0.1% solution is used for gastric lavage; the **crystals** must be completely dissolved — they burn the mucosa.

**Brilliant green 1–2%** — active against gram-positive bacteria (staphylococci); skin wounds, pyoderma, the umbilical wound. **Furacilin 0.02%** (1:5000) — irrigation of wounds and cavities; weak activity, many microorganisms are resistant.

parts.text: Common incorrect practices: 1) applying iodine and brilliant green **into an open wound** — this damages tissue and slows healing (only around the wound); 2) using boric acid in children — it is absorbed through the skin and may cause severe poisoning; 3) pouring alcohol onto an open wound. The most important thing in cleaning minor wounds is **irrigation with plenty of clean water or saline**.

blocks.text: 2.4. Hand disinfection

parts.text: According to the WHO, a large share of hospital-acquired infections is transmitted through the hands of health workers. **The 5 moments for hand hygiene** (WHO): 1) before touching a patient; 2) before an aseptic procedure; 3) after contact with body fluids; 4) after touching a patient; 5) after touching the patient's surroundings. If the hands are not visibly soiled, an **alcohol-based hand rub** (3–5 ml, rubbed for 20–30 seconds) is more effective than washing with soap; if they are visibly soiled, or after working with C. difficile or norovirus — soap and water (alcohol does not act on spores).

blocks.text: 2.5. Laboratory class: studying the mechanism of action of antiseptics
This section corresponds to the 6th-semester class “Laboratory study of the mechanism of action of antiseptic agents”.

**Experiment 1 (protein denaturation):** solutions of ethyl alcohol (70% and 96%), phenol, formaldehyde, silver nitrate and copper sulfate are added to egg white solution in test tubes — **precipitation (coagulation)** of the protein is observed. Conclusion: most antiseptics denature the proteins of the microbial cell.

**Experiment 2 (effect of oxidizing agents):** when hydrogen peroxide is added to blood or a piece of meat, **foam** (oxygen) forms under the action of catalase; potassium permanganate solution becomes colorless on contact with organic matter (manganese(IV) oxide precipitates). Conclusion: the action of oxidizing agents is short and ends quickly in an organic environment.

**Experiment 3 (effect of organic matter and concentration):** antiseptics of different concentrations are applied to a microbial culture (paper disk method) and the zones of growth inhibition are measured; when serum is added, the zones shrink.

parts.text: Laboratory conclusions: the effect of antiseptics depends on **concentration and contact time**; **organic matter** (blood, pus, protein) reduces the activity of most antiseptics — so a wound must first be cleaned mechanically.

parts.text: **Antimicrobial resistance** is a global threat that causes millions of deaths a year. Factors that worsen it: unjustified use of antibiotics in viral infections (ARVI, influenza), over-the-counter sales, wrong dose and duration, antibiotics in animal farming. The WHO **AWaRe** classification divides antibiotics into “Access” (can be widely used), “Watch” (use with caution) and “Reserve” groups.

blocks.text: 3.3. Basic principles of antimicrobial therapy

items: **Establishing the indication** — when a bacterial infection is likely (antibiotics do not act on viral infections).

**Identifying the pathogen** — where possible, take cultures before the antibiotic; first **empirical** therapy (according to the likely pathogens and local resistance), then switching to **targeted** therapy according to the results (de-escalation).
**Penetration of the drug into the site of infection** (urine, CNS, bone, prostate).
**Patient factors**: age, pregnancy, renal and hepatic function, allergy history, interactions.
**Optimal dose, route and duration** — the shortest effective course possible.
**Assessing effectiveness at 48–72 hours**.
Combinations only when indicated (tuberculosis, severe sepsis, H. pylori, prevention of resistance).

blocks.text: 4.1. Sulfonamides and co-trimoxazole

**Mechanism.** Bacteria synthesize folic acid themselves from **PABA** (para-aminobenzoic acid) (humans obtain it from food). Sulfonamides are structurally similar to PABA — they **competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthetase**. **Trimethoprim** inhibits **dihydrofolate reductase** at the next step. Together (**co-trimoxazole**) they produce sequential blockade, synergy and a bactericidal effect.

parts.text: Sources of PABA reduce the effect of sulfonamides: **pus and necrotic tissue** (much PABA) and drugs that form PABA — **procaine (Novocaine), benzocaine (Anesthesin)**. That is why sulfonamides are ineffective when used together with procaine or in a purulent wound.

blocks.text: **Uses of co-trimoxazole:** urinary tract infections (if local resistance is low), **Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia** (treatment and prevention — the drug of choice in HIV infection), nocardiosis, toxoplasmosis, skin infections caused by MRSA, shigellosis. **Sulfasalazine** — ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis (5-aminosalicylic acid is released in the intestine). **Sulfacetamide** eye drops (conjunctivitis), **silver sulfadiazine** — burns.

blocks.title: Table 16.4. Adverse effects of sulfonamides and co-trimoxazole
head: Adverse effect
Comment
rows: Allergic reactions, including Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
Precipitates in acidic urine — drink plenty of fluids
Hematologic: agranulocytosis, megaloblastic anemia (trimethoprim), hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Trimethoprim acts like amiloride (especially with ACE inhibitors)
Displaces bilirubin from albumin — contraindicated in late pregnancy and in infants under 2 months

blocks.text: 4.2. Fluoroquinolones

**Mechanism.** By inhibiting bacterial **DNA gyrase** (topoisomerase II; mainly in gram-negatives) and **topoisomerase IV** (mainly in gram-positives), they stop DNA replication — a **concentration-dependent bactericidal** effect.

blocks.title: Table 16.5. Generations and spectrum of fluoroquinolones
head: Generation
Preparations
Spectrum
Main use
rows: Gram-negatives (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa — ciprofloxacin), partly gram-positives, atypicals
Complicated urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, intestinal infections (salmonellosis, shigellosis), prostatitis, Pseudomonas infections, anthrax
+ pneumococci (including penicillin-resistant ones), atypicals (mycoplasma, chlamydia, legionella); moxifloxacin — anaerobes
Community-acquired pneumonia (alternative), severe sinusitis; drug-resistant tuberculosis (reserve)

parts.text: Because of **serious adverse effects of fluoroquinolones** (FDA and EMA warnings), they are **not recommended as first choice** in uncomplicated cystitis, acute bronchitis and mild sinusitis:

items: **tendinitis and tendon (Achilles) rupture** — especially in people over 60 and together with **glucocorticoids**;
peripheral neuropathy (may be irreversible), CNS disorders (dizziness, insomnia, psychosis, **seizures** — especially with NSAIDs);
**QT prolongation** and arrhythmias;
aortic aneurysm and dissection;
dysglycemia (hypo- and hyperglycemia), photosensitivity, C. difficile colitis;
contraindicated **in children and adolescents** (damage to growing joint cartilage) and **in pregnancy and breastfeeding** (except for special indications).

blocks.text: **Interactions: antacids, calcium, iron, zinc and dairy products** form chelates with fluoroquinolones and sharply reduce their absorption (take 2 hours before or 6 hours after); ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 and increases the concentrations of **theophylline** and caffeine; it enhances the effect of warfarin.
4.3. Nitrofurans

**Nitrofurantoin** reaches therapeutic concentrations **only in urine** (low in blood). The **first-line** drug for **uncomplicated cystitis** (in women) (5 days), prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection. Resistance develops rarely. Ineffective and toxic at GFR < 30–45 ml/min. Adverse effects: nausea, brown urine; with long-term use — **pulmonary reactions** (acute pneumonitis, chronic fibrosis), peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis; hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and in newborns.

**Nifuroxazide** — not absorbed from the intestine, used in bacterial diarrhea (in CIS countries). **Furazolidone** — intestinal infections, giardiasis; inhibits MAO, **disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol**. **Furazidin (Furagin)** — urinary tract.
4.4. Nitroimidazoles

In the cells of anaerobic microorganisms and protozoa, the nitro group of **metronidazole** is **reduced**, forming free radicals that damage DNA (this process does not occur in aerobic cells — the basis of its selective action).

**Spectrum: anaerobic bacteria** (Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridioides difficile, Fusobacterium), **protozoa** (Trichomonas vaginalis, Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica), Gardnerella (bacterial vaginosis), H. pylori.

**Uses:** anaerobic infections (abdominal, pelvic, abscesses — often with other antibiotics), **trichomoniasis** (both partners are treated), bacterial vaginosis, amebiasis, giardiasis, mild C. difficile colitis (vancomycin/fidaxomicin are now preferred), H. pylori eradication, prophylaxis in colorectal surgery.

**Adverse effects: metallic taste in the mouth**, nausea, dark urine, **disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol** (facial flushing, tachycardia, vomiting — no alcohol during treatment and for 48–72 hours afterward), peripheral neuropathy and encephalopathy (with long-term and high-dose use), enhances the effect of warfarin; caution in the 1st trimester of pregnancy.

parts.text: The spectrum of metronidazole — **“GET GAP on the Metro”**: **G**iardia, **E**ntamoeba, **T**richomonas, **G**ardnerella, **A**naerobes, **P** — H. pylori. In short: **“Anaerobes and protozoa — metronidazole”**.

blocks.text: 4.5. Oxazolidinones and others

**Linezolid** — active against gram-positive bacteria, including **MRSA** and **vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE)**; oral bioavailability ≈ 100%. A reserve antibiotic. Adverse effects: **myelosuppression** (thrombocytopenia — with use for more than 2 weeks), peripheral and optic neuropathy, lactic acidosis; inhibits MAO — **serotonin syndrome with SSRIs**, hypertension with tyramine.
**Nitroxoline** (5-NOK) — urinary tract infections; colors the urine bright yellow.
**Fosfomycin trometamol** — **a single dose in uncomplicated cystitis** (3 g), first line; also allowed in pregnant women.

skills.title: Skill 1. Hygienic hand disinfection with an alcohol-based hand rub (according to the WHO, 20–30 seconds)

items: Put 3–5 ml of antiseptic into the palm (an amount that wets the hands completely).
Rub palm to palm.
Right palm over the back of the left hand (including between the fingers), and vice versa.
Rub palm to palm with the fingers interlaced.
Rub the backs of the bent fingers against the opposite palm.
Rub the thumbs with a rotational movement.
Rub the fingertips against the opposite palm with a rotational movement.
Continue until the hands are dry (without wiping).
