cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 26-year-old woman (not pregnant) has complained of frequent painful urination and suprapubic discomfort for 1 day. No fever or back pain. No comorbidities. A friend advised her to take ciprofloxacin.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Optimal treatment? 3) Why is ciprofloxacin not the first choice?
cases.answer: 1) Uncomplicated acute cystitis. 2) Nitrofurantoin 100 mg 2 times a day for 5 days or fosfomycin trometamol 3 g once; plenty of fluids. 3) Fluoroquinolones are not recommended in uncomplicated cystitis because of the risk of serious adverse effects (tendons, nerves, aorta, QT) and their contribution to resistance — they are reserved for pyelonephritis and complicated infections.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 70-year-old man is taking levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia; he also takes prednisolone 30 mg/day for a COPD exacerbation. On day 5, while walking, he felt a “snap” and sharp pain above the heel and cannot push off with his foot.
cases.ask: 1) What complication? 2) Risk factors? 3) Management.
cases.answer: 1) Achilles tendon rupture — a serious adverse effect of fluoroquinolones. 2) Age > 60, concomitant use of glucocorticoids (especially dangerous); renal failure and transplantation are also risk factors. 3) Stop levofloxacin immediately and switch to an antibiotic of another group (beta-lactam + macrolide), immobilize the leg, an orthopedic consultation (conservative or surgical treatment); record the adverse effect in the medical records; avoid fluoroquinolones in the future.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 32-year-old woman has a frothy, yellow-green, malodorous vaginal discharge and itching. Microscopy shows motile trichomonads. She says she drinks a glass of wine with dinner every day.
cases.ask: 1) Treatment plan? 2) What special warning is given to the patient?
cases.answer: 1) Metronidazole (500 mg 2 times a day for 7 days or 2 g once) or tinidazole; the sexual partner is treated at the same time, abstinence from sex until treatment is completed; testing for other sexually transmitted infections. 2) No alcohol during treatment and for at least 48–72 hours after it ends — metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase and causes a disulfiram-like reaction (facial flushing, headache, palpitations, nausea, vomiting); explain that the metallic taste in the mouth and dark urine are harmless.

topics.cards_title: Table 16.8. Antiseptics and synthetic antibacterial agents — summary

topics.title: Antibiotics

goals.text: In 1928 A. Fleming discovered penicillin, in the 1940s it entered clinical practice, and mortality from bacterial infections fell sharply. Today antibiotics are the most prescribed group of drugs, but about half of them are prescribed without justification (mainly for viral infections). This leads to complications such as resistance, allergic reactions and C. difficile colitis. The most important skills for a GP are correctly determining whether an antibiotic is needed, choosing the first-line drug for common infections, and knowing the restrictions related to allergy and special groups (children, pregnant women, the elderly).
The student should know:

items: the classification of antibiotics (by chemical structure, mechanism, spectrum and type of action);
beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams) and beta-lactamase inhibitors;
glycopeptides, aminoglycosides, macrolides, tetracyclines, lincosamides, amphenicols, polymyxins and other antibiotics;
the main adverse effects of antibiotics and their prevention;
the principles of choosing antibiotics for common infections.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as benzylpenicillin, benzathine benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, amoxicillin/clavulanate, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, azithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, gentamicin, vancomycin and clindamycin;
choose an antibiotic in a patient with a history of penicillin allergy;
draw up an empirical treatment plan for acute tonsillitis, otitis and community-acquired pneumonia.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Drugs acting on **30S** — “**AT 30**” — **A**minoglycosides, **T**etracyclines. Drugs acting on **50S** — “**CELL at 50**” — **C**hloramphenicol, **E**rythromycin (macrolides), **L**incosamides (clindamycin), **L**inezolid.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Giving bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics together (for example, penicillin + tetracycline) is usually inappropriate: beta-lactams act only on the cell wall of **growing** bacteria, while bacteriostatic drugs stop growth — antagonism is possible. Exception: special combinations (for example, penicillin + clindamycin in severe streptococcal infections — to stop toxin synthesis).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Aminopenicillins and infectious mononucleosis**: when ampicillin or amoxicillin is given to patients with Epstein–Barr virus infection (often misdiagnosed as “tonsillitis”), a **maculopapular rash** appears in 70–100% of cases; this is not a true allergy, but it is the reason to exclude mononucleosis when treating “tonsillitis” in a young patient.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: With each generation: **gram-negative activity increases**, **gram-positive activity** (up to the 3rd generation) **decreases**, and resistance to beta-lactamases and penetration of the BBB increase. Cephalosporins do not act on **“LAME”**: **L**isteria, **A**typicals (mycoplasma, chlamydia), **M**RSA (except the 5th generation), **E**nterococci.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Ceftriaxone**: 1) in newborns (especially premature infants) it is not given intravenously together with **calcium-containing solutions** — ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates in the lungs and kidneys; 2) in newborns it displaces bilirubin from albumin (contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemia); 3) it may cause **pseudolithiasis** (sludge) in the gallbladder. **Cefoperazone** — a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol and hypoprothrombinemia.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The tradition of **intradermal penicillin testing** (before every injection in CIS countries) does not reliably predict allergy in patients without a history and may itself cause sensitization. Whenever any antibiotic is given for the first time, an **anaphylaxis kit** (epinephrine) must be ready and the patient must be observed for 30 minutes.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Adverse effects of aminoglycosides — “NOTN”**: **N**ephrotoxicity (proximal tubules, usually reversible), **O**totoxicity (cochlear — irreversible hearing loss; vestibular — dizziness, ataxia; even one dose in people with a mitochondrial DNA mutation), **T**eratogenicity (damage to the fetal auditory nerve — contraindicated in pregnancy), **N**euromuscular blockade (enhances the effect of muscle relaxants, dangerous in myasthenia; treatment — calcium preparations). **Once-daily dosing** (the same total dose) reduces toxicity while preserving effectiveness; monitoring of renal function and blood concentration; the course is as short as possible (5–7 days); caution together with furosemide, vancomycin and other nephrotoxic drugs.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Erythromycin and clarithromycin are strong CYP3A4 inhibitors** (azithromycin — very weak): they increase the concentrations of **statins** (simvastatin, atorvastatin — rhabdomyolysis), **warfarin**, carbamazepine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, colchicine, calcium antagonists, ergot alkaloids, some antiarrhythmics and DOACs. When there is a risk of interaction, **azithromycin** is preferred.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Tetracyclines are contraindicated in children under 8, pregnant women and breastfeeding women**: they bind calcium and accumulate in growing **bones and teeth** — **yellow-brown discoloration of tooth enamel**, enamel hypoplasia, slowed bone growth. Other adverse effects: **photosensitivity** (sun rash — doxycycline), esophageal ulcer (take the capsule with plenty of water, upright), gastrointestinal disturbances, candidiasis and superinfections, hepatotoxicity (in pregnant women), raised intracranial pressure; expired tetracycline — Fanconi syndrome. Absorption is reduced by chelation with **calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron and milk**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: According to modern data, **a short course of doxycycline** (≤ 21 days) hardly causes tooth discoloration in children under 8; therefore in life-threatening **rickettsioses** (for example, Rocky Mountain spotted fever) doxycycline is the drug of choice at any age.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Dangerous adverse effects of chloramphenicol (levomycetin): 1) **aplastic anemia** — dose-independent, idiosyncratic, often irreversible and fatal (one in 40,000 cases), described even after eye drops; 2) dose-dependent **reversible myelosuppression**; 3) **“gray baby syndrome”** in newborns — accumulation due to immature hepatic glucuronidation, with gray-bluish skin color, hypothermia, vomiting, abdominal distension and collapse. In CIS countries chloramphenicol tablets were widely used for diarrhea — this **is not recommended**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Antibiotics contraindicated in children: **tetracyclines** (under 8; a short course of doxycycline is an exception), **fluoroquinolones** (under 18, except for special indications — cartilage), **chloramphenicol** (newborns — gray baby syndrome), **ceftriaxone** (in newborns with hyperbilirubinemia and with calcium-containing solutions), **co-trimoxazole** and sulfonamides (under 2 months — kernicterus).

blocks.text: **Antibiotics** are substances produced by microorganisms (fungi, actinomycetes, bacteria), or their semisynthetic and synthetic analogs, that selectively inhibit the growth of other microorganisms or kill them.

blocks.title: Table 17.1. Classification of antibiotics by mechanism of action
head: Mechanism
Groups
Type of action
rows: Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams), glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin), fosfomycin
Macrolides, lincosamides, amphenicols (chloramphenicol), oxazolidinones, fusidic acid

parts.text: Drugs acting on **30S** — “**AT 30**” — **A**minoglycosides, **T**etracyclines. Drugs acting on **50S** — “**CELL at 50**” — **C**hloramphenicol, **E**rythromycin (macrolides), **L**incosamides (clindamycin), **L**inezolid.

Giving bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics together (for example, penicillin + tetracycline) is usually inappropriate: beta-lactams act only on the cell wall of **growing** bacteria, while bacteriostatic drugs stop growth — antagonism is possible. Exception: special combinations (for example, penicillin + clindamycin in severe streptococcal infections — to stop toxin synthesis).

blocks.text: **Pharmacodynamic characteristics: time-dependent** antibiotics (beta-lactams, vancomycin, macrolides) — effectiveness depends on the time the concentration stays above the MIC: frequent dosing or prolonged infusion; **concentration-dependent** antibiotics (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) — a high peak concentration is important: a large dose once a day; they have a **postantibiotic effect**.
2.1. General mechanism

Beta-lactams have a **beta-lactam ring** in their molecule. They bind to bacterial **penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)** — the **transpeptidases** that form the cross-links of peptidoglycan — and block the last step of cell wall synthesis. As a result, the growing bacterium cannot withstand the osmotic pressure and undergoes **lysis** (bactericidal). Human cells have no cell wall — that is why beta-lactams are **very little toxic**.
**Resistance: beta-lactamases** (break the beta-lactam ring), altered PBPs (**MRSA** — PBP2a; penicillin-resistant pneumococci), reduced porins and efflux in gram-negatives.
2.2. Penicillins

parts.text: **Amoxicillin is well absorbed orally** (≈ 90%, independent of food), while ampicillin is poorly absorbed (≈ 40%) — amoxicillin is preferred for oral use. **Benzathine benzylpenicillin** (Bicillin), given once intramuscularly, maintains a low concentration for 2–4 weeks — ideal for treating syphilis and preventing recurrences of rheumatic fever.

**Aminopenicillins and infectious mononucleosis**: when ampicillin or amoxicillin is given to patients with Epstein–Barr virus infection (often misdiagnosed as “tonsillitis”), a **maculopapular rash** appears in 70–100% of cases; this is not a true allergy, but it is the reason to exclude mononucleosis when treating “tonsillitis” in a young patient.

blocks.text: 2.3. Cephalosporins

Cephalosporins are derived from **cephalosporin C** (7-aminocephalosporanic acid); they are more resistant to beta-lactamases than penicillins. No cephalosporin acts on **enterococci or listeria**; only the 5th generation (ceftaroline) acts **on MRSA**.

parts.text: With each generation: **gram-negative activity increases**, **gram-positive activity** (up to the 3rd generation) **decreases**, and resistance to beta-lactamases and penetration of the BBB increase. Cephalosporins do not act on **“LAME”**: **L**isteria, **A**typicals (mycoplasma, chlamydia), **M**RSA (except the 5th generation), **E**nterococci.

**Ceftriaxone**: 1) in newborns (especially premature infants) it is not given intravenously together with **calcium-containing solutions** — ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates in the lungs and kidneys; 2) in newborns it displaces bilirubin from albumin (contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemia); 3) it may cause **pseudolithiasis** (sludge) in the gallbladder. **Cefoperazone** — a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol and hypoprothrombinemia.

blocks.text: 2.4. Carbapenems and monobactams

**Carbapenems** (meropenem, imipenem/cilastatin, ertapenem, doripenem) are **the broadest-spectrum** beta-lactams: gram-positives, gram-negatives (including **ESBL-producing** enterobacteria), anaerobes; meropenem and imipenem — Pseudomonas (not ertapenem). They do not act on MRSA, Stenotrophomonas or atypicals. **Reserve antibiotics** — severe hospital infections, sepsis, ESBL infections. **Imipenem** is broken down in the kidney by dehydropeptidase — it is given together with **cilastatin**; risk of seizures (especially with imipenem). Carbapenems sharply reduce valproate concentrations.

**Monobactams** — **aztreonam**: only against gram-negatives (including Pseudomonas); **almost no cross-allergy with penicillins** (except for the side chain it shares with ceftazidime) — an alternative for gram-negative infections in severe penicillin allergy.
2.5. Adverse effects of beta-lactams and allergy

blocks.title: Table 17.4. Adverse effects of beta-lactams
head: Adverse effect
Comment
rows: Urticaria, rash, angioedema, anaphylactic shock (0.01–0.05%), Stevens–Johnson syndrome, interstitial nephritis, hemolytic anemia, serum sickness
Very high doses (benzylpenicillin, imipenem), renal failure; intrathecal administration is prohibited
In the first hours of treating syphilis (and other spirochetoses) — fever, chills, worsening of the rash (mass death of spirochetes)
Benzylpenicillin potassium salt at large doses — hyperkalemia

parts.text: **“Penicillin allergy”** — about 10% of patients report it, but **more than 90%** of them are not actually allergic (often a viral rash in childhood or an adverse effect). A wrong label “condemns” the patient to less effective and more expensive antibiotics. The history must be clarified in detail: the type of reaction (urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis — true IgE-mediated; a mild rash — probably not) and its timing. In true severe allergy penicillins are contraindicated; **cross-reactivity with cephalosporins** depends mainly on **similar side chains** and is **less than 2%** (even less with the 2nd–3rd generations); in non-anaphylactic allergy, 3rd-generation cephalosporins are usually safe. Skin tests and a supervised drug challenge with an allergist make it possible to remove the “allergy” label.

The tradition of **intradermal penicillin testing** (before every injection in CIS countries) does not reliably predict allergy in patients without a history and may itself cause sensitization. Whenever any antibiotic is given for the first time, an **anaphylaxis kit** (epinephrine) must be ready and the patient must be observed for 30 minutes.

blocks.text: **Vancomycin** (and teicoplanin) binds to the D-alanyl-D-alanine part of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell wall synthesis. Only against **gram-positive** bacteria (it does not cross the outer membrane of gram-negatives): **MRSA**, coagulase-negative staphylococci, enterococci, **C. difficile**, penicillin-resistant pneumococci.

items: Intravenously — MRSA infections (bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia, osteomyelitis), penicillin-resistant pneumococcal meningitis (with ceftriaxone).
**Orally** (not absorbed) — **C. difficile colitis** (severe and recurrent).

The dose is monitored by the minimum (**trough**) blood concentration or the AUC. **Adverse effects: “red man syndrome”** (histamine release with rapid infusion — flushing of the face, neck and chest, itching, hypotension; prevention — infusion over at least 60 minutes), **nephrotoxicity** (especially with aminoglycosides and piperacillin/tazobactam), ototoxicity, phlebitis.

blocks.title: Table 17.5. Generations of aminoglycosides
head: Generation
Preparations
Property
rows: Streptomycin — tuberculosis (reserve), plague, tularemia; neomycin — only topical and intestinal (very toxic)

blocks.text: **Mechanism.** They bind irreversibly to the **30S** ribosomal subunit and cause misreading of mRNA and synthesis of nonfunctional proteins — **bactericidal**, concentration-dependent, with a strong postantibiotic effect. Their entry into the bacterium is **oxygen-dependent** — **they do not act on anaerobes**; their activity decreases in an acidic environment (abscess).
**Pharmacokinetics:** not absorbed from the intestine (parenteral or topical); cross the BBB poorly; excreted almost unchanged by the **kidneys**.

**Uses:** severe gram-negative infections (sepsis, pyelonephritis, hospital-acquired pneumonia) — usually in combination with a beta-lactam; **enterococcal and streptococcal endocarditis** (synergy — the beta-lactam damages the cell wall and makes it easier for the aminoglycoside to enter); plague, tularemia; tuberculosis (amikacin); topical — eye drops (tobramycin), skin ointments.

parts.text: **Adverse effects of aminoglycosides — “NOTN”**: **N**ephrotoxicity (proximal tubules, usually reversible), **O**totoxicity (cochlear — irreversible hearing loss; vestibular — dizziness, ataxia; even one dose in people with a mitochondrial DNA mutation), **T**eratogenicity (damage to the fetal auditory nerve — contraindicated in pregnancy), **N**euromuscular blockade (enhances the effect of muscle relaxants, dangerous in myasthenia; treatment — calcium preparations). **Once-daily dosing** (the same total dose) reduces toxicity while preserving effectiveness; monitoring of renal function and blood concentration; the course is as short as possible (5–7 days); caution together with furosemide, vancomycin and other nephrotoxic drugs.

blocks.text: **Preparations:** 14-membered — **erythromycin**, **clarithromycin**, roxithromycin; 15-membered (azalides) — **azithromycin**; 16-membered — josamycin, spiramycin, midecamycin.
**Mechanism. Binding to the 50S** subunit blocks translocation of the peptide chain — bacteriostatic (bactericidal at high concentrations).

**Spectrum:** gram-positive cocci (streptococci, pneumococci — resistance is growing), **atypical bacteria** (**Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, Legionella**), Bordetella pertussis, Campylobacter, H. pylori (clarithromycin), H. influenzae (azithromycin, clarithromycin), toxoplasma (spiramycin), mycobacteria (MAC — clarithromycin, azithromycin).

**Uses: community-acquired pneumonia** (atypical pathogens; in severe forms in combination with a beta-lactam), streptococcal tonsillitis and other infections **in penicillin allergy**, **whooping cough**, chlamydial infections (azithromycin 1 g once), H. pylori eradication (clarithromycin), campylobacteriosis, **trachoma**, travelers' diarrhea; azithromycin — long-term low-dose prevention of exacerbations in COPD and bronchiectasis (anti-inflammatory effect).
**Pharmacokinetics:** azithromycin reaches very high concentrations in tissues and inside cells, t½ — 68 hours; **short courses** (3–5 days).

**Adverse effects:** gastrointestinal disturbances (erythromycin is a **motilin agonist**, strongly so; it is also used as a prokinetic), **QT prolongation** and arrhythmias (especially with other QT-prolonging drugs), cholestatic hepatitis, ototoxicity (at high doses); in newborns, erythromycin and azithromycin — **pyloric stenosis**.

parts.text: **Erythromycin and clarithromycin are strong CYP3A4 inhibitors** (azithromycin — very weak): they increase the concentrations of **statins** (simvastatin, atorvastatin — rhabdomyolysis), **warfarin**, carbamazepine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, colchicine, calcium antagonists, ergot alkaloids, some antiarrhythmics and DOACs. When there is a risk of interaction, **azithromycin** is preferred.

blocks.text: **Preparations:** tetracycline, **doxycycline** (preferred — well absorbed, 1–2 times a day, no dose change in renal failure), **minocycline**; glycylcyclines — **tigecycline** (reserve, multidrug-resistant bacteria), omadacycline, eravacycline.
**Mechanism. Reversible binding to the 30S** subunit stops the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosome — bacteriostatic.

**Spectrum:** broad — gram-positives and gram-negatives, **intracellular and atypical pathogens**: rickettsiae (**drugs of choice**), chlamydiae, mycoplasmas, **borreliae (Lyme disease)**, brucellae (with streptomycin or rifampicin), Vibrio cholerae, anthrax, plague, tularemia, leptospirae, some protozoa (malaria prophylaxis — doxycycline), MRSA (doxycycline, minocycline), Propionibacterium acnes.

**Uses:** rickettsioses (epidemic typhus, Q fever), Lyme disease, brucellosis, chlamydial infections, atypical pneumonia, acne and rosacea, cholera, malaria prophylaxis, H. pylori (in a quadruple regimen).

parts.text: **Tetracyclines are contraindicated in children under 8, pregnant women and breastfeeding women**: they bind calcium and accumulate in growing **bones and teeth** — **yellow-brown discoloration of tooth enamel**, enamel hypoplasia, slowed bone growth. Other adverse effects: **photosensitivity** (sun rash — doxycycline), esophageal ulcer (take the capsule with plenty of water, upright), gastrointestinal disturbances, candidiasis and superinfections, hepatotoxicity (in pregnant women), raised intracranial pressure; expired tetracycline — Fanconi syndrome. Absorption is reduced by chelation with **calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron and milk**.

According to modern data, **a short course of doxycycline** (≤ 21 days) hardly causes tooth discoloration in children under 8; therefore in life-threatening **rickettsioses** (for example, Rocky Mountain spotted fever) doxycycline is the drug of choice at any age.

blocks.text: 7.1. Lincosamides

**Clindamycin** (and lincomycin) — act on the **50S** subunit; bacteriostatic. **Gram-positive cocci** (staphylococci, including some MRSA, streptococci) and **anaerobes** (Bacteroides, clostridia — except C. difficile). It penetrates bone tissue well and inhibits toxin synthesis.

**Uses:** skin and soft tissue infections, **osteomyelitis**, lung abscess and aspiration pneumonia, pelvic and abdominal anaerobic infections, odontogenic infections, **toxic shock syndrome** and necrotizing fasciitis (with penicillin — to stop toxin synthesis), streptococcal infections **in penicillin allergy**, acne (topical), bacterial vaginosis (vaginal cream), toxoplasmosis and pneumocystosis (with other drugs).
**Adverse effects: C. difficile colitis** (pseudomembranous colitis) — one of the antibiotics with the highest risk; diarrhea, rash.
7.2. Amphenicols

**Chloramphenicol (levomycetin)** — acts on the **50S** subunit; broad-spectrum, bacteriostatic; crosses the BBB well. Because of severe adverse effects it is now a **reserve** drug (bacterial meningitis — in severe penicillin allergy, enteric fever, rickettsioses — when there is no other option); topically — eye drops, ointments (Levomekol).

parts.text: Dangerous adverse effects of chloramphenicol (levomycetin): 1) **aplastic anemia** — dose-independent, idiosyncratic, often irreversible and fatal (one in 40,000 cases), described even after eye drops; 2) dose-dependent **reversible myelosuppression**; 3) **“gray baby syndrome”** in newborns — accumulation due to immature hepatic glucuronidation, with gray-bluish skin color, hypothermia, vomiting, abdominal distension and collapse. In CIS countries chloramphenicol tablets were widely used for diarrhea — this **is not recommended**.

blocks.text: 7.3. Polymyxins and others

items: **Polymyxin B** and **colistin (polymyxin E)** bind to the lipopolysaccharides and phospholipids of the gram-negative bacterial membrane and damage the membrane like a detergent — bactericidal. **The last reserve** in infections with gram-negative bacteria resistant to many drugs, including **carbapenems** (Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella). Nephrotoxic and neurotoxic. Topically — eye and ear drops.
**Daptomycin** — against gram-positives (MRSA, VRE); membrane depolarization; inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — **ineffective in pneumonia**; myopathy (CK monitoring).
**Fusidic acid** — staphylococci; a topical cream for skin infections.
**Mupirocin** — topical (nasal ointment) — eradication of staphylococcal carriage (including MRSA), impetigo.
**Rifamycins** (rifampicin, rifabutin, rifaximin) — in Topic 18; rifaximin is not absorbed from the intestine (travelers' diarrhea, hepatic encephalopathy).

blocks.text: 8.3. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea and C. difficile

Almost any antibiotic (especially **clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, amoxicillin/clavulanate**) can disrupt the intestinal flora and lead to overgrowth and toxin production by **Clostridioides difficile** — from watery diarrhea to **pseudomembranous colitis** and toxic megacolon. Treatment: stop the causative antibiotic; **oral vancomycin** or **fidaxomicin** (metronidazole only in mild cases when nothing else is available); in recurrent cases — fecal microbiota transplantation. Loperamide and other antiperistaltic agents are contraindicated. Prevention — no unjustified antibiotics, hand hygiene (with soap; alcohol does not act on spores).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 22-year-old student presents with fever (38.8 °C) for 2 days, severe sore throat and difficulty swallowing. No cough. The tonsils are enlarged with purulent exudate, and the anterior cervical lymph nodes are enlarged and tender. The rapid strep test is positive. At age 10 she had a “rash” after amoxicillin (no urticaria or swelling).
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Is an antibiotic needed, and which one? 3) How do you assess the “allergy” history?
cases.answer: 1) Acute streptococcal (group A) tonsillitis (Centor score 4, positive test). 2) Yes — to prevent complications (rheumatic fever, peritonsillar abscess) and to shorten the duration of symptoms. A mild childhood rash (without urticaria or anaphylaxis) is low-risk — probably a viral rash; it can be clarified with an allergist. Cephalexin (a 1st-generation cephalosporin) with caution, or phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days after allergy has been excluded; if the patient or doctor is worried — azithromycin for 5 days or clindamycin. 3) A detailed history: the type of reaction, its timing, its treatment; for low-risk rashes, allergy testing (a drug challenge) to remove the “allergy” label.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 65-year-old patient received clarithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia. He takes simvastatin 40 mg, amlodipine and warfarin. After 5 days he developed severe muscle pain and weakness, dark urine and nosebleeds. CK is markedly raised, INR 5.8.
cases.ask: 1) The cause of these conditions? 2) Management, and which antibiotic would have been preferable?
cases.answer: 1) Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor: the simvastatin concentration rose and rhabdomyolysis developed (muscle pain, myoglobinuria, raised CK); warfarin metabolism slowed and the INR rose — bleeding. The amlodipine concentration may also rise. 2) Stop clarithromycin and simvastatin, stop warfarin temporarily and give vitamin K (INR 4.5–10 with minor bleeding); in rhabdomyolysis — plenty of intravenous fluids, monitoring of creatinine and potassium. Replace the antibiotic with amoxicillin (± azithromycin — it hardly affects CYP3A4). Whenever an antibiotic is prescribed, interactions with the patient's other drugs must be checked.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 70-year-old woman received ceftriaxone and levofloxacin in hospital for pneumonia. On day 8 of treatment she developed watery diarrhea 8–10 times a day, abdominal pain, fever of 38.5 °C and leukocytosis of 18 × 10^9^/l. Stool C. difficile toxin is positive.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Treatment? 3) What must not be done?
cases.answer: 1) Clostridioides difficile infection (antibiotic-associated colitis), severe form (white cells > 15 × 10^9^/l is a severity criterion; creatinine is also monitored). 2) Stop other antibiotics where possible; oral vancomycin 125 mg 4 times a day for 10 days or fidaxomicin; fluid and electrolyte replacement; contact isolation, handwashing with soap (alcohol does not act on spores); stop the PPI if it is not needed. 3) Loperamide and other antiperistaltic agents — risk of toxic megacolon; intravenous vancomycin (it does not reach the intestine).

topics.title: Antituberculosis drugs. Antiviral drugs

goals.text: **Tuberculosis** ranks among the leading causes of death from infectious diseases; **drug-resistant tuberculosis** is a serious problem in Uzbekistan and the Central Asian region. Treating tuberculosis requires a long-term combination of several drugs and strict adherence by the patient. **Antiviral drugs** have changed radically in recent decades: HIV infection has become a chronic, manageable disease, and hepatitis C is cured completely with 8–12 weeks of tablets. At the same time, many “immunomodulators” and “antivirals” are widely sold without proven effectiveness — a GP must be able to tell evidence-based treatment apart.
The student should know:

items: the classification of antituberculosis drugs, and the mechanism, adverse effects and interactions of the main (first-line) drugs;
the principles of treating tuberculosis, standard regimens and approaches to treating drug-resistant tuberculosis;
the stages of viral replication and the targets of antiviral drugs;
drugs against influenza, herpes, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B and C, HIV and COVID-19;
the place of interferons and interferon inducers.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: write prescriptions for drugs such as isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, acyclovir, valacyclovir and oseltamivir;
recognize and manage the adverse effects of antituberculosis drugs;
determine the indications for antiviral treatment in influenza and herpes infections.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The basic principles of tuberculosis treatment**: 1. **Combination therapy** — at least 3–4 drugs: with monotherapy, **resistance** develops quickly. 2. **Long-term treatment** — to eliminate persistent forms (in drug-susceptible tuberculosis — at least 4–6 months). 3. **Two phases**: **intensive** (2 months — rapid reduction of the number of mycobacteria) and **continuation** (4 months — elimination of the rest). 4. **Directly observed therapy (DOT)** — a health worker watches every dose being taken (or video observation). 5. **Drug susceptibility testing** before treatment (rapid molecular tests — Xpert MTB/RIF detects rifampicin resistance in 2 hours).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Older textbooks divided antituberculosis drugs into “first-line” and “second-line (reserve)”, and streptomycin and kanamycin were widely used. Current WHO recommendations do not recommend injectable drugs (kanamycin, capreomycin) for drug-resistant tuberculosis because of **ototoxicity** and low effectiveness; **oral regimens** (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) are used instead.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The first-line drugs — **“RIPE”**: **R**ifampicin, **I**soniazid, **P**yrazinamide, **E**thambutol. Their adverse effects: **R** — **R**ed urine and **R**aised (induced) enzymes; **I** — **I**nflamed nerves (neuropathy) and liver; **P** — **P**odagra (gout) and liver; **E** — **E**yes. Three drugs (H, R, Z) are hepatotoxic, while ethambutol is harmless to the liver.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Rifampicin has very many interactions**: it sharply **reduces** the concentrations of **oral contraceptives** (unexpected pregnancy — nonhormonal contraception is needed), warfarin, DOACs, glucocorticoids, sulfonylureas, antiretroviral drugs (protease inhibitors, most integrase inhibitors), azole antifungals, methadone, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, digoxin, beta-blockers and calcium antagonists. In tuberculosis with HIV, **rifabutin** (a weak inducer) is sometimes used instead of rifampicin.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Stopping treatment on one's own or taking drugs incorrectly is the main cause of **drug-resistant tuberculosis**. A patient infected with a resistant strain transmits it to others. That is why explaining to the patient the need for the full course of treatment and ensuring DOT are of crucial importance.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The effectiveness of **umifenovir (Arbidol), Ingavirin, Kagocel, oxolinic ointment, tilorone** and similar “antiviral” and “immunomodulatory” preparations widely sold in CIS countries **has not been proven in quality randomized trials** for influenza and ARVI; they are not included in WHO or international clinical recommendations. For most ARVIs (rhinovirus, adenovirus) there is no specific antiviral treatment — symptomatic treatment is enough.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The main adverse effect of acyclovir** is **crystalluria and acute kidney injury** with large intravenous doses (prevention — adequate hydration, slow infusion, dosing according to renal function); rarely neurotoxicity (in the elderly and in renal failure). Herpesviruses **are never completely eliminated** from the body — the drugs only stop replication and do not act on latent infection.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Hepatitis C used to be treated with pegylated interferon and ribavirin for 24–48 weeks — low effectiveness and severe adverse effects (flu-like syndrome, depression, cytopenias, hemolytic anemia). Now **interferon-free DAA regimens** are the standard; the WHO aims to eliminate hepatitis C by 2030.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Principles of antiretroviral therapy (ART)**: ART is started **as soon as possible in every patient diagnosed with HIV, regardless of the CD4 count**. The standard first-line regimen (WHO) is **tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine) + dolutegravir** (TLD, in a single tablet, once a day). The goal is to suppress the viral load to an undetectable level: **“Undetectable = Untransmittable”** (U = U). ART is taken for life; adherence prevents resistance.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Intranasal and rectal interferon preparations** and **interferon inducers** (tilorone, Kagocel, Cycloferon) are widely used in CIS countries to treat and prevent ARVI and influenza, but their effectiveness has not been confirmed in studies that meet the standards of modern evidence-based medicine.

blocks.text: 1.1. Features of mycobacteria and principles of treatment

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slowly multiplying bacterium (division time 18–24 hours) whose cell wall is rich in **mycolic acids** (acid-fast, impermeable to many drugs) and which can live inside macrophages. The disease focus contains different populations: rapidly multiplying (in cavities), slowly multiplying (in an acidic environment, inside macrophages) and “dormant” (persistent) forms.

parts.text: **The basic principles of tuberculosis treatment**: 1. **Combination therapy** — at least 3–4 drugs: with monotherapy, **resistance** develops quickly. 2. **Long-term treatment** — to eliminate persistent forms (in drug-susceptible tuberculosis — at least 4–6 months). 3. **Two phases**: **intensive** (2 months — rapid reduction of the number of mycobacteria) and **continuation** (4 months — elimination of the rest). 4. **Directly observed therapy (DOT)** — a health worker watches every dose being taken (or video observation). 5. **Drug susceptibility testing** before treatment (rapid molecular tests — Xpert MTB/RIF detects rifampicin resistance in 2 hours).

blocks.text: 1.4. Drugs for treating drug-resistant tuberculosis

items: **Bedaquiline** inhibits mycobacterial **ATP synthase** (a new mechanism); bactericidal. Adverse effects: **QT prolongation**, hepatotoxicity.
**Pretomanid** and **delamanid** — nitroimidazooxazines; they disrupt mycolic acid synthesis and cellular respiration. QT prolongation, neuropathy.
**Linezolid** — 50S ribosome (Topic 16); **myelosuppression**, peripheral and **optic neuropathy** (with long-term use).
**Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin** — DNA gyrase (Topic 16).
**Clofazimine** — red-brown skin pigmentation, QT prolongation.
**Cycloserine** — cell wall synthesis; **neuropsychiatric** adverse effects (depression, psychosis, seizures) — given with pyridoxine.

parts.text: **Hepatotoxicity of antituberculosis drugs** is the most common reason for stopping treatment. Liver enzymes are measured before treatment; in risk groups (alcoholism, hepatitis B and C, HIV, old age, pregnancy) they are monitored regularly. If symptoms appear (nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain) or transaminases rise more than 3-fold with symptoms (more than 5-fold without symptoms), **all hepatotoxic drugs are stopped**, and once the enzymes normalize they are restarted one by one.

Stopping treatment on one's own or taking drugs incorrectly is the main cause of **drug-resistant tuberculosis**. A patient infected with a resistant strain transmits it to others. That is why explaining to the patient the need for the full course of treatment and ensuring DOT are of crucial importance.

blocks.text: 2.1. Stages of viral replication and drug targets

Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites — they use the mechanisms of the host cell. That is why it is difficult to create drugs that act selectively on viruses; drugs target **virus-specific enzymes and processes**.

blocks.text: 2.2. Anti-influenza drugs

items: **Neuraminidase inhibitors** — **oseltamivir** (oral), zanamivir (inhaled): by inhibiting neuraminidase they stop the release of new virions from the infected cell and their spread. They act on influenza A and B. Effective when started **within 48 hours** of symptom onset — they shorten the illness by ≈ 1 day and reduce complications and hospitalizations **in risk groups** (the elderly, pregnant women, children under 2, chronic diseases, immunosuppression); in severe and hospitalized patients at any time. Prophylaxis — after contact. Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting; rarely neuropsychiatric disorders in children. Zanamivir — bronchospasm in asthma and COPD.
**Baloxavir marboxil** inhibits the cap-dependent endonuclease of the viral polymerase; a single dose.
**Amantadine, rimantadine** — influenza A only; almost all modern strains are **resistant** — not recommended (amantadine is used in Parkinson's disease).

parts.text: The most effective prevention of influenza is **annual vaccination**, especially for risk groups and health workers. Antiviral drugs do not replace vaccination.

The effectiveness of **umifenovir (Arbidol), Ingavirin, Kagocel, oxolinic ointment, tilorone** and similar “antiviral” and “immunomodulatory” preparations widely sold in CIS countries **has not been proven in quality randomized trials** for influenza and ARVI; they are not included in WHO or international clinical recommendations. For most ARVIs (rhinovirus, adenovirus) there is no specific antiviral treatment — symptomatic treatment is enough.

blocks.text: 2.3. Drugs against herpesviruses

**Acyclovir** is a guanosine analog and a **prodrug**: viral **thymidine kinase** (only in the infected cell) converts it into the monophosphate, and then cellular kinases phosphorylate it to the triphosphate. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits the viral **DNA polymerase** and, by being incorporated into the DNA chain, stops its elongation. It has almost no effect on uninfected cells — **high selectivity**, low toxicity.

parts.text: **The main adverse effect of acyclovir** is **crystalluria and acute kidney injury** with large intravenous doses (prevention — adequate hydration, slow infusion, dosing according to renal function); rarely neurotoxicity (in the elderly and in renal failure). Herpesviruses **are never completely eliminated** from the body — the drugs only stop replication and do not act on latent infection.

blocks.text: 2.4. Drugs against viral hepatitis

items: **Hepatitis B** (chronic): **tenofovir** (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or alafenamide) and **entecavir** — nucleoside/nucleotide analogs; highly effective, with very little resistance; usually taken **long term** (often for life); they suppress the virus and reduce the risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Tenofovir is also used **in pregnancy** (to prevent mother-to-child transmission). Pegylated interferon alfa — a finite course in selected patients. Abrupt withdrawal — a severe flare of hepatitis.

**Hepatitis C**: **direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)** — **sofosbuvir** (an NS5B polymerase inhibitor) + **velpatasvir** or daclatasvir (NS5A inhibitors), glecaprevir/pibrentasvir; an **8–12-week** course eliminates the virus (cure) in **more than 95%** of patients. Pangenotypic regimens do not require genotyping. Screening for hepatitis B before treatment is mandatory (risk of HBV reactivation); sofosbuvir with amiodarone — severe bradycardia.

parts.text: Hepatitis C used to be treated with pegylated interferon and ribavirin for 24–48 weeks — low effectiveness and severe adverse effects (flu-like syndrome, depression, cytopenias, hemolytic anemia). Now **interferon-free DAA regimens** are the standard; the WHO aims to eliminate hepatitis C by 2030.

blocks.text: 2.5. Drugs against HIV infection (antiretroviral therapy)
HIV is a retrovirus; its RNA is converted into DNA by **reverse transcriptase** and integrated into the host genome by **integrase**; new viral proteins mature with the help of **protease**.

Efavirenz — CNS (strange dreams, depression); nevirapine — hepatotoxicity, rash

parts.text: **Principles of antiretroviral therapy (ART)**: ART is started **as soon as possible in every patient diagnosed with HIV, regardless of the CD4 count**. The standard first-line regimen (WHO) is **tenofovir + lamivudine (or emtricitabine) + dolutegravir** (TLD, in a single tablet, once a day). The goal is to suppress the viral load to an undetectable level: **“Undetectable = Untransmittable”** (U = U). ART is taken for life; adherence prevents resistance.

blocks.text: **Prevention: post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)** — a 28-day course of ART **within 72 hours** (ideally within 2 hours) after a risky contact (including a needlestick injury in a health worker); **pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)** — tenofovir/emtricitabine in high-risk groups; prevention of mother-to-child transmission — ART in pregnancy.
2.6. Drugs against COVID-19

items: **Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir** — an inhibitor of the main protease (Mpro) of SARS-CoV-2; ritonavir slows its metabolism. In patients **at high risk** of severe disease, **within 5 days** of symptom onset. **Ritonavir is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor**: dangerous interactions with statins, antiarrhythmics, DOACs and some anticonvulsants.
**Remdesivir** — an RNA polymerase inhibitor; intravenous; in hospitalized patients and in high-risk outpatients.
**Molnupiravir** — introduces mutations into the viral RNA; when there are no other options; contraindicated in pregnancy.
Anti-inflammatory treatment in severe COVID-19 — **dexamethasone** (reduces mortality in patients requiring oxygen), tocilizumab, baricitinib; anticoagulants (thrombosis prevention).

blocks.text: 2.7. Interferons

**Interferons** are proteins produced by cells in response to a virus; they induce an antiviral state in cells (enzymes that break down viral RNA, inhibition of protein synthesis) and enhance the immune response.

items: **Interferon alfa** (pegylated) — chronic hepatitis B (selected patients), some tumors (hairy cell leukemia, melanoma); **interferon beta** — multiple sclerosis; **interferon gamma** — chronic granulomatous disease.
**Adverse effects** (parenteral): flu-like syndrome (fever, myalgia), depression and suicidal thoughts, cytopenias, autoimmune thyroid disease, fatigue.

parts.text: **Intranasal and rectal interferon preparations** and **interferon inducers** (tilorone, Kagocel, Cycloferon) are widely used in CIS countries to treat and prevent ARVI and influenza, but their effectiveness has not been confirmed in studies that meet the standards of modern evidence-based medicine.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 34-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis (mycobacteria in sputum, Xpert MTB/RIF — rifampicin-susceptible) is being treated with the HRZE regimen. In week 5 he developed nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite and yellowing of the sclerae. ALT is 6 times the upper limit of normal, bilirubin is raised. The patient drinks alcohol every day.
cases.ask: 1) Condition? 2) Which drugs may be the cause? 3) Management.
cases.answer: 1) Drug-induced hepatitis (during antituberculosis treatment). 2) Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are hepatotoxic; alcohol increases the risk; other causes (viral hepatitis) must be excluded. 3) Stop all hepatotoxic drugs; if the patient's condition and the severity of the disease require it — a temporary liver-sparing regimen (ethambutol + levofloxacin ± linezolid); when the enzymes and bilirubin approach normal, restart the drugs one by one (rifampicin first, then isoniazid; do not restart pyrazinamide and extend the continuation phase); abstinence from alcohol; DOT.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 28-year-old woman is being treated for tuberculosis with a rifampicin-containing regimen. She takes a combined oral contraceptive and does not want to become pregnant.
cases.ask: What advice would you give?
cases.answer: Rifampicin is a strong CYP3A4 inducer; it speeds up the metabolism of estrogens and progestins and sharply reduces contraceptive effectiveness. During treatment and for at least 4 weeks after rifampicin is stopped, nonhormonal contraception (a copper intrauterine device, condoms) or a method not affected by inducers (depot medroxyprogesterone injection, a levonorgestrel intrauterine system) is recommended. She should also be warned that rifampicin colors urine and other fluids red and stains soft contact lenses.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 68-year-old man has had severe burning pain along the intercostal spaces of the right half of the chest for 2 days, followed by clusters of blisters on reddened skin in the same area.
cases.ask: 1) Diagnosis? 2) Treatment? 3) Prevention.
cases.answer: 1) Herpes zoster (shingles) — reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. 2) Valacyclovir 1 g 3 times a day for 7 days (or acyclovir 800 mg 5 times a day) — within 72 hours of the onset of the rash (over 50 years — to reduce the risk of postherpetic neuralgia); analgesics for pain (paracetamol, NSAIDs; for severe pain — gabapentinoids or a low-dose TCA); dose adjustment according to renal function. If the ophthalmic branch is involved — an urgent ophthalmologist. 3) Vaccination with the recombinant zoster vaccine for people over 50.
